conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is pelvic organ prolapse (POP)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of one or more pelvic organs into the vagina due to weakness of the pelvic floor support (fascia, ligaments and muscles), so the vaginal walls (with the organ behind them) bulge downwards. It is very common (up to 40% of postmenopausal women) and impairs quality of life.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is the core mechanism of pelvic organ prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: The pelvic organs are held up by the pelvic floor (levator ani) muscles and endopelvic fascia/ligaments; childbirth, ageing and oestrogen loss weaken these, so the organs descend, pushing the vaginal walls ahead of them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is a cystocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall (anterior compartment) — associated with urinary symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is a rectocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of the rectum into the posterior vaginal wall (posterior compartment) — associated with constipation and incomplete emptying.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is uterine prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of the uterus into the vagina (apical/central compartment).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is a vault prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of the top of the vagina (vault) after hysterectomy (apical compartment).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is an enterocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Descent of the small bowel into the upper posterior vaginal wall (apical compartment).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is a urethrocele, and how is it often described?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Urethral descent, often combined with a cystocele as a cysto-urethrocele.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: List the risk factors for pelvic organ prolapse.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Increasing age and menopause (oestrogen loss), multiparity/vaginal deliveries (the biggest — especially instrumental/prolonged, large babies), obesity, chronic cough/constipation/heavy lifting (raised intra-abdominal pressure), spina bifida/connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos), and previous pelvic surgery (e.g. hysterectomy → vault prolapse).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is the biggest risk factor for pelvic organ prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Vaginal delivery/multiparity (especially instrumental/prolonged deliveries and large babies).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is the hallmark symptom of pelvic organ prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: A sensation of pressure, heaviness, or 'something coming down'/'bearing down' — worse at the end of the day or on standing, ± a palpable/visible vaginal lump.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What urinary and bowel symptoms occur with prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Cystocele: urinary incontinence, frequency, urgency, incomplete emptying. Rectocele: constipation, incomplete evacuation, splinting. Sexual dysfunction (discomfort, reduced sensation) can also occur.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: How is prolapse assessed on examination (NICE NG123)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Speculum/bimanual examination (a Sims speculum helps visualise each wall) to identify the compartment, examining while the woman bears down and, if needed, standing (prolapse may only show upright); assess pelvic floor strength, look for vaginal atrophy, and exclude a pelvic mass.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: How is pelvic organ prolapse staged?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: With POP-Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification), or the older Baden-Walker grading — broadly graded by how far the leading edge descends relative to the hymen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: How is asymptomatic prolapse managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: No treatment is needed — observation is reasonable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What are the first-line conservative measures for prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Lifestyle (weight loss, treat constipation and chronic cough, avoid heavy lifting), pelvic floor muscle training (supervised, ≥16 weeks — most useful for mild POP-Q stage 1–2), and topical vaginal oestrogen for associated atrophy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is a vaginal pessary, and who is it offered to?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: A device (e.g. a ring) inserted vaginally to support the prolapse, sitting around the cervix/vault. Offer it to any woman with symptomatic prolapse — especially if she wishes to preserve fertility, is unfit for surgery, or prefers to avoid it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: How often should a vaginal pessary be changed, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: At least every 6 months, to prevent erosion, discharge, bleeding and fistula.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What surgical procedure is used for a cystocele (anterior wall prolapse)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Anterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair, without mesh).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What surgical procedure is used for a rectocele (posterior wall prolapse)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Posterior colporrhaphy (posterior repair, without mesh).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What surgical procedures are used for uterine prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Vaginal hysterectomy (± apical support) or sacrohysteropexy (uterus-preserving).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What surgical procedures are used for vault prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Sacrocolpopexy (abdominal/laparoscopic, with mesh) or sacrospinous fixation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is colpocleisis, and who is it for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Vaginal closure — for frail women not wishing to retain sexual function.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.front: What is the current position on transvaginal mesh for prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.back: Its use is highly restricted/paused in the UK (research-only per NICE IPG599) due to serious complications (mesh erosion, chronic pain); native-tissue (non-mesh) repairs are first-line, with mesh reserved for specific procedures (e.g. sacrocolpopexy) after MDT discussion and a decision aid, with a 6-month post-op review.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is termination of pregnancy (TOP), and what two things does the topic hinge on?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: The medical or surgical ending of a pregnancy. The topic hinges on the legal grounds and choosing the method by gestation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Which law governs abortion in England, Scotland and Wales, and the usual upper limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: The Abortion Act 1967 (as amended by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990); the upper limit for most abortions is 24 weeks (23⁺⁶).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: How many doctors must agree to an abortion, and what is the emergency exception?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Two registered medical practitioners must agree, in good faith, that a legal ground is met; ONE is sufficient in an emergency (to save the woman's life or prevent grave permanent injury).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is Ground A of the Abortion Act, and its time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Continuing the pregnancy risks the woman's life — no time limit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is Ground B of the Abortion Act, and its time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: To prevent grave permanent injury to the woman's physical/mental health — no time limit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is Ground C of the Abortion Act, and its time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A greater risk to the woman's physical/mental health than termination — the ground used for the vast majority; time limit <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is Ground D of the Abortion Act, and its time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A greater risk to the physical/mental health of existing children; time limit <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is Ground E of the Abortion Act, and its time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality — no time limit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Which abortion grounds have NO upper time limit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Grounds A (risk to life), B (grave permanent injury), and E (serious fetal abnormality).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: How does abortion law differ in Northern Ireland?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: It has a separate framework (the Abortion (NI) Regulations 2020) — broadly up to ~12 weeks on request, with different certification.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is the current telemedicine ('pills by post') provision?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Since the COVID provisions were made permanent (2022), early medical abortion at home (up to 9⁺⁶ weeks) can follow a remote consultation, with both mifepristone and misoprostol taken at home.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What assessment is done before TOP (NICE NG140)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Confirm and date the pregnancy (ultrasound as needed); bloods (blood group & Rhesus status, FBC); STI screening (chlamydia and others); non-judgemental discussion of options with informed consent and counselling; and discussion of future contraception to start immediately after.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Up to what gestation are both medical and surgical TOP options, and what determines the choice?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Both are options up to 23⁺⁶ weeks; the choice depends on gestation and patient preference.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Describe the medical TOP regimen and mechanism.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Mifepristone (an anti-progesterone) blocks progesterone, breaking down the decidua and sensitising the uterus; misoprostol (a prostaglandin analogue) is given 24–48h later to cause uterine contractions that expel the pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is the mechanism of mifepristone in medical TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: It is an anti-progesterone that blocks progesterone, breaking down the decidua and sensitising the uterus to prostaglandins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is the mechanism of misoprostol in medical TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A prostaglandin analogue that causes uterine contractions to expel the pregnancy, given 24–48h after mifepristone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What surgical TOP methods are used, and at what gestations?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Vacuum aspiration — manual (MVA) or electric (EVA) — typically up to ~14 weeks; dilatation & evacuation (D&E) for later gestations (after ~14 weeks). Cervical priming with misoprostol ± mifepristone beforehand softens/dilates the cervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Why is cervical priming used before surgical TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Misoprostol ± mifepristone softens and dilates the cervix beforehand, reducing trauma during the procedure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: How is the success of medical TOP confirmed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A follow-up pregnancy test at ~2 weeks, ideally a multi-level/quantitative (serum β-hCG) test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: How long can a urine pregnancy test stay positive after TOP, and what does a positive test beyond 4 weeks suggest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: A urine test can stay positive up to ~4 weeks; a positive test beyond 4 weeks suggests incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast (investigate for retained products or gestational trophoblastic disease).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What are the anti-D prophylaxis rules for TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Give anti-D to RhD-negative women having a surgical abortion, and medical abortion after 10 weeks; it is no longer required for early medical abortion before 10 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: What is the approach to contraception after TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Start immediately — an IUD/IUS can be inserted immediately after surgical evacuation; an implant, injection or pills can be started at the time of medical TOP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: Is routine follow-up needed after TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: No routine follow-up is needed if the pregnancy test/protocol confirms success (NICE NG140), with analgesia and safety-netting for complications.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.front: List the complications of TOP.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.back: Incomplete abortion/retained products (may need a repeat procedure), infection (endometritis), haemorrhage, uterine perforation (surgical), cervical trauma, failed termination/continuing pregnancy, and psychological impact.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What are reduced fetal movements (RFM), and why do they matter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: A decrease or cessation of the mother's perception of her baby's movements. They matter because they can be a warning sign of fetal compromise (a hypoxic fetus reduces activity to conserve oxygen) and are associated with stillbirth and fetal growth restriction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What is the core physiological logic of RFM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: A fetus with chronic hypoxia redistributes blood to vital organs and reduces movement to lower oxygen consumption — a compensatory mechanism — so RFM is a non-specific but important surrogate marker of fetal condition.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: When is quickening (first perception of movements) usually felt?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Around 18–20 weeks (earlier in multiparous women).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: How do fetal movements change through pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: They increase until ~32 weeks, then plateau — they change in character but should NOT reduce at the end of pregnancy (the myth that late movements decrease is wrong). There is no single normal number; each baby has its own pattern.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: List the benign/perceptual causes of reduced fetal movements.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Posture/distraction/being busy (movements are more noticeable lying down and focused), an anterior placenta (<28 weeks, cushions movements), an anterior fetal position (movements directed backwards), maternal obesity (harder to feel), and medication (alcohol/sedatives temporarily reduce movements).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: List the concerning/pathological causes of reduced fetal movements.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Fetal growth restriction/SGA (linked with ~29% of RFM cases), placental insufficiency, oligohydramnios (polyhydramnios can also alter perception), fetal hypoxia/distress, impending stillbirth, fetomaternal haemorrhage, and infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: How is RFM primarily assessed, and what confirms fetal viability?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Primarily on maternal perception; a handheld Doppler or ultrasound is used to confirm the fetal heartbeat.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: How is RFM managed if movements have never been felt by 24 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Refer to a fetal medicine unit; confirm the heartbeat with a handheld Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: How is RFM managed at 24–28 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Confirm the fetal heartbeat with a handheld Doppler, and take a history for stillbirth/FGR risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What is the assessment pathway for RFM after 28 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Handheld Doppler (no heartbeat → immediate ultrasound to confirm viability); if a heartbeat is present, CTG for ≥20 minutes to assess fetal wellbeing; then ultrasound (growth, amniotic fluid, umbilical artery Doppler) if concern persists.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: When is ultrasound performed in the RFM pathway after 28 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: If RFM persists despite a normal CTG, there are FGR/stillbirth risk factors, or there has been no scan in 2 weeks — assessing growth, amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What advice is given to a mother concerned about reduced movements after 28 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Lie on the left side and focus on movements for 2 hours — if fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours, contact the maternity unit immediately. Do NOT wait until the next day and do NOT rely on home Doppler/apps for reassurance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What should be done if RFM investigations (CTG and growth/liquor) are normal?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Reassure, and advise the woman to re-present immediately if RFM recurs — recurrent RFM warrants ultrasound and closer surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What is the management if the CTG is abnormal in RFM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Senior obstetric review; decisions about delivery weigh gestation against the degree of abnormality.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: How is RFM with SGA/abnormal Doppler/abnormal liquor managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: As fetal growth restriction (RCOG Green-top 31) — increased surveillance and timed delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: Why is recurrent RFM significant?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: It is itself a risk factor, warranting a lower threshold for scanning and a delivery discussion near term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What did the AFFIRM trial show about formal awareness-of-fetal-movement packages?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: A formal 'awareness of fetal movements' care package did NOT significantly reduce stillbirth and increased inductions and caesareans — so routine formal kick-counting with fixed alarm limits is NOT recommended.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: What is the recommended approach to fetal movement awareness (rather than formal kick-counting)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Women are advised to be aware of their baby's individual pattern and to report any reduction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: Which guideline covers the investigation and management of reduced fetal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: RCOG Green-top Guideline 57.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.front: Give the reflex approach to a woman reporting reduced fetal movements at 32 weeks.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.back: Confirm the heartbeat with a handheld Doppler (no heartbeat → immediate USS), then CTG for ≥20 minutes; arrange ultrasound (growth/liquor/Doppler) if concern persists or risk factors are present, and advise immediate re-presentation if RFM recurs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the organising principle for preterm birth & PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Identify preterm labour/PPROM early to deliver interventions that improve neonatal outcome — antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate (neuroprotection), and consideration of tocolysis/in-utero transfer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes — spontaneous rupture of the fetal membranes before 37 weeks and before the onset of labour. It causes ~30–40% of preterm births.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: Define PROM, PPROM and 'prolonged' rupture.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: PROM = rupture before labour at/after 37 weeks (term). PPROM = rupture before labour before 37 weeks (preterm). Prolonged = >24 hours between rupture and delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: From which three directions does PPROM put the fetus at risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Prematurity, infection (chorioamnionitis), and cord problems (prolapse, compression from oligohydramnios).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the core management tension in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: The intact sac is a barrier against ascending infection and cushions the cord; once it ruptures preterm, management navigates the trade-off between delivering (prematurity) and waiting (rising infection/cord risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What are the clinical features of PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: A gush or trickle of fluid from the vagina ('waters breaking'), a persistent feeling of dampness/wetness, ± mild irregular contractions; reduced fetal movements or signs of infection are red flags.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the key diagnostic test for PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: A sterile speculum examination looking for pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior vaginal fornix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: Why is digital vaginal examination avoided in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Because it introduces infection and shortens the latency period.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What biochemical tests are used if no pooling of fluid is seen on speculum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: PAMG-1 (placental alpha-microglobulin-1, e.g. Amnisure) or IGFBP-1 on vaginal fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the role of ultrasound in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: It may show oligohydramnios — supportive, but not diagnostic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is a woman with PPROM monitored for chorioamnionitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Maternal observations (temperature, HR), CRP/WCC, CTG (fetal tachycardia), uterine tenderness, and offensive discharge; swabs including for group B Streptococcus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What prophylactic antibiotic is given in PPROM, and for how long (RCOG Green-top 73)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days (or until established labour) — it reduces chorioamnionitis and delays delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: Which antibiotic must be avoided in PPROM, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Co-amoxiclav — it is associated with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in this setting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: When are antenatal corticosteroids offered in PPROM, and their benefit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks — they reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, IVH, NEC, and death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: When is IV magnesium sulphate offered in PPROM, and its benefit?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: For neuroprotection (reducing cerebral palsy), offered 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶) if birth is expected within 24 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the recommended timing of birth in stable PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Expectant management until 37⁺⁰ weeks (current RCOG — better outcomes than early birth) if there are no contraindications; NOT 34 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: When should immediate delivery occur in PPROM, regardless of gestation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: If chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, cord prolapse, or abruption develops.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: Is tocolysis recommended in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: No — tocolysis is not recommended (no clear benefit and it may mask infection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What are the maternal complications of PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Chorioamnionitis (the main one), postpartum endometritis, and sepsis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What are the fetal/neonatal complications of PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Prematurity and its sequelae (RDS, IVH, NEC), cord prolapse (from loss of fluid), cord/limb compression and pulmonary hypoplasia from severe/early oligohydramnios (Potter sequence if very early), and neonatal sepsis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What signs indicate chorioamnionitis requiring immediate delivery in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Maternal fever/tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, raised CRP/WCC, uterine tenderness, and offensive discharge.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is preterm birth, and preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Preterm birth is delivery before 37⁺⁰ weeks — the leading cause of neonatal death and long-term disability (the earlier, the higher the risk). Preterm labour is the process (regular contractions + cervical change before 37 weeks) that leads to it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is preterm birth classified by gestation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Extremely preterm: <28 weeks; very preterm: 28–31⁺⁶ weeks; moderate to late preterm: 32–36⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is low birth weight classified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Low birth weight <2500 g; very low <1500 g; extremely low <1000 g.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the strongest risk factor for preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: A previous preterm birth (and previous late miscarriage).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: List the risk factors for preterm labour.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Previous preterm birth (strongest)/late miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, PPROM, infection (chorioamnionitis, UTI, BV, GBS), cervical incompetence/previous cervical surgery (LLETZ, cone biopsy), uterine anomalies/fibroids, antepartum haemorrhage, smoking, low BMI, extremes of maternal age, and short inter-pregnancy interval.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is preterm labour diagnosed clinically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Regular painful contractions plus cervical change (dilatation/effacement) before 37 weeks; a speculum exam assesses dilatation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: When should a fetal fibronectin swab be taken relative to a digital examination?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: BEFORE any digital examination (a digital exam alters the result).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is uncertain suspected preterm labour with intact membranes managed at ≤29⁺⁶ weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: If clinical assessment suggests preterm labour, treat (steroids ± tocolysis) without needing further tests.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is uncertain suspected preterm labour managed at ≥30⁺⁰ weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Offer a diagnostic test for likelihood of birth within 48h — transvaginal ultrasound cervical length (>15 mm = unlikely; ≤15 mm = likely) OR fetal fibronectin (≥50 ng/mL positive = increased risk within 7 days; negative = strong reassurance). Do NOT use both together.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the interpretation of transvaginal cervical length in suspected preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: >15 mm makes preterm labour unlikely; ≤15 mm makes it likely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the interpretation of fetal fibronectin in suspected preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Positive (≥50 ng/mL) indicates increased risk of birth within 7 days; a negative result is strongly reassuring.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the role and timing of corticosteroids in preterm labour (NICE NG25)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Two doses of IM betamethasone/dexamethasone accelerate fetal lung maturity (reducing RDS, IVH, NEC, neonatal death), offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the role and timing of magnesium sulphate in preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: IV magnesium reduces cerebral palsy (neuroprotection), given when birth is expected within 24h at 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶); monitor for toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression → calcium gluconate).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What is the aim and first-line agent for tocolysis in preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: The aim is to delay birth ~48h so steroids can work and allow in-utero transfer (it does not improve outcomes alone). First-line is nifedipine (a calcium channel blocker), used 26⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks with intact membranes; atosiban is an alternative if nifedipine is contraindicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What are the contraindications to tocolysis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Infection, significant bleeding, and fetal compromise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: When are antibiotics given in preterm labour (ORACLE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Erythromycin ONLY if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM) — do NOT give it if membranes are intact.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What group B streptococcus prophylaxis is given in established preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Intrapartum benzylpenicillin (GBS prophylaxis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What intrapartum measures apply in preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: In-utero transfer, delayed cord clamping (≥60s) if stable, caesarean for breech at 26–36⁺⁶ weeks, and avoiding fetal scalp electrodes before 34 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: How is preterm birth prevented in high-risk women (previous preterm birth, short cervix)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Vaginal progesterone and/or cervical cerclage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: List the complications of prematurity by system.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Respiratory: RDS (surfactant deficiency), chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia). Neurological: intraventricular haemorrhage. GI: necrotising enterocolitis. Eyes: retinopathy of prematurity (<32 weeks; over-oxygenation → abnormal retinal neovascularisation). Also hearing impairment, hypothermia, feeding problems, infection/sepsis, and jaundice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.front: What causes retinopathy of prematurity, and in whom?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.back: Over-oxygenation causing abnormal retinal neovascularisation, in infants born <32 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the organising principle for postpartum complications?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: The postnatal woman (in the puerperium) can deteriorate rapidly; work through the common causes by system — bleeding (PPH), fever/sepsis (puerperal pyrexia), mood/psychosis, and endocrine (thyroiditis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Excessive bleeding from the genital tract after delivery — the leading cause of maternal death worldwide and a core obstetric emergency; the response is a time-critical, protocolised escalation (mechanical → medical → surgical).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the core principle explaining uterine atony as the commonest cause of PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: After the placenta delivers, the uterus must contract to clamp the spiral arteries at the placental bed (the 'physiological ligature'); if it doesn't (uterine atony), those vessels bleed freely, so a 'boggy' uterus that won't contract is the commonest cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is PPH defined by volume (RCOG Green-top 52)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Blood loss ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the difference between primary and secondary PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Primary PPH occurs within 24 hours of birth; secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours to 6–12 weeks postpartum, typically from retained placental tissue or endometritis (infection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is PPH severity classified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Minor = 500–1000 mL (no shock); major = >1000 mL or any volume with shock (moderate 1000–2000 mL / severe >2000 mL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is lochia distinguished from PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Lochia is the normal postpartum discharge that reduces over ~6 weeks; bleeding <500 mL with no shock is likely lochia. Ultrasound is done if lochia persists beyond 6 weeks (?retained products).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the 4 T's causing PPH, and which is commonest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Tone (uterine atony — commonest, ~70%), Trauma (genital tract tears/episiotomy/uterine rupture/haematoma), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes), and Thrombin (coagulopathy — e.g. abruption, pre-eclampsia, sepsis/DIC).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why does retained tissue ('Tissue') cause PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because retained placenta or membranes prevent the uterus from contracting effectively.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: List the risk factors for PPH.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Previous PPH (biggest single predictor), an overdistended uterus (prolonged labour, macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy → atony), pre-eclampsia, placenta praevia/accreta, emergency caesarean, increased maternal age, grand multiparity, and chorioamnionitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the biggest single predictor of PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: A previous PPH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is PPH prevented at delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Active management of the third stage — prophylactic IM oxytocin 10 IU at delivery reduces PPH by ~60%; tranexamic acid at caesarean for women at increased risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is every birth managed proactively for PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because most PPH occurs in women with NO identifiable risk factors, so active third-stage management (prophylactic oxytocin) is used for everyone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the immediate resuscitation steps in PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: An A-E approach; call senior help (obstetrics, anaesthetics, midwifery, haematology); two large-bore IV cannulae; bloods (FBC, coagulation, cross-match 4 units); IV fluids/warmed blood products (major haemorrhage protocol if severe); catheterise; and monitor closely — resuscitate and treat the cause in parallel.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the first-line (mechanical) step to stop bleeding in PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: 'Rub up' the fundus (bimanual uterine massage) and empty the bladder (a full bladder inhibits contraction).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the medical (uterotonic) sequence for PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Oxytocin (first) → ergometrine → carboprost → misoprostol; plus tranexamic acid 1 g IV given early.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What surgical/tamponade options are used if medical measures fail in PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: An intrauterine balloon (Bakri) → B-Lynch brace suture → uterine/internal iliac artery ligation → interventional radiology embolisation → hysterectomy as a last resort (life-saving).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the cautions for ergometrine and carboprost in PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia; carboprost (PGF2α) should be avoided in asthma (risk of bronchospasm).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What does the WOMAN trial show about tranexamic acid in PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: TXA 1 g IV given early (within 3 hours) reduces death from PPH, so it is now given early in all significant PPH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is secondary PPH managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Treat the cause — antibiotics for endometritis, and evacuation of retained products (ERPC) if retained tissue; ultrasound guides this.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is Sheehan's syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Severe PPH → hypovolaemic shock → pituitary ischaemic necrosis → hypopituitarism; classically failure of postpartum lactation (↓prolactin) plus amenorrhoea (↓gonadotrophins) after a haemorrhagic delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is Sheehan's syndrome diagnosed and treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Diagnosed by inadequate pituitary hormone stimulation (prolactin, gonadotrophins); treated by replacing the missing hormones (hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, oestrogen/progesterone, ± growth hormone).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is puerperal pyrexia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Fever in the postpartum period — traditionally a temperature ≥38°C in the first 14 days after delivery (some definitions span the puerperium to 6 weeks). It matters because postpartum sepsis remains a leading cause of maternal death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is the postpartum uterus a portal for infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: It has a raw placental bed and an open cervix — a ready portal for ascending infection; genital tract sepsis can escalate rapidly (especially Group A Streptococcus), so a febrile new mother is treated with urgency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the single most important cause of puerperal pyrexia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Endometritis (genital tract infection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: List the sources to consider in puerperal pyrexia and their clues.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Endometritis (commonest — lower abdominal/uterine pain, tender bulky uterus, offensive lochia, secondary PPH); UTI/pyelonephritis (dysuria, frequency, loin pain); wound infection (caesarean/perineal wound erythema/discharge); mastitis/breast abscess (unilateral tender red swollen breast); VTE/DVT (calf swelling/pain, low-grade fever, breathlessness); chest infection (cough, especially post-GA/caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is postpartum endometritis, and its typical organisms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Uterine infection, usually from bacteria ascending from the lower genital/GI tract — typically polymicrobial (mixed aerobes + anaerobes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the risk factors for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Caesarean section (the biggest), prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, retained products, multiple vaginal examinations, group B Streptococcus carriage, obesity, and diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the clinical features of postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Fever, lower abdominal/uterine tenderness, offensive/heavy lochia, secondary PPH, and malaise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What investigations are done in puerperal pyrexia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Observations/sepsis screen (temp, HR, RR, BP; MEOWS chart); bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E, lactate, blood cultures); high vaginal + endocervical swabs (± placental swab); MSU; wound swab; breast exam; ± ultrasound (retained products/pelvic collection), CTPA/Doppler if VTE suspected, and throat swab if Group A Strep suspected.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the initial approach to a febrile postpartum woman with signs of severe sepsis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Assess severity using the sepsis pathway; if severe sepsis (hypotension, tachycardia, raised lactate, breathlessness), initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently (RCOG GTG64).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the first-line antibiotic treatment for postpartum endometritis/genital tract sepsis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Admit and give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — clindamycin + gentamicin IV first-line, continued until afebrile for >24 hours (oral continuation usually not needed).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is severe genital tract sepsis treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Broader cover — IV piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem ± clindamycin (for its antitoxin effect in Group A Strep) — following local microbiology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is clindamycin included in severe genital tract sepsis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: For its antitoxin effect against Group A Streptococcus (reducing toxin production).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is a non-endometritis source of puerperal pyrexia treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Treat the specific source — antibiotics for UTI/wound/mastitis, anticoagulation for VTE, and ERPC if retained tissue is driving endometritis; plus supportive care (fluids, antipyretics, monitoring).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) particularly dangerous postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: It is a highly virulent, rapidly-progressive genital-tract pathogen — warranting a low threshold for aggressive treatment and infection-control precautions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Give the reflex approach to a febrile postpartum woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Treat with urgency (not reassurance) — sepsis screen, find the source (endometritis commonest → uterine tenderness/offensive lochia), and start IV antibiotics; Sepsis Six if severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the biggest risk factor for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Caesarean section.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What chart is used to flag maternal deterioration in the postpartum period?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: A MEOWS (Modified Early Obstetric Warning Score) chart.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Which secondary complication of endometritis relates to bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage (from the infected/poorly-contracting uterus, often with retained products).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is puerperal (postpartum) psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: A severe, acute psychiatric emergency in the early postpartum period, characterised by psychosis, mania and mood disturbance — the most serious psychiatric disorder of childbirth, carrying real risk of suicide and infanticide/harm to the baby, and demanding immediate psychiatric admission (ideally to a Mother & Baby Unit).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is puerperal psychosis strongly linked to?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Bipolar affective disorder — it is often the first presentation of, or a relapse of, bipolar illness triggered by childbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the biggest risk factor for puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: A personal/family history of bipolar disorder or previous puerperal psychosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Compare the frequency, onset and management of baby blues, postnatal depression and puerperal psychosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Baby blues: ~60–70%, days 3–7, mild/self-limiting → reassurance. Postnatal depression: ~10–15%, within a month/peaks ~3 months, moderate → CBT ± SSRI. Puerperal psychosis: ~1–2/1000, within 2–3 weeks (often days), severe emergency → admit (Mother & Baby Unit).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Describe the baby blues.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Affecting ~60–70% of women, onset days 3–7, with tearfulness, anxiety, irritability and lability; self-limiting (~2 weeks) → reassurance and support, no drugs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: When does postnatal depression typically start, and how is it screened?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Most start within a month and peak around 3 months, with features like major depression; screened with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS, 10-item, max 30; >13 = likely depressive illness).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is postnatal depression managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: CBT first-line (mild-moderate); an SSRI if needed — sertraline/paroxetine (paroxetine preferred in breastfeeding); avoid fluoxetine (long half-life → infant accumulation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Which SSRIs are preferred and avoided in breastfeeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Sertraline and paroxetine are preferred (paroxetine particularly); fluoxetine is avoided because of its long half-life leading to infant accumulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Describe the presentation of puerperal psychosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Onset within ~2–3 weeks of birth (often abrupt, within the first few days), with severe mood swings (mania and/or depression), hallucinations (e.g. auditory) and delusions (often bizarre, may centre on the baby), plus confusion, perplexity, disorientation, rapidly fluctuating symptoms, insomnia and restlessness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: List the risk factors for puerperal psychosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Personal or family history of bipolar disorder (strongest), previous puerperal psychosis (high recurrence), first pregnancy (primiparity), and discontinuation of psychiatric medication in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the immediate management of puerperal psychosis (NICE CG192)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: It is a psychiatric emergency → urgent assessment and admission, ideally to a specialist Mother & Baby Unit (keeping mother and baby together to support bonding and safety).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What risk assessment is essential in puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Assess and manage risk to the mother (suicide) and to the baby (harm/neglect).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What must be ruled out in a woman with suspected puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Organic causes — infection, thyroid disorder, and medication effects.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What pharmacological treatments are used in puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine) for psychotic/manic symptoms; a mood stabiliser — lithium (effective and for relapse prevention); short-term benzodiazepines for agitation/sleep; and ECT for severe/resistant cases or high suicide risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: When is ECT considered in puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: For severe or treatment-resistant illness, or where there is a high suicide risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the red-flag distinction for puerperal psychosis vs baby blues?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Any new mother with rapid-onset confusion, mania, hallucinations, or delusions (especially involving the baby) has puerperal psychosis — an emergency, NOT baby blues.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the prognosis and recurrence risk of puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Generally good with prompt treatment (most recover fully), but there is a high recurrence in future pregnancies and a risk of subsequent bipolar episodes — so pre-conception counselling and a perinatal mental health plan matter.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is a Mother & Baby Unit the preferred admission setting?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because it keeps the mother and baby together, supporting bonding while maintaining safety.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is postpartum thyroiditis (PPT)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: A transient autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid within 12 months of delivery in a previously euthyroid woman (no Graves' or toxic nodule). It is common (~5–10%) and easily missed, classically producing a hyperthyroid phase then a hypothyroid phase, each managed differently.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the core mechanism of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Autoimmune lymphocytic destruction of thyroid follicles → preformed hormone leaks out → a transient thyrotoxic phase (release, not overproduction — which is why antithyroid drugs don't work). Once stores deplete → a hypothyroid phase → then usually recovery. TPO antibodies drive it (~90%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the three phases of postpartum thyroiditis, their timing and biochemistry?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: 1. Thyrotoxic (~1–4 months, lasts 1–3 months): ↑T4/T3, ↓TSH. 2. Hypothyroid (~3–12 months): ↓T4, ↑TSH. 3. Euthyroid (usually by 12 months): normal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Does every woman with PPT go through all three phases?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: No — roughly a third have both phases, a third only thyrotoxic, and a third only hypothyroid; the classic teaching pattern is hyper → hypo → recovery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What antibodies drive postpartum thyroiditis, and their predictive value?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: TPO (thyroid peroxidase) antibodies, present in ~90%; TPO-positivity in pregnancy predicts who develops PPT (about 50% of TPO-positive women do).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What are the risk factors for postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Type 1 diabetes, previous PPT, and a personal/family history of autoimmune thyroid disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How does PPT differ from Graves' disease in mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: PPT is destructive (hormone release from a damaged gland); Graves' is stimulatory (hormone overproduction driven by TSH-receptor antibodies).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How do the antibodies differ between PPT and Graves'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: PPT: TPO antibodies. Graves': TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How does radioiodine uptake differ between PPT and Graves'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: PPT: LOW uptake (the gland is not working — it's leaking stored hormone). Graves': HIGH uptake (the gland is overactive).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How does the T3:T4 ratio and eye signs differ between PPT and Graves'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: PPT: lower T3:T4 ratio (leaked stored T4), no eye signs. Graves': higher T3:T4 ratio (>20:1) and may have thyroid eye disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why must antithyroid drugs NOT be given in the thyrotoxic phase of PPT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because the thyroid isn't overproducing hormone — it's leaking stored hormone from destruction; antithyroid drugs block synthesis, which is not the problem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is the thyrotoxic phase of PPT managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: First-line propranolol (a β-blocker) to control palpitations/tremor/anxiety (safe in breastfeeding); do NOT give antithyroid drugs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: How is the hypothyroid phase of PPT managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Levothyroxine if symptomatic or trying to conceive; taper at ~6–12 months (monitoring TSH), as it is usually transient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the prognosis of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Most women recover to euthyroid within 12 months, but up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism in later years (especially if strongly TPO-positive), so annual TSH monitoring is advised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is annual TSH monitoring recommended after PPT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism in later years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: What is the recurrence risk of PPT in future pregnancies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: High — approximately 20–70%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Why is postpartum thyroiditis often missed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Because symptoms are frequently attributed to normal postnatal fatigue/stress ('new-baby stress').

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.front: Give the reflex approach to a woman with hyperthyroid symptoms a few months postpartum.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Consider postpartum thyroiditis (destructive release) — check TFTs and TPO antibodies, treat the thyrotoxic phase with propranolol (not antithyroids), and monitor for a subsequent hypothyroid phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the organising principle for pelvic & vaginal infections?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Discharge character + upper vs lower tract: BV = thin grey fishy (not an STI); trichomonas = frothy yellow-green (STI); PID = ascending infection with pain, fever and cervical excitation → treat empirically to protect fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract — uterus (endometritis), fallopian tubes (salpingitis), ovaries (oophoritis) and surrounding peritoneum — usually from an STI ascending from the endocervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is the classic sign of PID cervical motion tenderness?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because infection ascends from the endocervix upwards, so moving the inflamed upper-tract structures (on cervical motion) hurts — 'cervical excitation'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the examinable essence of managing PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A LOW threshold to treat empirically (don't wait for confirmation, as the cost of missing it is high) plus knowing the antibiotic regimens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the most common causative organism of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Chlamydia trachomatis — often asymptomatic and insidious.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Which organism causes more severe PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Which organisms besides chlamydia and gonorrhoea cause PID, and why is metronidazole included?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Mycoplasma genitalium (increasingly recognised) and anaerobes/Gardnerella/endogenous flora — the anaerobic involvement is why metronidazole is included.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the risk factors for PID.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Non-barrier contraception/not using condoms, multiple/new sexual partners, young age (<25), previous PID or STI, and recent instrumentation including IUD insertion (risk highest in the first ~3 weeks after fitting).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the symptoms of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Lower abdominal pain (typically bilateral), deep dyspareunia, abnormal vaginal/cervical discharge, abnormal bleeding (intermenstrual, postcoital, or menstrual irregularity), fever, and dysuria.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the examination findings in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Cervical motion tenderness ('cervical excitation') — the classic sign — plus adnexal/pelvic tenderness, cervicitis, and purulent discharge.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What investigation must always be done in a sexually active woman with pelvic pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A pregnancy test (β-hCG) — to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What swabs/tests are used in suspected PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A NAAT endocervical/vulvovaginal swab (chlamydia and gonorrhoea), a high vaginal swab (BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis), and microscopy (absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely); CRP/ESR are often raised (supportive).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is a useful microscopy rule-out for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: The absence of pus cells on microscopy of a vaginal/endocervical swab makes PID unlikely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Is PID a clinical or laboratory diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A clinical diagnosis — investigations support it, but a negative swab does not exclude it, so treat empirically on clinical suspicion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line (BASHH) treatment regimen for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the second-line (fluoroquinolone) regimen for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (or moxifloxacin 400 mg OD, particularly for suspected M. genitalium).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why are fluoroquinolones now second-line for PID (BASHH 2019/MHRA)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Following 2019 MHRA safety advice about disabling tendon, muscle, joint and neurological effects, so the ceftriaxone-based regimen is preferred first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: When should quinolones be avoided in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: If there is a high risk of gonococcal PID (partner has gonorrhoea, severe disease, contact abroad) — because of high quinolone resistance in gonorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is an IUD managed in a woman with PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: In mild PID the device can usually be left in situ; consider removal in severe cases or if there is no improvement in 48–72h.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What general measures accompany antibiotic treatment of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Analgesia, rest, avoiding intercourse until treatment is completed, referral to GUM for specialist management and contact tracing/partner treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: When is inpatient/IV treatment indicated in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Severe disease, a tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, failure of oral therapy, or inability to tolerate oral treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the complications of PID.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Tubo-ovarian abscess (may need drainage), infertility (tubal scarring, risk rising with each episode), ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Perihepatitis — RUQ pain from liver-capsule inflammation with 'violin-string' adhesions — a classic complication of chlamydial/gonococcal PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is bacterial vaginosis (BV)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: An overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria in the vagina caused by loss of the protective lactobacilli — the commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age. It is NOT a sexually transmitted infection but a disturbance of the vaginal flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the core mechanism of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Healthy lactobacilli produce lactic acid keeping the pH acidic (<4.5) and suppressing other bacteria; when lactobacilli are lost, the pH rises (alkaline), favouring overgrowth of anaerobes — chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Is bacterial vaginosis a sexually transmitted infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — it is a disturbance of the vaginal flora (loss of lactobacilli), although sexual activity can disrupt the flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How does BV discharge differ from candida and trichomonas?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: BV: thin, white/grey, homogenous, fishy odour, pH >4.5, minimal itch, not an STI. Candida: thick white 'cottage cheese', no odour, normal pH, prominent itch, not an STI. Trichomonas: frothy yellow-green, offensive odour, pH >4.5, itch/soreness, an STI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the risk factors for BV.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Multiple/new sexual partners (sexual activity disrupts flora), excessive vaginal cleaning/douching, recent antibiotics, smoking, and a copper IUD.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the clinical features of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: ~50% are asymptomatic; otherwise a thin, white, homogenous discharge coating the vaginal walls, with a fishy odour (often worse after sex/menstruation, as alkaline semen/blood raises pH) and NO significant itching or soreness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is the fishy odour of BV worse after sex or menstruation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because alkaline semen and menstrual blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing the fishy amine odour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the whiff test?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Adding potassium hydroxide (KOH) to the discharge releases a fishy amine odour — a positive whiff test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are Amsel's criteria for diagnosing BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Diagnose BV if ≥3 of 4 are present: thin white homogenous discharge, vaginal pH >4.5, clue cells on microscopy, and a positive whiff test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are clue cells?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Vaginal epithelial cells stippled with adherent bacteria, giving a 'granular/moth-eaten' cell border — the microscopy hallmark of BV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the laboratory alternative to Amsel's criteria for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: The Nugent score / Hay-Ison Gram-stain grading.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the complications of BV outside pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: An increased risk of acquiring STIs (including HIV) from the raised pH and loss of protection, and post-procedural infection (e.g. after termination/surgery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the pregnancy-related complications of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Miscarriage, preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM), chorioamnionitis, low birth weight, and postpartum endometritis (a uterine infection — not endometriosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Does asymptomatic BV usually need treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — usually not, except before some gynaecological procedures or in pregnancy with risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line treatment for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the alternative treatments for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Metronidazole 2 g single oral dose (aids adherence but slightly less effective), or topical metronidazole gel or topical clindamycin cream.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What advice is given about metronidazole and alcohol?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after metronidazole, because of a disulfiram-like reaction (nausea, vomiting, flushing) — the exam-safe answer, even though newer evidence questions the mechanism.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What key preventive advice reduces BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid vaginal douching, soaps and shower gels inside the vagina, as these disrupt the protective flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Should sexual partners be treated in BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — treating male partners does not reduce recurrence, so partners are not routinely treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is BV managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Treat symptomatic BV (given adverse outcomes) with oral metronidazole (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen) or topical treatment; metronidazole is considered low-risk in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How common is recurrence of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Common — approximately 50–70% within a year; consider avoiding triggers and, in some, suppressive regimens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is trichomoniasis, and what organism causes it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis — a flagellated protozoan parasite (not a bacterium). It classically causes a frothy yellow-green discharge with a 'strawberry cervix'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why does it matter that trichomonas is a true STI (unlike BV)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because it requires partner treatment and contact tracing (referral to GUM), whereas BV is a flora disturbance and partners are not treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How do trichomonas, BV and candida differ in pH and STI status?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Trichomonas: pH >4.5, an STI (treat partners). BV: pH >4.5, not an STI. Candida: pH <4.5 (normal), not an STI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Contrast the discharge in trichomonas, BV and candida.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Trichomonas: frothy, yellow-green, offensive/fishy, with itch. BV: thin, white/grey, fishy, minimal itch. Candida: thick, white, curdy, no odour, prominent itch.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Describe Trichomonas vaginalis and its transmission.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A motile, flagellated protozoan (parasite) spread by sexual contact; it infects the vagina, urethra and paraurethral glands in women, and the urethra in men. Incubation is ~3–9 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What proportion of trichomonas infections are asymptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Up to ~50% (a reservoir for transmission); men are usually asymptomatic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the clinical features of trichomoniasis in women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Frothy, yellow-green discharge with a fishy/offensive smell, vulval itching/soreness, dysuria, dyspareunia, and a 'strawberry cervix' (colpitis macularis) — punctate cervical haemorrhages, highly specific but rarely seen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is a 'strawberry cervix'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Punctate cervical haemorrhages (colpitis macularis) seen in trichomoniasis — highly specific but rarely observed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How does trichomoniasis present in men?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Usually asymptomatic; it may cause urethral discharge/discomfort, dysuria, or balanitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis diagnosed in women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Vaginal pH >4.5; a charcoal swab from the posterior fornix → microscopy (wet-mount) showing motile flagellated trophozoites; NAAT is the most sensitive test and increasingly first-line (same sample as chlamydia/gonorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis diagnosed in men?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: With a urethral swab or first-catch urine (NAAT is the most sensitive test).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is a Pap (cervical) smear not used to diagnose trichomonas?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Trichomonas may be an incidental finding on a Pap smear, but the Pap is not a diagnostic test (false positives/negatives) — confirm with a proper test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line treatment for trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 5–7 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the alternative treatment for trichomoniasis, and its caveats?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Metronidazole 2 g single oral dose — but the 7-day course is generally preferred (especially in HIV), and the single dose is less favoured/avoided in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What advice about alcohol accompanies metronidazole for trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction) during and shortly after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why must sexual partners be managed in trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because it is an STI — partners must be treated and contact-traced, with GUM referral (the key contrast with BV, where partners are not treated).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What additional screening is recommended in trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Screen for other STIs (co-infection is common — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV); a test of cure is done if symptoms persist.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the associations/complications of trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Increased HIV transmission risk, and adverse pregnancy outcomes — preterm birth and low birth weight.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis treated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole can be used (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen); topical/gel treatment is not effective for trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of trichomoniasis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Frothy yellow-green offensive discharge with vulval itch, pH >4.5, ± a strawberry cervix → charcoal swab/NAAT → oral metronidazole + treat partners/contact-trace.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A gynaecological surgical emergency in which the ovary (usually with the fallopian tube — 'adnexal torsion') twists around its supporting ligaments, cutting off its blood supply and threatening ovarian viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the exam essence of managing ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Suspect it clinically, image with ultrasound, and operate promptly — and don't be reassured by normal Doppler flow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: On which two ligaments does the ovary twist in torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: The infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament (carrying the ovarian vessels) and the utero-ovarian ligament.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Explain the venous-first mechanism of ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Twisting first occludes the low-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage → ovarian congestion and oedema (enlargement); as swelling worsens, arterial inflow is compromised → ischaemia → infarction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why can arterial Doppler flow still be present in early/partial ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because venous obstruction precedes arterial compromise (the venous-first sequence), so arterial flow may persist early — the key diagnostic trap.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: In whom does torsion of an ovarian mass vs a normal ovary typically occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Torsion with a mass/cyst (~85–95%) occurs in adults with an ovarian cyst/dermoid/tumour (a mass acts as a lever point; ~5 cm is a classic size). Torsion of a normal ovary occurs in prepubertal girls (longer ligaments, mobile ovaries).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the risk-factor logic for ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Anything that enlarges the ovary or makes it more mobile predisposes to torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: List the risk factors for ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Ovarian cyst/mass (the biggest — especially dermoid cysts and cysts ~5 cm+), OHSS/ovulation induction (enlarged ovaries), pregnancy (corpus luteum cyst, ligament laxity), reproductive age, prepubertal girls (long ligaments), and previous torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the cardinal presenting feature of ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Sudden-onset, severe, unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain — often colicky/intermittent (if it partially twists and untwists) then constant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What associated symptoms and signs occur in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Prominent nausea and vomiting (vagal/peritoneal), pain radiating to the flank/groin, adnexal tenderness ± a palpable mass, and possibly low-grade fever and mild leukocytosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Give the classic stem for ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A young woman with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain and vomiting, and a known ovarian cyst → ovarian torsion until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What investigation must ALWAYS be done first in suspected ovarian torsion, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A pregnancy test (β-hCG) — always — to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the first-line imaging for ovarian torsion, and its findings?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — showing an enlarged, oedematous ovary (commonest finding) ± an underlying cyst/mass, peripherally displaced follicles ('string of pearls'), a 'whirlpool sign' (twisted vascular pedicle), and free pelvic fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the #1 diagnostic trap in ovarian torsion imaging?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Doppler flow may be NORMAL or present in up to ~50% of torsions (venous obstruction precedes arterial), so normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: How is the definitive diagnosis of ovarian torsion made?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: At surgery — if clinical suspicion is high despite equivocal imaging, proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy.
