conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the definitive treatment of ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Prompt surgery, usually laparoscopy, to visualise and untwist (detort) the ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why is ovarian conservation (detorsion) preferred even if the ovary looks ischaemic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because intra-operative visual assessment of viability is highly inaccurate (only ~18–20% of 'necrotic-looking' ovaries are truly necrotic; blackened ovaries frequently recover follicular function), so conserving preserves fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What adjunctive procedures accompany detorsion in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Cystectomy (remove an underlying cyst at the same time, once detorted) and oophoropexy (fixing the ovary) — for recurrent torsion or torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: When is oophorectomy indicated in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: For a frankly necrotic/non-viable ovary or a suspicious mass (possible malignancy), particularly in postmenopausal women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why is timing critical in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because the sooner detorsion happens, the greater the chance of salvaging the ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Which key differentials overlap with ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian cyst accident (rupture/haemorrhage) — with ectopic being the must-not-miss one (hence β-hCG first).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is antenatal care, and why is its schedule high-yield?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: The structured programme of monitoring throughout pregnancy that keeps mother and baby well, screens for complications and prepares for birth. Its schedule and checks are a fixed, examinable framework — booking bloods, scans, supplements, and 'what's checked when'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How many antenatal appointments are recommended for uncomplicated pregnancies (NICE NG201)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 10 for nulliparous women and 7 for parous women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens at the booking appointment (~8–12 weeks)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Lifestyle advice, BP, urine dipstick, BMI, and booking bloods (ideally by 10 weeks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the dating scan, and what does it establish?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 10–13⁺⁶ weeks — to confirm dates, exclude multiple pregnancy, and determine chorionicity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the combined test done, and what does it measure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 11–13⁺⁶ weeks — Down syndrome screening using nuchal translucency + βhCG + PAPP-A.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the anomaly scan performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 18–20⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is checked at the 28-week appointment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: BP, urine, symphysis-fundal height; a second anaemia and antibody screen (Hb <10.5 → iron); and the first anti-D dose if RhD-negative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens at the 34-week and 36-week appointments?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 34 weeks: routine care, second anti-D, and birth-plan discussion. 36 weeks: check presentation and offer ECV if breech, plus breastfeeding/vitamin K/baby-blues information.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are the booking bloods?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: FBC, blood group & Rhesus status, red-cell antibodies, haemoglobinopathies, hepatitis B, syphilis, HIV, and a urine culture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Which screening test was removed from the booking panel in 2016?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Rubella screening (it is no longer part of the booking bloods).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the folic acid recommendation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 400 micrograms daily from before conception to 12 weeks (reducing neural tube defects); 5 mg (high dose) if obesity, epilepsy (on antiepileptics), personal/family history of NTD, coeliac disease, diabetes, or thalassaemia trait.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Which women should take high-dose (5 mg) folic acid?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Those with obesity, epilepsy (on antiepileptics), a personal/family history of NTD, coeliac disease, diabetes, or thalassaemia trait.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the vitamin D recommendation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 10 micrograms daily for ALL pregnant women (note the unit is micrograms, not mg).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Is iron routinely offered in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: No — iron is only given if the woman is anaemic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Why is high-dose vitamin A avoided in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It is teratogenic — avoid high-dose vitamin A (>700 mcg) and avoid liver (very high in vitamin A).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is blood pressure monitored antenatally, and what triggers referral?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: BP at every appointment; refer a woman >20 weeks with new BP ≥140/90 within 24h, and same-day for ≥160/110.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens to blood pressure physiologically in the first half of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It FALLS (vasodilation + increased volume), returning to baseline by term — so a rising BP is abnormal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When are fetal movements discussed, and what advice is given?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: After 24 weeks; women are advised to report reduced fetal movements.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: From when is symphysis-fundal height plotted, and what does a small measurement prompt?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From 24–28 weeks; a small SFH prompts a growth scan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When are anti-D doses given antenatally in RhD-negative women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 28 and 34 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is labour, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: The process of expelling the fetus, placenta and membranes — diagnosed by regular, painful uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change (effacement and dilatation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is true labour distinguished from false labour/Braxton Hicks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Braxton Hicks are irregular contractions (~every 20 min) with NO progressive cervical change → reassure and, if term and well, send home. True labour has progressive cervical change.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are other signs of labour besides contractions?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: A 'show' (blood-stained mucus plug) and rupture of the membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the first stage of labour and its phases.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From onset to full dilatation (10 cm). Latent phase: up to ~4 cm — slow, irregular painful contractions with cervical effacement/early dilatation. Active/established phase: from ~4 cm — regular contractions dilating the cervix ~0.5–1 cm/hour to full dilatation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the second stage of labour and its phases.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From full dilatation to delivery of the baby. Passive phase: full dilatation before/without an urge to push. Active phase: active pushing → delivery. The mechanism of labour (cardinal movements) occurs here.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the third stage of labour.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is active management of the third stage, and its benefit (NICE NG235)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: A prophylactic uterotonic (IM oxytocin/Syntocinon) + controlled cord traction + delayed cord clamping — it reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is physiological management of the third stage, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: No drugs and spontaneous delivery of the placenta — only if the birth is uncomplicated and the woman chooses it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: List the cardinal movements of labour in order.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is engagement and flexion in the cardinal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Engagement: the head enters the pelvic brim. Flexion: chin to chest, presenting the smallest diameter of the head.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is internal rotation and extension in the cardinal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Internal rotation: the occiput rotates anteriorly. Extension: the head delivers under the symphysis pubis (crowning).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is restitution and external rotation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Restitution: the head realigns with the shoulders. External rotation: the shoulders rotate to the anteroposterior position.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is a partogram?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: A graphical record of labour progress (cervical dilatation vs time), contractions, fetal heart and maternal observations; a 'flag' is raised when progress crosses the alert/action line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is the fetal heart monitored in low-risk vs high-risk labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Intermittent auscultation in low-risk labour; continuous CTG if there are risk factors or concerns.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are the '3 P's' of failure to progress in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Power (inadequate uterine contractions — the commonest cause, correctable with oxytocin), Passage (the pelvis — cephalopelvic disproportion), and Passenger (the fetus — size, malposition/malpresentation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the commonest cause of failure to progress, and how is it corrected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Inadequate uterine contractions ('Power') — correctable with oxytocin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What analgesia options are available in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Non-pharmacological measures → Entonox → epidural.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What rate does the cervix dilate in the active first stage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Approximately 0.5–1 cm per hour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is a multiple pregnancy, and why is it high-risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A pregnancy carrying more than one fetus (most commonly twins). It is high-risk across the board — higher rates of nearly every obstetric complication (preterm birth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, PPH) plus, for monochorionic types, dangerous shared-placenta complications. Rates have risen with IVF and older maternal age.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the single organising concept that determines the risk profile of a multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Chorionicity (how many placentas) — NOT zygosity — because it decides whether the babies share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the difference between zygosity and chorionicity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Zygosity (identical vs non-identical) is the underlying biology; chorionicity + amnionicity (how many placentas and sacs) is the clinically decisive classification, as it determines whether the babies share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe dizygotic twins and their chorionicity.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Two ova fertilised by two sperm (non-identical); they are ALWAYS DCDA (2 placentas, 2 sacs). They make up ~2/3 of twins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe monozygotic twins and what determines their chorionicity.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: One fertilised ovum splits (identical); the TIMING of the split determines chorionicity — they can be DCDA, MCDA, or MCMA.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What are the three chorionicity types, their placenta/sac count, and risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: DCDA (2 placentas, 2 sacs, no shared circulation — lowest risk); MCDA (1 placenta, 2 sacs, shared circulation — TTTS/TAPS risk); MCMA (1 placenta, 1 sac, shared circulation — cord entanglement, highest risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why is the monochorionic group the dangerous one?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because a shared (mono)placenta means a shared circulation, allowing complications like twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), TAPS and (for MCMA) cord entanglement.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When and how is chorionicity best determined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Best assessed before 14 weeks on first-trimester ultrasound (a key reason for the early dating scan), as the membrane junction is clearer then (NICE NG137).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the lambda (λ)/'twin peak' sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A thick membrane (4 layers) with a wedge of placenta between the sacs at the junction — indicating a DICHORIONIC pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the T-sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A thin membrane (2 layers) meeting the placenta at a right angle with no wedge — indicating a MONOCHORIONIC pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: List the risk factors for (dizygotic) twins.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Previous twins, family history (maternal side), increasing maternal age, multigravidity, assisted conception (IVF/ovulation induction — the biggest modern driver), and ethnicity (higher in Afro-Caribbean, lower in East Asian populations).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What are the maternal complications of multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Anaemia, pre-eclampsia/pregnancy-induced hypertension, gestational diabetes, hyperemesis (higher β-hCG), antepartum and postpartum haemorrhage (overdistended uterus → atony), and polyhydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the dominant fetal risk in multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Preterm birth — about 60% of twins deliver before 37 weeks; also growth restriction, malformations and higher perinatal mortality.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A monochorionic complication where unbalanced blood flow across placental anastomoses leaves the donor twin hypovolaemic (anaemic, oligohydramnios, growth-restricted — the 'stuck twin') and the recipient twin hypervolaemic (polycythaemic, polyhydramnios, cardiac overload/hydrops).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe the donor and recipient twins in TTTS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Donor: hypovolaemic — anaemic, oligohydramnios, growth-restricted (the 'stuck twin'). Recipient: hypervolaemic — polycythaemic, polyhydramnios, at risk of cardiac overload/hydrops.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: How is TTTS treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the shared communicating placental vessels.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is TAPS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence — a chronic, subtler haemoglobin imbalance between monochorionic twins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why do MCMA twins deliver early by caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because of the risk of cord entanglement (both twins in a single sac).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What antenatal care/supplements are recommended in multiple pregnancy (NICE NG137)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Early ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis, determine chorionicity and date; consultant-led care with more frequent visits; iron and folate supplementation; aspirin for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis (a moderate risk factor); and serial growth scans.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the surveillance schedule for monochorionic vs dichorionic twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Monochorionic twins: fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks with amniotic-fluid/Doppler assessment to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR (refer to fetal medicine). Dichorionic twins: less intensive scanning (~4-weekly growth).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the planned timing of birth for uncomplicated DCDA, MCDA and MCMA twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: DCDA: 37+0 weeks; MCDA: 36+0 weeks; MCMA: 32+0 to 33+6 weeks (by caesarean, due to cord-entanglement risk). Triplets ~35 weeks. Offer antenatal corticosteroids if delivering preterm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When can vaginal birth be offered in twins, and what is required?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: If twin 1 is cephalic, vaginal birth can be offered — with 2 obstetricians present, continuous CTG, and epidural often advised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When is caesarean indicated for twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: If twin 1 is non-cephalic (breech/transverse), or for any MCMA pregnancy (always caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why is prophylactic oxytocin used at delivery of twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because the overdistended uterus carries a high PPH risk (atony), so active third-stage management with prophylactic oxytocin is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Excessive menstrual loss that interferes with quality of life — defined by IMPACT, not millilitres (the old '≥80 mL' figure is obsolete).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is the term 'dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB)' obsolete?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because HMB is a symptom; the cause is classified with PALM-COEIN rather than labelled DUB.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does the PALM part of PALM-COEIN represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The STRUCTURAL causes: Polyp (endometrial/cervical), Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma (fibroids), and Malignancy & hyperplasia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does the COEIN part of PALM-COEIN represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The NON-structural causes: Coagulopathy (e.g. von Willebrand), Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, perimenopause, thyroid), Endometrial (primary endometrial dysfunction), Iatrogenic (copper coil, anticoagulants), and Not otherwise classified.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What examination findings suggest fibroids vs adenomyosis as a cause of HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A bulky, irregular ('knobbly') uterus suggests fibroids (Leiomyoma); a tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus with dysmenorrhoea suggests adenomyosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of HMB is suggested by heavy bleeding since menarche plus easy bruising?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Coagulopathy (e.g. von Willebrand disease).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of HMB is suggested by irregular cycles and hirsutism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovulatory dysfunction (e.g. PCOS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What symptoms in HMB should prompt exclusion of malignancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intermenstrual, postcoital, or postmenopausal bleeding (± persistent intermenstrual bleeding or cancer risk factors).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should a physical (including pelvic/speculum) examination be done in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Before all investigations or before fitting an LNG-IUS; the exception is a low-risk history with a non-LNG-IUS treatment, which can start without examination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What blood test should be done for ALL women with HMB, and when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A full blood count for all women, in parallel with starting treatment, to detect anaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is coagulation testing (e.g. for von Willebrand) indicated in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only if the history suggests it — HMB since menarche and a personal/family bleeding history.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which tests are NOT done routinely in HMB (NICE NG88)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Serum ferritin is not routinely tested, routine female-hormone testing is not done, and thyroid function is tested only if there are other thyroid signs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is outpatient hysteroscopy indicated in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: When submucosal fibroids/polyps or endometrial pathology are suspected — e.g. persistent intermenstrual bleeding or cancer risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy used in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Transvaginal ultrasound for larger structural abnormality; endometrial biopsy if cancer/hyperplasia is a concern (persistent intermenstrual bleeding, or age ≥45 with treatment failure).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first-line treatment for HMB (NICE NG88)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The LNG-IUS (Mirena) — if there is no pathology, fibroids <3 cm not distorting the cavity, or adenomyosis, and long-term use is acceptable. It is the most effective medical option and the clear first choice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-hormonal options treat HMB when contraception is NOT wanted?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic with no cycle effect) or NSAIDs (mefenamic acid — reduce bleeding AND dysmenorrhoea, useful if pain co-exists).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What hormonal options treat HMB when contraception IS wanted (LNG-IUS declined)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill or cyclical oral progestogens (e.g. norethisterone).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What surgical/procedural options exist for HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Endometrial ablation (family complete, not if future fertility desired), hysteroscopic removal of submucosal fibroids/polyps, uterine artery embolisation or myomectomy (fibroids, fertility-sparing), and hysterectomy (definitive but a last resort).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is endometrial ablation unsuitable for women wanting future fertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because it destroys the endometrium, so it is only used when the family is complete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the overall management sequence for HMB.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Physical exam → FBC (not routine ferritin/hormones/TFTs) → LNG-IUS first-line; else tranexamic acid/NSAIDs (no contraception) or COCP/cyclical progestogens (contraception wanted) → surgery (ablation/hysterectomy) if medical treatment fails and family is complete. Treat the underlying cause and any anaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is dysmenorrhoea, and what does the approach hinge on?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Painful menstruation — the commonest cause of school/work absence in adolescent girls. The approach hinges on separating primary (no pathology → treat symptomatically) from secondary (a pelvic disease is causing it → find and treat the cause).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The endometrium releases prostaglandins (especially PGF2α) → myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia → cramping pain. This is why NSAIDs (prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors) are first-line and so effective.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the onset of primary vs secondary dysmenorrhoea differ?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: young, 6–12 months after menarche. Secondary: older (20s–30s+), often after years of pain-free periods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the pain timing differ between primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: pain with or just before the period, lasting 1–3 days. Secondary: often begins days before, persists through and after the period, and may occur at other times.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What associated features suggest secondary (rather than primary) dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Deep dyspareunia, menorrhagia, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, and subfertility; examination may be abnormal (mass, tenderness, fixed uterus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What examination findings are expected in primary vs secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: normal examination. Secondary: examination may be abnormal — a pelvic mass, tenderness, a fixed/retroverted uterus, or adnexal masses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the secondary causes of dysmenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Endometriosis (classic — cyclical pain, dyspareunia, subfertility), adenomyosis (boggy tender uterus, HMB), fibroids, PID (especially new-onset in under-25s — chlamydia), ovarian cysts, copper IUD (iatrogenic), and cervical stenosis/outflow anomalies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What key history points help distinguish primary from secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Age of onset relative to menarche, the timing/pattern of pain, associated symptoms (dyspareunia, HMB, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, subfertility, discharge/fever → PID), impact, and contraception (copper coil).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is a pelvic examination performed in dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In primary dysmenorrhoea it can be deferred (normal); if secondary is suspected, perform an abdominal and pelvic (bimanual/speculum) examination for masses, tenderness, a fixed/retroverted uterus, and adnexal masses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What investigations are used if secondary dysmenorrhoea is suspected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy test (exclude ectopic); STI screen/high vaginal + endocervical swabs (PID/chlamydia, especially under-25s); transvaginal ultrasound (fibroids, adenomyosis, cysts, endometrioma); and laparoscopy (gold standard for endometriosis, though empirical medical treatment first is supported).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Are investigations needed for typical primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — primary dysmenorrhoea needs no investigations if the history is typical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) started from the onset of pain — they inhibit prostaglandins; paracetamol can be added.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the second-line (hormonal) treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Hormonal treatment — the combined oral contraceptive pill (cyclical or extended/tricycling; check UKMEC), with LNG-IUS/progestogen as alternatives; NSAIDs and hormonal treatment can be combined if single agents are insufficient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-drug measures help primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Local heat, TENS, and gentle exercise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is secondary dysmenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Treat the cause — e.g. endometriosis (analgesia → hormonal suppression → GnRH analogues → laparoscopic surgery), PID (antibiotics), fibroids/adenomyosis (cause-specific), copper coil (consider removal/alternative); refer to gynaecology if specialist workup is needed or symptoms are severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is mefenamic acid now less favoured as the NSAID of choice?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It is no better in efficacy, has a narrow therapeutic window, and carries a higher seizure risk in overdose — so ibuprofen/naproxen are preferred.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key rule when dysmenorrhoea fails to respond to NSAIDs plus hormonal contraception?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Suspect a secondary cause (especially endometriosis) → investigate/refer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What should new-onset pelvic pain/dysmenorrhoea in an under-25-year-old prompt consideration of?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PID/chlamydia — with STI screening/swabs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is amenorrhoea, and how should it be approached?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Absence of menstruation — a symptom, not a diagnosis. Work backwards through the axis: hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH/LH) → ovaries (oestrogen) → endometrium → patent outflow tract. A break at any level causes amenorrhoea, and the FSH/LH pattern indicates where. Always exclude pregnancy first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define primary amenorrhoea and its thresholds.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menstruation never established — no period by age 15 (with normal secondary sexual characteristics) OR by age 13 (with none).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define secondary amenorrhoea and its thresholds.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menstruation stopped after being established — for 3–6 months if previously regular, or 6–12 months if there was previous oligomenorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the commonest cause of primary amenorrhoea, and its features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Gonadal dysgenesis — Turner syndrome (45,XO) → streak ovaries, high FSH/LH, and short stature.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the primary causes of amenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Gonadal dysgenesis (Turner syndrome, commonest), androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY female phenotype), outflow malformations (imperforate hymen, transverse septum, Müllerian agenesis/MRKH), functional hypothalamic (anorexia), congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and constitutional delay.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What must be excluded first in any secondary amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy (β-hCG) — also consider lactation and menopause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the commonest pathological cause of secondary amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the secondary causes of amenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy/lactation/menopause (exclude first); hypothalamic (stress, excessive exercise, low weight/anorexia → hypogonadotropic); PCOS; hyperprolactinaemia; POI; thyroid disease; Sheehan's syndrome (pituitary necrosis after PPH); and Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions after D&C).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What blood tests are done first in amenorrhoea (after excluding pregnancy)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: FBC, U&E, TFTs, and a coeliac screen; then the key hormones (FSH/LH, prolactin, testosterone) to localise the lesion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does a LOW FSH/LH (hypogonadotropic) pattern indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A hypothalamic/pituitary cause — stress, low weight, excessive exercise, Sheehan's, or a prolactinoma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does a HIGH FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic) pattern indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: An ovarian cause — premature ovarian insufficiency or gonadal dysgenesis (Turner's).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is a raised prolactin interpreted and investigated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Repeat it (stress/food falsely raise it); if persistently raised, arrange a pituitary MRI (hyperprolactinaemia/prolactinoma).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What hormone pattern suggests PCOS in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Raised testosterone and a raised LH:FSH ratio.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is a karyotype indicated in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: If FSH is high — to confirm Turner's syndrome/gonadal dysgenesis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the role of pelvic ultrasound in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: To check whether the uterus and ovaries are present, assess the outflow tract, and look for polycystic ovaries.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is amenorrhoea from gonadal dysgenesis/POI managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: HRT — to develop/maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is hypothalamic amenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Weight restoration, reducing excessive exercise, managing stress/an eating disorder, and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PCOS-related amenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Weight management, cycle regulation (COCP/progestogen for endometrial protection), and treatment of hyperandrogenism/subfertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is hyperprolactinaemia causing amenorrhoea treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With a dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is amenorrhoea from outflow obstruction (e.g. imperforate hymen) or Asherman's managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Outflow obstruction → surgery; Asherman's syndrome → hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is Sheehan's syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pituitary necrosis following a postpartum haemorrhage, causing hypopituitarism (including amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is Asherman's syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intrauterine adhesions (typically after a D&C) causing amenorrhoea, treated with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of hypothalamic amenorrhoea is classically 'the athlete'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Low weight/over-exercise/stress → reduced GnRH → low FSH/LH (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is premenstrual syndrome (PMS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Psychological, physical and behavioural symptoms in the LUTEAL phase (the ~2 weeks before the period) that resolve once menstruation starts. It is common (~40%), with ~5–8% severe; the severest form is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core concept underlying PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptoms are triggered by normal cyclical ovarian hormone CHANGES (not abnormal levels) — susceptible women over-respond to the fluctuations. This is why suppressing ovulation (COCP, GnRH) and modulating serotonin (SSRIs) both work.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PMS distinguished from a primary mood disorder by timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS symptoms occur ONLY in the luteal phase, resolve with menstruation, and there is a symptom-free week after the period; a primary mood disorder is present throughout the cycle with no symptom-free interval.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key teaching point about diagnosing PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS is defined by the cyclical pattern, confirmed PROSPECTIVELY (not by symptoms alone, as retrospective recall over-diagnoses it). If symptoms don't clear after the period, it is NOT PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the difference between PMS and PMDD?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS is the broad syndrome (physical + psychological + behavioural, in the luteal phase); PMDD is the severe, predominantly affective form — a formal psychiatric diagnosis (DSM-5/ICD-11).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the psychological, physical and behavioural symptoms of PMS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Psychological: mood swings, irritability, depression, anxiety, tension. Physical: breast tenderness, bloating, headache, fatigue, cravings. Behavioural: poor concentration, sleep disturbance, withdrawal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PMS diagnosed (RCOG GTG48)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With a prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles — the DRSP (Daily Record of Severity of Problems) is RCOG-recommended — showing symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom-free interval, while excluding other diagnoses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which other diagnoses must be excluded when assessing PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Depression/bipolar disorder, thyroid disease, and perimenopause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is done if the diagnosis of PMS is unclear?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A 3-month GnRH-analogue trial (which switches off ovarian hormones); resolution of symptoms confirms it is ovulation-driven PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the first-line management options for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Lifestyle measures (exercise, sleep, diet, reducing alcohol/caffeine) and CBT; a continuous drospirenone-containing COCP (e.g. Yasmin) to suppress ovulation; and SSRIs (citalopram/escitalopram) — continuous OR luteal-phase only — for moderate-severe PMS/PMDD.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is distinctive about SSRI dosing in PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: SSRIs can be given continuously OR only in the luteal phase (they have a rapid onset in PMS, unlike in depression).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the second-line options for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Higher-dose SSRIs (continuous or luteal), or transdermal oestradiol plus a progestogen (for endometrial protection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the third-line (specialist) treatment for PMS, and its requirement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: GnRH analogues — potent ovulation suppression producing a hypo-oestrogenic state, so they require 'add-back' HRT to protect bone and cardiovascular health; used only for severe/resistant cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the fourth-line (last resort) treatment for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Hysterectomy plus bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (± HRT) — removing ovarian cycling; reserved for the most severe/resistant cases when the family is complete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What other treatments may help specific PMS symptoms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Spironolactone (for bloating/breast tenderness), some evidence for vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), and CBT throughout.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the underlying logic of the PMS treatment ladder?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: You are either suppressing ovulation (COCP → GnRH → surgery, escalating potency) or modulating serotonin (SSRIs) — the two mechanistic levers.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is a symptom-free week after the period essential to the diagnosis of PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because PMS symptoms are confined to the luteal phase and resolve with menstruation; the absence of a symptom-free interval points to a primary mood disorder instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why do both ovulation-suppressing and serotonin-modulating treatments work in PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because PMS results from over-response to normal cyclical hormone changes — suppressing ovulation removes the trigger, while SSRIs modulate the serotonergic response to it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is menopause, and its retrospective definition?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function — retrospectively defined as 12 months after the last period (average UK age ~51).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is premature ovarian insufficiency (POI)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menopause occurring before age 40 — where the calculus flips so that HRT becomes a replacement (not just an optional symptom treatment).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core hormonal mechanism of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian follicles deplete → oestrogen falls → loss of negative feedback → FSH and LH rise. Every symptom flows from oestrogen deficiency, and the high FSH is the biochemical fingerprint.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define perimenopause, menopause, postmenopause, POI and early menopause.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Perimenopause: the transition (irregular cycles + symptoms, up to 12 months after the last period). Menopause: 12 months amenorrhoea. Postmenopause: after that. POI: menopause <40. Early menopause: 40–45.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is menopause diagnosed in a woman ≥45 with typical symptoms (NICE NG23)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Clinically — with NO blood tests, because FSH fluctuates and does not change management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should FSH be checked in suspected menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only if the woman is 40–45 with symptoms, under 40 (POI), or has atypical features.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is POI diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptoms plus an elevated FSH (>30) on 2 samples taken 4–6 weeks apart.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of POI.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Idiopathic (commonest), iatrogenic (chemotherapy/radiotherapy/oophorectomy), autoimmune, and genetic (Turner syndrome, Fragile X).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the vasomotor and menstrual features of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Vasomotor: hot flushes and night sweats (the hallmark). Menstrual: irregular then absent periods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What genitourinary and psychological features occur in menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: GSM: vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency/urgency, recurrent UTIs. Psychological: mood/anxiety/low mood, 'brain fog', poor sleep, reduced libido.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the long-term health consequences of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Osteoporosis (fractures) and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-hormonal options are used for menopausal symptoms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Lifestyle measures (exercise, weight, reducing alcohol/caffeine/smoking); CBT (now recommended for vasomotor symptoms and low mood — 2024 NICE update); SSRIs/SNRIs for flushes (cautiously); and topical vaginal oestrogen/moisturisers-lubricants for GSM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the 'golden rule' of HRT regarding the uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: If the uterus is present → combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen), as the progestogen protects the endometrium (unopposed oestrogen causes hyperplasia/cancer). If no uterus → oestrogen-only HRT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is unopposed oestrogen dangerous in a woman with a uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, so a progestogen is added for endometrial protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is transdermal HRT preferred over oral, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In women with VTE risk or BMI >30 — transdermal oestrogen does not raise VTE risk (no first-pass metabolism), whereas oral oestrogen does.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the main benefits of HRT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptom relief and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the breast cancer risk with HRT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A small increase with COMBINED HRT (duration-related, falling after stopping); oestrogen-only HRT carries little/no increase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the VTE/stroke risks of HRT, and how does route affect them?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: VTE and stroke are raised with ORAL HRT but not with transdermal HRT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Should HRT be offered to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — HRT should NOT be offered for prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia (2024 NICE); it is for symptoms and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What sex-steroid replacement is offered in POI, and until when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: HRT or the combined oral contraceptive pill, until at least ~51 — replacing the oestrogen a young woman should have, protecting bone and cardiovascular health; the older-woman HRT-risk narrative does not apply.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why do women with POI still need contraception, and which option is contraceptive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because they may occasionally ovulate and rarely conceive; HRT is NOT contraceptive, but the COCP is.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What additional issues should be addressed in POI?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Fertility (e.g. donor eggs), bone health (DEXA), and psychological support.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex diagnostic and management summary for POI.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menopause <40 → diagnose with FSH ×2 (4–6 weeks apart) → offer HRT/COCP until ~51 for bone and cardiovascular protection, with contraception still needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is subfertility, and how common is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse — affecting ~1 in 7 couples. Both partners are investigated, organised around whether the problem is sperm, egg (ovulation), or the plumbing (tubes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What proportion of couples conceive within a year, reframing subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Over 80% conceive within a year (and about half the rest in the second year) — most couples are subfertile (reduced, not zero fertility), so the workup is as much reassurance and timing as pathology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the approximate proportions and core tests for the causes of subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Male factor ~30% (semen analysis); ovulatory disorder ~25% (mid-luteal/day-21 progesterone); tubal/pelvic ~20% (HSG/laparoscopy); unexplained ~25% (all tests normal).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of male-factor subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Low count/motility/morphology from varicocele, cryptorchidism, mumps orchitis, Klinefelter's, obstruction, hypogonadism, and drugs/heat/smoking.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of ovulatory subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PCOS (commonest anovulation), hypothalamic dysfunction (low weight/exercise/stress), hyperprolactinaemia, POI, and thyroid disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of tubal/pelvic subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PID (chlamydia — the big one), previous ectopic/surgery, endometriosis, and fibroids/adhesions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What preconception advice applies to a couple trying to conceive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Folic acid, stop smoking/alcohol, optimise BMI (~19–30; lose weight if ≥30), and have intercourse every 2–3 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core investigation for male-factor subfertility, and when is it repeated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Semen analysis; repeat at ~3 months if abnormal (spermatogenesis takes ~74 days).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the WHO reference values for semen analysis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Volume ≥1.5 mL, concentration ≥15 million/mL, motility ≥40%, and normal forms ≥4%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is ovulation confirmed biochemically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A mid-luteal progesterone taken 7 days before the expected period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle, adjusted for cycle length); a raised level confirms ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What further blood tests are done if a woman's cycles are irregular?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: FSH/LH (day 2–5), prolactin, TSH, testosterone (for PCOS), ± AMH (ovarian reserve).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the tests for tubal patency, and what is done before instrumentation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: HSG (first-line), HyCoSy, or laparoscopy + dye (if pelvic pathology). Screen for chlamydia before any instrumentation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should a subfertile couple be investigated, and when referred earlier?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Investigate after 1 year; refer earlier (before 1 year) if the woman is ≥36, there is a known cause, or a predisposing history (PID, cancer treatment, amenorrhoea, undescended testes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the dominant prognostic factor in fertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The woman's age.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is ovulatory subfertility due to PCOS managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Weight optimisation; ovulation induction with letrozole (increasingly first-line) or clomifene (± metformin); gonadotrophins if oral treatment fails; and dopamine agonists (cabergoline/bromocriptine) for hyperprolactinaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is tubal-factor subfertility managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Tubal surgery (for mild disease) or IVF, which bypasses the tubes and is often preferred for significant tubal damage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is male-factor subfertility managed by severity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Mild → IUI/IVF; severe → ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection); surgical sperm retrieval; or donor sperm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is intrauterine insemination (IUI), and its uses?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Placing prepared sperm directly into the uterus — used for mild male factor, same-sex couples, and donor sperm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the steps of IVF?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian stimulation → egg retrieval → in-vitro fertilisation → embryo transfer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is ICSI, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection — a single sperm injected directly into the egg, used for severe male-factor subfertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is unexplained infertility managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Do NOT offer clomifene/letrozole (no benefit); continue regular intercourse and offer IVF after 2 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key complication of ovulation induction/IVF?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which infection is the leading cause of tubal-factor subfertility, and what precaution follows?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Chlamydia — screen for it before instrumentation (e.g. HSG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: An iatrogenic, systemic complication of fertility treatment — an exaggerated ovarian response to controlled stimulation. It is the most serious complication of ovulation induction/IVF (has caused maternal deaths); the central danger is a massive fluid shift plus a prothrombotic state → VTE.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stimulated ovaries exposed to hCG (the trigger injection, or endogenous hCG of an early pregnancy) release VEGF → increased vascular permeability → fluid leaks into the 'third space'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the VEGF/fluid-shift mechanism explain the OHSS picture?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Third-space loss (ascites, effusions, oedema); intravascular depletion (hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration, hypotension, AKI); haemoconcentration + prothrombotic state → VTE; and ovarian enlargement (pain, torsion/rupture risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is OHSS described as hCG-driven, and why does pregnancy worsen it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: OHSS is rare without hCG and worsens if pregnancy occurs, because endogenous hCG keeps the ovaries stimulated — 'late' OHSS is pregnancy-associated and more severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of MILD OHSS (RCOG GTG5)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Abdominal bloating/discomfort and mild nausea, with ovaries <8 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of MODERATE OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Moderate pain, nausea/vomiting, and ascites on ultrasound, with ovaries 8–12 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of SEVERE OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Clinical ascites (± hydrothorax), oliguria, haemoconcentration (haematocrit >45%), hypoproteinaemia, and ovaries >12 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of CRITICAL OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Tense ascites/large effusions, haematocrit >55%, WCC >25, oligo/anuria, VTE, ARDS, and organ failure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors for OHSS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PCOS (many follicles), young age, low BMI, high antral follicle count/high AMH, previous OHSS, high follicle number/oestradiol during stimulation, hCG trigger + luteal support, and pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does OHSS present?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Abdominal bloating, distension and pain (ovarian enlargement + ascites); nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea; reduced urine output; shortness of breath (ascites/effusion); and signs of VTE (including unusual sites such as upper-limb/neck veins). It develops within days of the hCG trigger/egg collection, or later if pregnant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What investigations are used in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: FBC (haematocrit for haemoconcentration/severity, WCC); U&Es (AKI/electrolytes), LFTs, albumin, coagulation; ultrasound (enlarged ovaries, ascites); CXR if respiratory compromise; and β-hCG (pregnancy predicts worsening).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which conditions must be excluded when diagnosing OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian torsion, ovarian rupture, and ectopic pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the general management principle for OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It is usually self-limiting → supportive care while awaiting resolution; priorities are fluid balance, symptom control, and VTE prevention.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is mild-moderate OHSS managed (outpatient)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Analgesia (paracetamol/codeine — avoid NSAIDs if renal compromise), antiemetics, oral fluids to thirst, monitoring of symptoms/weight/urine output, safety-netting, and VTE risk assessment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is severe/critical OHSS managed (inpatient)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: IV fluids to correct hypovolaemia with monitoring of fluid balance/U&Es/haematocrit; paracentesis for tense/symptomatic ascites; essential VTE prophylaxis (LMWH + stockings); human albumin (plasma expander) in some; and HDU/ICU for critical cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is VTE prophylaxis essential in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because OHSS is strongly prothrombotic (haemoconcentration) and kills via thrombosis — including at unusual sites (neck/arm veins) — and the risk often extends into pregnancy if she conceives.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the role of paracentesis in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Draining tense/symptomatic ascites relieves pain and breathing and improves renal perfusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is surgery indicated in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only for ovarian torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy — otherwise the fragile enlarged ovaries are left alone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How can OHSS be prevented?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Identify high-risk women (PCOS, high AMH), use lower stimulation doses, antagonist protocols with a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG, 'freeze-all' embryos (avoiding pregnancy hCG that cycle), and cabergoline (reduces the VEGF effect).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is a GnRH-agonist trigger used instead of hCG to prevent OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because hCG is the driver of OHSS; a GnRH-agonist trigger avoids the prolonged hCG stimulation, reducing OHSS risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the organising principle for medical disorders in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy alters physiology and drug safety, so many conditions need screening (e.g. GDM), prophylaxis (VTE), or specific treatment — always weighing maternal and fetal wellbeing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is gestational diabetes (GDM)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy, driven by the insulin resistance that placental hormones (human placental lactogen, cortisol, progesterone) create to divert glucose to the fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does maternal hyperglycaemia in GDM affect the fetus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperinsulinaemia and macrosomia → shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. GDM is also a red flag for future type 2 diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the '5678' diagnostic thresholds for GDM on the 75g OGTT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L — either value alone is diagnostic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How are women screened for GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With a 75g OGTT — previous GDM: OGTT as soon as possible after booking and repeated at 24–28 weeks; any other risk factor: OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors for gestational diabetes.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: BMI >30, a previous macrosomic baby (≥4.5 kg), previous GDM, a first-degree relative with diabetes, and high-prevalence ethnicity (South Asian, Black Caribbean, Middle Eastern).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the 'glycosuria trap' in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A trace of glucose on urine dipstick is NORMAL in pregnancy (increased GFR and reduced tubular reabsorption). Do NOT screen with urinalysis/fasting glucose/HbA1c — use the OGTT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first step for GDM diagnosed with a fasting glucose <7 mmol/L and no complications?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A trial of diet and exercise, adding metformin if targets are missed, and insulin if glucose remains high.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first step for GDM with a fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L at diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Immediate insulin (± metformin) — too high to wait for diet/exercise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the approach when fasting glucose is 6.0–6.9 mmol/L with complications (macrosomia/polyhydramnios)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Consider immediate insulin (± metformin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Within what timeframe should a newly diagnosed woman with GDM be seen, and what is taught?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Seen in a joint diabetes/antenatal clinic within 1 week, and taught capillary blood glucose self-monitoring.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Outline the glucose-lowering ladder in GDM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Diet + exercise first (fasting <7, no complications; review in 1–2 weeks) → metformin if targets not met → insulin if metformin insufficient, or first-line if fasting ≥7 (or 6.0–6.9 with complications).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the capillary glucose targets in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Fasting <5.3 mmol/L; 1 hour post-meal <7.8; 2 hours post-meal <6.4; and keep >4 mmol/L if on insulin (to avoid hypos).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What fetal surveillance is used in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Growth scans to detect macrosomia/polyhydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is delivery timed in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Timed delivery by ~40–41 weeks (elective birth offered no later than 40⁺⁶), earlier if on treatment or with complications.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What should happen to glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stop all glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth — GDM resolves with delivery of the placenta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What neonatal monitoring is needed after a GDM pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Monitor the neonate for hypoglycaemia (fetal hyperinsulinaemia persists briefly after birth).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What postnatal maternal follow-up is needed after GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Maternal fasting glucose or HbA1c at 6–13 weeks postnatally, then annual HbA1c, given the high future risk of type 2 diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is GDM a 'red flag' for the mother's future health?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because it predicts a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes later, warranting ongoing surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which placental hormones drive the insulin resistance of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Human placental lactogen (hPL), cortisol, and progesterone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP/obstetric cholestasis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A liver disorder unique to pregnancy in which bile acids accumulate in the maternal circulation, causing intense itch (typically in the third trimester) that resolves after delivery. At high bile-acid levels it raises stillbirth risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of harm in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Impaired bile flow raises serum bile acids, which are thought to cross to the fetus and, at high concentrations, trigger fetal cardiac arrhythmia/placental vasospasm → sudden stillbirth. The bile-acid LEVEL, not the symptoms, drives risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the cardinal (often only) clinical feature of ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pruritus — classically worse on the palms and soles and worse at night, with NO rash (only excoriations).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the severity classification of ICP by peak bile acids (RCOG GTG43 2022)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Mild: 19–39 micromol/L; moderate: 40–99 micromol/L; severe: ≥100 micromol/L.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: At what bile-acid level is the stillbirth risk significantly raised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ≥100 micromol/L (severe ICP) — this is the key threshold; mild ICP does not significantly raise stillbirth risk above background.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the paradigm shift in understanding ICP stillbirth risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It was previously taught that ICP raised stillbirth risk in everyone; current evidence concentrates the excess risk at bile acids ≥100, so mild ICP is now managed much more conservatively.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the key investigations in suspected ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Serum bile acids (the key diagnostic and prognostic test) and LFTs (transaminases ALT/AST often raised, using pregnancy-adjusted ranges — ALP rises physiologically so is not useful).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is ICP a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because other causes must be ruled out — viral hepatitis, liver autoantibodies, liver ultrasound, and pre-eclampsia/HELLP; the diagnosis is confirmed retrospectively by resolution after delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the significance of a normal ALP in interpreting LFTs in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ALP rises physiologically in pregnancy (placental source), so it is not useful for diagnosing ICP; transaminases (ALT/AST) with pregnancy-adjusted ranges are used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) routinely recommended in ICP, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — the PITCHES RCT showed it does not prevent stillbirth and has only limited/insignificant benefit on itch, so routine use is superseded (it may be considered on an individual basis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What supportive measures are used for the itch of ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Topical emollients (e.g. menthol in aqueous cream — safe, may soothe) and a sedating antihistamine (chlorphenamine) to help sleep, though the effect on itch is limited.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is vitamin K given in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Water-soluble vitamin K only if there is prolonged clotting or severe cholestasis (impaired fat-soluble vitamin absorption creating a bleeding risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is the timing of birth stratified by bile-acid level in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ≥100 (severe): planned birth ~35–36 weeks; 40–99 (moderate): ~38–39 weeks; <40 (mild): ~40 weeks. Co-existing GDM/pre-eclampsia/multiple pregnancy prompts earlier delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What monitoring guides delivery timing in ICP, and what is the limitation of CTG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Serial bile acids and LFTs guide delivery timing; CTG is offered but cannot reliably predict or prevent the sudden stillbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the postnatal follow-up for ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Confirm resolution with an LFT/bile-acid check at ~4+ weeks; note the high recurrence (~45–90%) and a small increased lifetime hepatobiliary risk (gallstones).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the recurrence rate of ICP in future pregnancies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: High — approximately 45–90%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of ICP.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Third-trimester pruritus of the palms and soles with NO rash and raised bile acids, resolving after birth → measure bile acids and stratify delivery timing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What jaundice/bilirubin findings occur in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Bilirubin is raised in ~90%, but clinical jaundice occurs in only ~20%; dark urine, pale stools, RUQ discomfort and fatigue may also occur variably.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is bile-acid-stratified delivery timing used rather than a flat 37–38 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because stillbirth risk is concentrated at bile acids ≥100, so severe ICP is delivered earlier (~35–36 weeks) while mild ICP can be managed to ~40 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is VTE important in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: VTE (DVT + pulmonary embolism) is a leading direct cause of maternal death; pregnancy is a major prothrombotic state, and diagnosis/prevention deliberately differ from the non-pregnant pathway.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does pregnancy fulfil all three arms of Virchow's triad?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Hypercoagulability (oestrogen raises clotting factors and lowers protein S), stasis (uterine venous compression), and endothelial injury (at delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is VTE risk highest in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In the third trimester and the puerperium (first 6 weeks) — the puerperium carries the greatest daily risk of all.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is every woman VTE risk-assessed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: At booking, on any admission, intrapartum, and postnatally — because the risk is dynamic (RCOG uses a cumulative risk-factor score).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors used in VTE risk scoring.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Age >35, BMI >30, parity ≥3, smoking, gross varicose veins, current pre-eclampsia, immobility, multiple pregnancy, IVF, family history of unprovoked VTE, thrombophilia, medical comorbidities (SLE, IBD, cancer), and transient factors (hyperemesis/dehydration, OHSS, surgery, long-haul travel).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for a woman with previous VTE (any)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: She is highest risk — LMWH throughout the antenatal period plus 6 weeks postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for an antenatal risk score of ≥4?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH from the first trimester plus 6 weeks postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for an antenatal risk score of 3?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH from 28 weeks plus 6 weeks postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for a postnatal risk score of ≥2?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH for at least 10 days postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the anticoagulant of choice for VTE prophylaxis/treatment in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Low molecular weight heparin (e.g. enoxaparin) — it does not cross the placenta. DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated (warfarin is teratogenic — fetal warfarin syndrome).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is anti-Xa monitoring used with LMWH in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only at body-weight extremes (<50 or ≥90 kg) or in renal impairment — not routinely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What thromboprophylaxis applies after a caesarean with additional risk factors or emergency caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Postnatal LMWH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What mechanical/general measures support VTE prevention?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Anti-embolism stockings, mobilisation, and hydration.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why are D-dimer and the Wells score NOT used to diagnose VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy (so is not useful), and the Wells score is not validated in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is suspected DVT investigated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Compression duplex ultrasound (DVT is more often left-sided/iliofemoral); if negative but suspicion remains, repeat on days 3 and 7.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is suspected PE investigated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ECG and CXR first; if there are DVT signs, do a leg ultrasound first (avoids radiation); otherwise a V/Q scan or CTPA, guided by the CXR.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should treatment be started in suspected VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Start treatment-dose LMWH immediately on suspicion — do not wait for imaging, and do not delay for a thrombophilia screen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How long is LMWH continued when treating VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: For at least 3 months AND until at least 6 weeks postnatal (whichever is longer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is massive/life-threatening PE managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With IV unfractionated heparin or thrombolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What must happen to LMWH around labour/delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stop LMWH at the onset of labour or before planned delivery, to allow safe timing of regional anaesthesia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex for suspected PE in a pregnant woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Start treatment-dose LMWH on suspicion, then investigate (ECG + CXR first, then leg ultrasound or V/Q/CTPA) — without using D-dimer or the Wells score.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)?
