conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Antibiotics DURING labour (intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, IAP) — to stop the baby being colonised as it passes through the birth canal. Timing is everything: GBS prophylaxis only works intrapartum, not antenatally.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How does a baby acquire early-onset GBS disease?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: GBS lives in the maternal vagina/rectum, and the baby is exposed during vaginal delivery, leading to invasive disease in the first days of life.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Contrast early-onset and late-onset GBS disease.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Early-onset (<7 days, usually <24–48h): vertical spread from the maternal genital tract during birth, presenting with sepsis/pneumonia/respiratory distress, and preventable by intrapartum antibiotics. Late-onset (7 days–3 months): environmental/postnatal contact, more often meningitis, and NOT preventable by IAP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which type of GBS disease does intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Early-onset GBS disease only — late-onset disease is not targeted by this strategy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Does the UK use universal GBS screening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: No — the UK uses a RISK-FACTOR-based approach, offering IAP on risk factors rather than screening all pregnant women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why does the UK not screen all pregnant women for GBS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because most carriers' babies are born safely, a late swab cannot reliably predict disease, and screening everyone would give huge numbers of women unnecessary antibiotics (anaphylaxis and resistance risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How does the US approach to GBS differ from the UK?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The USA uses universal rectovaginal swab screening at 35–37 weeks, whereas the UK uses a risk-factor-based approach (a classic exam-comparison trap).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the GBS3 trial?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A UK cluster-randomised trial evaluating whether to switch to universal GBS screening (rather than the current risk-factor-based approach).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: List the risk factors that warrant offering intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS (RCOG GTG36).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A previous baby with invasive GBS disease; GBS detected in the current pregnancy (vaginal/rectal swab or GBS bacteriuria); preterm labour (<37 weeks); intrapartum fever ≥38°C (or suspected chorioamnionitis); and prolonged rupture of membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Treat it at diagnosis (e.g. amoxicillin) AND offer intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a woman with known GBS colonisation in a PREVIOUS pregnancy managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Offer either IAP in this labour, OR testing (enriched culture medium, ECM) in late pregnancy with IAP if positive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a woman whose PREVIOUS baby had invasive GBS disease managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Offer IAP in this labour — no swab is needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic for GBS prophylaxis, and its dosing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: IV benzylpenicillin, given as soon as labour starts and repeated 4-hourly until delivery (adequate dosing before birth matters).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What GBS intrapartum antibiotic is used for non-severe penicillin allergy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A cephalosporin (e.g. cefuroxime).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What GBS intrapartum antibiotic is used for severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Vancomycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is clindamycin no longer recommended for GBS prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because of rising GBS resistance to clindamycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Is intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis needed for a planned caesarean with intact membranes before labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: No — there is no passage through the birth canal, so IAP is not required.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How are neonates managed after GBS risk in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Babies who received adequate IAP and are well have routine observation; babies with risk factors but inadequate/no IAP, or signs of infection, have observation ± investigation and antibiotics per neonatal early-onset sepsis pathways (NICE).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why should an MSU be sent antenatally in relation to GBS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because GBS bacteriuria found on urine testing triggers both treatment at diagnosis and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the organising principle for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Timing + proteinuria + organ features. New hypertension after 20 weeks: without proteinuria/organ involvement = gestational hypertension; with proteinuria or organ dysfunction = pre-eclampsia; with seizures = eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A multisystem disorder defined by NEW hypertension plus end-organ dysfunction (classically proteinuria) after 20 weeks of pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the unifying pathophysiological concept of pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: The placenta is the problem — abnormal spiral-artery remodelling → a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta → release of anti-angiogenic factors → widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction → hypertension, proteinuria, oedema and multi-organ complications. This is why delivering the placenta is curative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is eclampsia, and when can seizures occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Pre-eclampsia plus a tonic-clonic seizure. Seizures can occur antenatally, intrapartum, or POSTNATALLY (a classic trap — pre-eclampsia does not end at delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What defines severe pre-eclampsia by blood pressure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Blood pressure ≥160/110 mmHg (with pre-eclampsia), or pre-eclampsia with severe features — an emergency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the severe/impending-eclampsia red-flag features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Severe frontal headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights/blurring), epigastric or RUQ pain (liver-capsule stretch), brisk reflexes/clonus, sudden facial/hand oedema, and reduced urine output.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the diagnostic BP threshold for pre-eclampsia (NICE NG133)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions after 20 weeks, PLUS at least one feature of proteinuria or organ dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is proteinuria quantified in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) ≥30 mg/mmol (or ACR ≥8); do not use a first-morning void to quantify it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the organ-dysfunction features that (with hypertension) define pre-eclampsia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Renal (raised creatinine/proteinuria), hepatic (raised transaminases ± RUQ/epigastric pain), neurological (visual disturbance, severe headache, clonus), haematological (thrombocytopenia, DIC, haemolysis), and uteroplacental (fetal growth restriction).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the role of PLGF-based testing in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Placental growth factor (PLGF) testing, between 20 and 36⁺⁶ weeks, helps RULE OUT pre-eclampsia in suspected disease (low PLGF supports the diagnosis, as it is the anti-angiogenic marker).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the HIGH-risk factors for pre-eclampsia (any ONE → aspirin).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes (type 1 or 2), and autoimmune disease (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the MODERATE-risk factors for pre-eclampsia (TWO or more → aspirin).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: First pregnancy (nulliparity), age ≥40, BMI ≥35, family history of pre-eclampsia, multiple pregnancy, and a pregnancy interval >10 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the aspirin prophylaxis regimen for pre-eclampsia, and its indication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Aspirin 75–150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth (many use 150 mg at night; start before 16 weeks for maximal effect). Given for one high-risk OR two or more moderate-risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What surveillance is used in a woman with diagnosed pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Serial BP and urine PCR/dipstick; bloods (FBC — falling platelets worrying, U&Es/creatinine, LFTs, and coagulation/LDH/haptoglobin/blood film if HELLP suspected); PLGF testing; and fetal surveillance (growth-scan ultrasound, umbilical artery Doppler, CTG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Delivery of the fetus and placenta; all other treatment temporises to allow fetal maturity while keeping the mother safe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the first-line antihypertensive for pre-eclampsia/gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Labetalol (oral, or IV in severe disease).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the second-line antihypertensive if labetalol is unsuitable (e.g. asthma)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Nifedipine; methyldopa is third-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the target blood pressure in pre-eclampsia?
Which antihypertensives are contraindicated in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ACE inhibitors and ARBs — they cause fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios (a classic trap).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures, and its dual role?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Magnesium sulfate — it both treats AND prevents eclamptic seizures (superior to diazepam/phenytoin), given in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (IV loading then maintenance infusion).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the features and antidote of magnesium sulfate toxicity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Toxicity progresses from loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign) → respiratory depression → cardiac arrest. The antidote is IV calcium gluconate; monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is an eclamptic seizure managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ABCDE, protect the airway, IV magnesium sulfate (loading + maintenance), control BP (IV labetalol/hydralazine), then expedite delivery once the mother is stabilised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is HELLP syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A severe variant/complication of pre-eclampsia — Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — presenting with RUQ/epigastric pain, nausea and malaise ± the pre-eclampsia picture; it risks liver haematoma/rupture and DIC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is HELLP syndrome managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Stabilise the mother and deliver.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why must BP monitoring and treatment continue postnatally in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Because the disease and seizures can worsen after delivery — pre-eclampsia does not end at delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What should new hypertension BEFORE 20 weeks make you think of?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension or another cause — or a molar pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: New hypertension arising after 20 weeks of pregnancy WITHOUT proteinuria or organ dysfunction (the presence of which would make it pre-eclampsia). Also called pregnancy-induced hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why is gestational hypertension described as 'pre-eclampsia's antechamber'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Because up to a quarter (~15–25%) of women with gestational hypertension go on to develop pre-eclampsia, so it is defined as much by what you watch for as by what it is.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How does gestational hypertension differ from chronic hypertension in timing and resolution?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Gestational hypertension arises AFTER 20 weeks and usually resolves after birth (by ~6–12 weeks postpartum); chronic hypertension is present before 20 weeks (or pre-pregnancy) and does not resolve.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How does gestational hypertension differ from pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Both are new hypertension after 20 weeks, but gestational hypertension has NO proteinuria and NO organ dysfunction, whereas pre-eclampsia has proteinuria or organ/uteroplacental dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the two 'negatives' that define gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: No proteinuria (urine PCR <30 mg/mmol) and no maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for gestational hypertension (NICE NG133)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: New hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks on two occasions, with no proteinuria (PCR <30) and no organ/uteroplacental dysfunction; severity graded as mild-moderate up to <160/110 and severe at ≥160/110.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the key investigation at each visit in gestational hypertension, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Urine dipstick/protein:creatinine ratio — the key test to catch the transition to pre-eclampsia (the development of proteinuria).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What surveillance is undertaken in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: BP monitoring (frequency scaled to severity), urine dipstick/PCR at each visit, bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) as indicated, PLGF-based testing if pre-eclampsia is suspected (20–36⁺⁶ weeks), and fetal monitoring (growth scans/Doppler) if concern arises.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the antihypertensive ladder for gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: The same as pre-eclampsia: first-line labetalol, second-line nifedipine (if labetalol unsuitable, e.g. asthma), third-line methyldopa; target BP ≤135/85.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Which antihypertensives are contraindicated in gestational hypertension, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ACE inhibitors and ARBs — they cause fetal renal damage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the target blood pressure in gestational hypertension?
What is the approach to timing of birth in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Aim to continue to term where BP is controlled and there are no complications; deliver earlier if it progresses to pre-eclampsia or BP becomes uncontrolled.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What happens to blood pressure postnatally after gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: It usually normalises but must be monitored, with antihypertensive treatment weaned.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What long-term health risk does gestational hypertension flag?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A higher lifetime risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease — warranting long-term follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why does a hypertensive disorder in a previous pregnancy affect the next pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: It is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks is indicated in any subsequent pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Give the exam framing for distinguishing the three hypertensive states by presentation.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: High BP first detected at 28 weeks with clear dipstick and normal bloods = gestational hypertension; the same BP with proteinuria or deranged LFTs/platelets = pre-eclampsia; high BP already present at booking (before 20 weeks) = chronic hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is severe gestational hypertension defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: BP ≥160/110 mmHg (mild-moderate is up to <160/110), graded as for pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What proportion of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Roughly 15–25% (up to about a quarter).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the four gynaecological cancers and their hallmarks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Endometrial (postmenopausal bleeding, unopposed oestrogen); ovarian (vague late symptoms + raised CA-125); cervical (HPV, screened/vaccine-preventable, post-coital bleeding); vulval (VIN/lichen sclerosus, elderly, vulval lump/itch/ulcer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the single highest-yield reflex in gynae-oncology?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise → urgent (2-week-wait) referral for transvaginal ultrasound ± biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is endometrial cancer and how common is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A malignancy of the uterine lining — the commonest gynaecological cancer in the UK and the 4th commonest cancer in women. It is overwhelmingly a disease of postmenopausal women (peak 60s–70s).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does endometrial cancer usually present at a curable stage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because it announces itself early and loudly through abnormal (postmenopausal) bleeding, so it is usually diagnosed at an early, curable stage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the central through-line explaining Type 1 endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Unopposed oestrogen — oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation and progesterone opposes it, so anything raising the oestrogen-to-progesterone ratio raises risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe Type 1 endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: ~80% of cases; oestrogen-dependent; endometrioid adenocarcinoma (grade 1–2); precursor is atypical endometrial hyperplasia; typical patient is obese, peri-/postmenopausal; better prognosis; usually p53 wild-type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe Type 2 endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: ~20% of cases; oestrogen-independent; serous, clear cell, or carcinosarcoma histology; precursor serous intraepithelial carcinoma; typically older, thinner, often multiparous women; worse prognosis (aggressive, spreads early); often p53-mutated (serous).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does obesity increase endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Adipose tissue aromatises androgens into oestrogen, increasing unopposed oestrogen exposure — it is the biggest modifiable driver.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the reproductive risk factors for endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Nulliparity, early menarche, and late menopause — all increasing lifetime oestrogen exposure; also PCOS (chronic anovulation → unopposed oestrogen).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does tamoxifen increase endometrial cancer risk (the 'tamoxifen trap')?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Tamoxifen is anti-oestrogenic in the breast but pro-oestrogenic on the endometrium, so it protects against breast cancer but raises endometrial cancer risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which hormonal exposures increase endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Oestrogen-only HRT (without a progestogen, in a woman with a uterus) and tamoxifen; diabetes and hypertension also cluster with it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which factors are protective against endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill, the Mirena/LNG-IUS, and pregnancy; smoking is anti-oestrogenic (the one context it 'protects' — never a recommendation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What hereditary syndrome predisposes to endometrial cancer, and its implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — lifetime risk up to ~40–60%. Consider it in younger patients; it prompts mismatch-repair (MMR) testing (now routine on biopsy) and colorectal cancer screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the cardinal symptom of endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) — over 90% present this way.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does endometrial cancer present in premenopausal women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Intermenstrual bleeding, or heavier/irregular menstrual bleeding; also abnormal discharge or (postmenopausal) pyometra, and in late disease pelvic pain and weight loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the 2-week-wait referral criterion for suspected endometrial cancer (NICE NG12)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Refer on the suspected-cancer pathway (seen within 2 weeks) any woman ≥55 with postmenopausal bleeding; consider a 2WW referral in women <55 with PMB.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the role and cutoff of transvaginal ultrasound in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: TVUS measures endometrial thickness: ≤4 mm is reassuring (>99% negative predictive value); >4 mm warrants endometrial biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the first-line tissue diagnosis in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: An outpatient Pipelle endometrial biopsy (a 'blind' aspiration sampler).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: When is hysteroscopy ± biopsy used in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: If the Pipelle sample is inadequate, there is a focal lesion (polyp/submucosal fibroid) to target, or bleeding persists despite a normal blind sample — allowing directed biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the PMB triage pathway in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: 2-week-wait referral → transvaginal ultrasound → if >4 mm, Pipelle biopsy → if inadequate or a focal lesion, hysteroscopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What imaging is used for staging endometrial cancer once confirmed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: MRI pelvis to assess myometrial invasion, and CT for distant spread.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the surgical cornerstone of treatment for early-stage endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total hysterectomy plus bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH+BSO), typically laparoscopic, ± pelvic lymphadenectomy/sentinel node depending on stage and grade.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What adjuvant therapies are used in endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Radiotherapy (vaginal brachytherapy/external beam) for higher-risk early disease; chemotherapy ± radiotherapy for advanced/high-grade disease; and immunotherapy (dostarlimab or pembrolizumab with carboplatin-paclitaxel), guided by MMR/microsatellite status, in advanced/recurrent disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the role of progestogens (high-dose oral or LNG-IUS) in endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A fertility-sparing option in selected young women with early, low-grade disease or atypical hyperplasia who wish to conceive; and palliative treatment for women unfit for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is atypical endometrial hyperplasia (the Type 1 precursor) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total hysterectomy is definitive; the LNG-IUS/progestogen with surveillance is used if fertility is desired or the woman is unfit for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What updated approach did FIGO introduce for endometrial cancer staging in 2023?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Incorporation of histological subtype, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), and molecular classification (POLE-mutated, MMR-deficient, p53-abnormal, no-specific-molecular-profile) alongside anatomical extent — a shift toward prognostic/molecular staging.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is ovarian cancer called the 'silent killer'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It is the leading cause of gynaecological-cancer death in the UK; it presents late with vague symptoms mistaken for IBS or ageing, so about two-thirds are diagnosed at an advanced stage — the mirror of endometrial cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the 'incessant ovulation' hypothesis of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Each ovulation ruptures and repairs the ovarian surface; cumulative lifetime ovulations drive malignant transformation, so anything reducing lifetime ovulations is protective.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which cell of origin accounts for ~90% of ovarian cancers, and give examples?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Epithelial tumours — high-grade serous (commonest), mucinous, endometrioid, and clear cell; typically in postmenopausal women (60s); the marker is CA-125.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Where is high-grade serous ovarian cancer now thought to originate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: From the fallopian tube fimbriae (not primarily the ovarian surface).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe germ-cell ovarian tumours and their markers.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 5% of cases, in young women (teens–30s); examples include dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour and teratoma; markers are AFP, βhCG and LDH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe sex cord-stromal ovarian tumours and their hormonal effects.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 5% of cases, any age; granulosa cell tumours (oestrogen → postmenopausal bleeding) and Sertoli-Leydig tumours (androgen → virilisation); markers include inhibin and oestrogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a Krukenberg tumour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A metastatic tumour of the ovary (classically from a gastric — or breast — primary), characteristically bilateral with signet-ring cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is Meigs syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The triad of a benign ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion, all of which resolve after removal of the tumour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the risk factors that increase ovarian cancer risk.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, increasing age (postmenopausal), BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (biggest genetic driver), Lynch syndrome, a family history of ovarian/breast cancer, and endometriosis (clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the biggest genetic risk factor for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (BRCA1 lifetime risk ~40%); Lynch syndrome also increases risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which factors are protective against ovarian cancer, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The COCP (major, persisting years after stopping), pregnancy/multiparity, and breastfeeding — all reduce the number of lifetime ovulations.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What persistent symptoms should raise suspicion of ovarian cancer (especially in women ≥50)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent (>12×/month) abdominal distension/bloating ('clothes don't fit'), early satiety/loss of appetite, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency, change in bowel habit, weight loss, and fatigue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is new-onset 'IBS' in a woman over 50 a red flag?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because IBS rarely presents for the first time at that age, so new IBS-type symptoms in an older woman should prompt investigation for ovarian cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the late signs of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Ascites, a palpable pelvic/abdominal mass, pleural effusion, and bowel obstruction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the first-line investigation in a woman with persistent possible ovarian-cancer symptoms (NICE CG122)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Serum CA-125; if it is ≥35 IU/mL, arrange an ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What additional markers should be measured in women under 40 with an ovarian mass?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: AFP and βhCG, to detect germ-cell tumours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI), and its referral threshold?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: RMI = U × M × CA-125. Refer to the gynae-oncology MDT if RMI ≥250.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the components of the RMI?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: U (ultrasound score: 1 point each for multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites, intra-abdominal metastases → U=0/1/3); M (menopausal status: premenopausal=1, postmenopausal=3); and CA-125 (absolute value in IU/mL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is CA-125 non-specific, and what is its role?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It is also raised in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, menstruation, pregnancy, ascites of any cause and other cancers. It is a triage and monitoring tool, not a diagnostic test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What imaging and staging system are used for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: CT abdomen/pelvis for staging, using FIGO staging (stage I confined to the ovaries → stage IV distant metastases).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the NICE ovarian cancer pathway in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent symptoms → CA-125 → if ≥35, ultrasound → calculate RMI → if ≥250, gynae-oncology MDT referral (add AFP + βhCG in under-40s).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the surgical management of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total abdominal hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy + omentectomy with maximal cytoreduction ('debulking'); the goal is no visible residual disease (the strongest prognostic factor). Fertility-sparing surgery is possible in young women with early germ-cell or borderline/stage IA epithelial disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the strongest prognostic factor in ovarian cancer surgery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Achieving no visible residual disease after cytoreductive ('debulking') surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What chemotherapy is used for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin) ± paclitaxel — adjuvant for most, or neoadjuvant in advanced disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What maintenance therapies are used in advanced high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: PARP inhibitors — olaparib if BRCA-positive, and niraparib/rucaparib in defined (HRD-dependent) settings; bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) in selected cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What causes nearly all cervical cancer, and which types are most important?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection; types 16 and 18 cause ~70% of cases. Cervical cancer affects young women (peak 30s–40s) and is largely preventable by vaccination and screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Explain the HPV oncoprotein mechanism in cervical cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: HPV E6 inhibits p53 (the guardian of the genome) and E7 inhibits Rb (retinoblastoma suppressor); losing both tumour-suppressor 'brakes' allows uncontrolled cervical epithelial proliferation → CIN → invasive cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the two main histological types of cervical cancer and where do they arise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Squamous cell carcinoma (~70–80%) arising at the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction), best detected by screening; and adenocarcinoma (~20%), glandular and arising higher in the canal, so harder to catch on screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is CIN and how do its grades differ?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia — a pre-invasive precursor. CIN I = dysplasia of the lower third (often regresses); CIN II = lower two-thirds; CIN III = full-thickness (carcinoma in situ), which is treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the classic trap distinguishing CIN from dyskaryosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: CIN is a HISTOLOGICAL (biopsy) diagnosis; dyskaryosis is the CYTOLOGICAL (cell) term used on the smear result.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the risk factors for cervical cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent high-risk HPV (the cause), smoking (independent risk and impairs HPV clearance), immunosuppression (HIV, transplant), early first intercourse/multiple partners/non-barrier contraception (HPV exposure), long-term COCP use, multiparity, and non-engagement with screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the biggest determinant of who develops cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Non-engagement with (non-attendance at) cervical screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Who is invited for NHS cervical screening and at what interval (from July 2025)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Women and anyone with a cervix aged 25–64. Ages 25–49: every 5 years if HPV-negative (changed from every 3 years on 1 July 2025); ages 50–64: every 5 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is HPV primary screening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Since 2019, the cervical sample is tested FIRST for high-risk HPV, and cytology is examined only if HPV-positive ('reflex cytology') — reversing the old cytology-first order.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for a hrHPV-negative screening result?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Routine recall (in 5 years, or 3 years if there was a recent prior HPV-positive result).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for hrHPV-positive with normal cytology?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Repeat the test in 12 months.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for hrHPV-positive with abnormal cytology (dyskaryosis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Refer for colposcopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What happens if a woman is hrHPV-positive at 3 consecutive annual tests?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: She is referred for colposcopy regardless of cytology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the cervical screening algorithm in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: HPV first → if negative, done → if positive, look at the cells → abnormal cells (or persistent HPV) = colposcopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is seen at colposcopy, and how are abnormal areas identified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Acetic acid turns abnormal areas white ('acetowhite'); iodine (Schiller's test) stains normal epithelium brown while abnormal areas do not take it up; a directed biopsy confirms the CIN grade.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the standard treatment for CIN, and its main future-pregnancy risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone); it carries a small increased risk of preterm birth in future pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What HPV vaccine is used, what does it cover, and who is offered it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Gardasil 9 — covering HPV 16 and 18 (plus 31/33/45/52/58, and 6/11 for warts); offered to all children in school Year 8 (~age 12–13), both girls and boys.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the current HPV vaccine schedule for the routine cohort?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A single-dose schedule (since September 2023); MSM up to 45 and immunocompromised people have separate schedules.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is HPV vaccination given before sexual debut?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: To vaccinate before HPV exposure, giving maximum protective benefit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the symptomatic red flags of cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Abnormal bleeding — postcoital, intermenstrual, or postmenopausal (the classic triad); blood-stained/offensive discharge; dyspareunia; and late features such as pelvic pain, leg oedema, ureteric obstruction/renal failure and fistula.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What should be done for an abnormal-looking cervix (mass/ulcer/contact bleeding) on speculum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Urgent 2-week-wait referral (NICE NG12) regardless of screening status — do NOT wait for a smear.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is cervical cancer investigated and staged once suspected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Colposcopy + biopsy confirms invasive disease; examination under anaesthesia (EUA), MRI pelvis (local/parametrial spread), and CT/PET for nodal/distant disease; it is FIGO staged (2018 revision incorporating imaging and nodal status).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the management principle by stage in cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Early disease → surgery; locally advanced disease → chemoradiation. Radical surgery and radiotherapy are not combined, to avoid stacking morbidity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a radical trachelectomy, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Removal of the cervix with pelvic lymphadenectomy while preserving the uterus — a fertility-sparing option for early cervical cancer (stage IA2–IB1) when fertility is desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a Wertheim's hysterectomy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy, used for early cervical cancer (IA2–IIA) when fertility is not desired (± ovarian preservation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is locally advanced cervical cancer (IB3/IIB–IVA) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Chemoradiation — cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is metastatic (IVB)/recurrent cervical cancer managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Palliative chemotherapy ± bevacizumab, with immunotherapy (pembrolizumab) in defined settings.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is vulval cancer, who does it affect, and the commonest type?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A malignancy of the external female genitalia — rare, a disease of elderly women (peak 70s+); ~90% are squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the central organising concept ('two roads') of vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It arrives by two separate routes — a younger HPV road and an older lichen-sclerosus road — and almost everything (age, precursor, p53 status, prognosis) follows from which road the patient is on.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe the HPV-dependent road to vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Caused by high-risk HPV (mainly type 16); the precursor is usual-type VIN (uVIN, now called vulval HSIL); typically younger women (40s–50s); p53 wild-type; risk factors include smoking, immunosuppression and other HPV lesions (CIN); slower progression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe the HPV-independent road to vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Caused by chronic inflammation — lichen sclerosus (± lichen planus); the precursor is differentiated VIN (dVIN); typically older women (70s+); p53-mutated; faster progression with much higher cancer risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which vulval cancer road is the more dangerous, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The HPV-independent (lichen sclerosus/dVIN) road — dVIN progresses faster (~2–3 years vs ~6–7), carries a much higher cancer risk, and is easily mistaken for a benign dermatosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the VIN terminology trap?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Usual-type VIN (uVIN, HPV-driven) is now often called vulval HSIL; differentiated VIN (dVIN, HPV-independent, lichen-sclerosus-associated) retains its name and is more dangerous.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is lichen sclerosus and its typical appearance?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A chronic inflammatory dermatosis — intensely itchy white/porcelain atrophic ('cigarette-paper') plaques, in a figure-of-eight perianal distribution, with architectural loss (labial fusion, buried clitoris).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the malignancy risk of lichen sclerosus, and via what precursor?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 4–5% lifetime risk of progression to vulval squamous cell carcinoma, via differentiated VIN (dVIN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is lichen sclerosus managed, and why does treatment matter for cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Potent/ultrapotent topical steroids (e.g. clobetasol), which also reduce cancer risk, plus long-term surveillance; biopsy any non-healing/ulcerated/thickened area to exclude dVIN/cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does vulval cancer typically present?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Vulval itching (pruritus, often long-standing especially on the lichen-sclerosus road); a lump, ulcer or plaque (raised/warty/eroded); bleeding, pain or discharge; a non-healing sore; sometimes an enlarged groin (inguinal) node.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is vulval cancer often advanced at diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Presentation is frequently delayed through embarrassment, so it is often advanced by the time of diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the essential investigation for any suspicious vulval lesion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Biopsy — every suspicious vulval lesion, and any suspicious area within lichen sclerosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why should the whole lower genital tract be inspected in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because HPV-related disease is often multifocal, so the cervix and vagina should also be checked.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the referral pathway for an unexplained vulval lump/ulceration/bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Urgent 2-week-wait referral (NICE NG12).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does vulval cancer spread, and what is the dominant prognostic factor?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It spreads via the inguinal (groin) lymph nodes, and nodal status is the dominant prognostic factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is uVIN (vulval HSIL) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Local surgical excision, or topical imiquimod in selected counselled women (after excluding occult invasion); laser in some cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is dVIN managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Excision, treated more aggressively because of its high, fast progression risk, alongside optimising lichen sclerosus treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the cornerstone of treatment for invasive vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Surgery — wide local excision (or radical vulvectomy for larger/multifocal disease) aiming for clear margins, extended to include adjacent dVIN/lichen sclerosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How are the groin nodes managed in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Sentinel lymph node biopsy for early unifocal tumours; inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy if nodes are involved or the tumour is high-risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: When are radiotherapy/chemotherapy used in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy for node-positive/high-risk disease, or primary chemoradiation for advanced/unresectable disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is each road of vulval cancer prevented/addressed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: HPV vaccination (Gardasil 9) protects against the HPV-dependent road; treating lichen sclerosus with steroids plus surveillance addresses the HPV-independent road.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Give the reflex stem for vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: An elderly woman with long-standing vulval itch who now has a lump/ulcer → vulval cancer until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the hallmark of each of the four gynaecological cancers.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Cervical = young/HPV; endometrial = obese/postmenopausal bleeding; vulval = elderly/itch; ovarian = late/silent.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the definition of female genital mutilation (FGM)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: All procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, or other injury to the female genital organs, for NON-MEDICAL reasons. It has no health benefits, causes serious harm, is a form of child abuse and a human-rights violation, and is illegal in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does FGM have any health benefits or religious basis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — it has no health benefits and no religious basis; it is culturally rooted and performed on girls (often young), causing physical and psychological harm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the three key threads in approaching FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: (1) Classify it (WHO Types 1–4); (2) know the legal framework (illegal under the FGM Act 2003, FGM Protection Orders, and the mandatory reporting duty); and (3) manage the acute and long-term consequences (including deinfibulation for Type 3).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 1 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Clitoridectomy — partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 2 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Excision — partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, ± excision of the labia majora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 3 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Infibulation — narrowing of the vaginal orifice with a covering seal (cutting and appositioning the labia, ± excision of the clitoris). It is the most extensive type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 4 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: All other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical reasons — pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, or cauterisation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Which type of FGM causes the most obstetric/gynaecological problems, and what may be needed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Type 3 (infibulation) — causing obstructed flow, intercourse and delivery problems; it may require deinfibulation (surgical opening).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the acute complications of FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Severe pain, haemorrhage, shock, infection (including tetanus, HIV/hepatitis from shared instruments), urinary retention, genital tissue injury, and death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the long-term complications of FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Urinary (recurrent UTIs, dysuria, obstruction/retention), menstrual/gynaecological (dysmenorrhoea, haematocolpos, difficult examinations), sexual (dyspareunia, reduced function), obstetric (obstructed labour, perineal tears, PPH, need for deinfibulation), and psychological (PTSD, anxiety, depression).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What UK law makes FGM illegal, and what does it criminalise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: The Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 (amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) — it is a criminal offence to perform FGM, to assist/arrange it, or to fail to protect a girl from it, including taking a girl abroad for FGM (extraterritorial).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the maximum penalty for FGM offences in the UK?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: 14 years' imprisonment; there is also a separate offence of failing to protect a girl (under 16) from FGM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is an FGM Protection Order (FGMPO)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: A civil court order to protect a girl at risk of FGM — for example, by removing/surrendering her passport to prevent her being taken abroad.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What legal protection exists for FGM survivors regarding identity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Lifelong anonymity for FGM survivors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the mandatory reporting duty for FGM (who and what)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Regulated healthcare professionals, social care workers, and teachers (England and Wales) have a PERSONAL duty to report KNOWN cases of FGM in a girl UNDER 18.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What does 'known' mean for the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Either the girl DISCLOSES she has had FGM, OR you VISUALLY IDENTIFY physical signs of FGM in the course of your work.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: How and when is a case reported under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Report to the POLICE — call 101 (999 if there is immediate risk); the statutory limit is within 1 month, but best practice is as soon as possible (ideally by close of the next working day).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does the mandatory reporting duty apply to girls 'at risk' or 'suspected' cases?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — it applies only to KNOWN cases in girls under 18; at-risk or suspected cases are managed with a normal safeguarding referral to children's services, not the police duty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does the mandatory reporting duty apply when an adult (≥18) discloses FGM she had as a child?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — the duty applies only to girls under 18; an adult disclosure is managed via local safeguarding, considering risk to other girls.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does a disclosure by a parent/relative (not the girl herself) trigger the mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — the mandatory police duty is not triggered by a third-party disclosure, though safeguarding still applies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Summarise the key decision on FGM reporting.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: KNOWN FGM (disclosed by, or visibly identified in, a girl under 18) → mandatory report to POLICE (101). At risk/suspected/adult → safeguarding referral (children's services), NOT the mandatory police duty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the principles of clinical management of a woman with FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Sensitive, non-judgemental, culturally-aware care; use professional interpreters (not family); careful documentation; psychological support for trauma/PTSD; assess risk to other girls; specialist FGM services; and deinfibulation for Type 3.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is deinfibulation, and when can it be done?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Surgical opening of a Type 3 infibulation — done antenatally, in labour, or when non-pregnant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Why must re-infibulation never be performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Because re-closing (re-infibulating) after delivery is illegal in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the organising principle for any reproductive-age woman with bleeding/pain and a positive pregnancy test?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Exclude ectopic pregnancy. Use transvaginal ultrasound plus serial βhCG to locate the pregnancy and assess viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is an ectopic pregnancy and its commonest site?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Implantation outside the uterine cavity — most commonly the fallopian tube (~95%, especially the ampulla). The tube cannot sustain the pregnancy, so it eventually ruptures, causing life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the classic triad of ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Amenorrhoea (6–8 weeks) + unilateral lower abdominal pain + vaginal bleeding (dark/'prune juice'). However, presentations are commonly atypical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why should you pregnancy-test every reproductive-age woman with pain, GI symptoms or collapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because ectopic presentations are commonly atypical, and a positive test with no intrauterine pregnancy is ectopic until proven otherwise; missing it risks fatal rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What signs indicate a ruptured/unstable ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Sudden severe pain, collapse and shock, with peritonism, shoulder-tip pain, tachycardia and hypotension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why does shoulder-tip pain occur in a ruptured ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Intraperitoneal blood irritates the diaphragm, causing referred shoulder-tip pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the immediate management of a ruptured/unstable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Resuscitate (ABC, IV access, fluids/blood, crossmatch) and proceed to immediate surgery (laparoscopy/laparotomy) — usually salpingectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the key examination signs of a (stable) ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Cervical motion tenderness ('cervical excitation') and adnexal tenderness/mass.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: List the main risk factors for ectopic pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Previous ectopic (strongest), PID/salpingitis (especially chlamydia), tubal surgery/ligation, endometriosis, adhesions, IUD/IUS in situ, assisted reproduction (IVF), smoking, and older age. (Anything that damages the tube.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line investigation once pregnancy is confirmed in suspected ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — to locate the pregnancy; findings include an adnexal mass/tubal sac, NO intrauterine pregnancy, and free fluid (blood) in the pouch of Douglas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is a 'pregnancy of unknown location' (PUL)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A positive pregnancy test with NO intrauterine pregnancy seen on transvaginal ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How are serial serum βhCG levels interpreted in a PUL?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Taken 48h apart: a normal intrauterine pregnancy roughly DOUBLES; an ectopic or failing pregnancy rises slowly, plateaus, or falls.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Where should a woman with a positive pregnancy test and pain/pelvic/cervical-motion tenderness be referred?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Immediately to the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria for EXPECTANT management of a stable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Clinically stable AND pain-free AND a tubal ectopic <35 mm AND no fetal heartbeat AND hCG <1500 IU/L (and falling) AND able to attend follow-up — with monitoring by serial hCG.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria for MEDICAL management (methotrexate) of an ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Stable, no significant pain, unruptured, mass <35 mm, no fetal heartbeat, hCG <1500 IU/L, no intrauterine pregnancy, and able to attend follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is methotrexate given and monitored in ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A single IM dose; serum hCG is monitored on days 4 and 7 for an adequate fall (~15% between days 4–7); repeat dose or surgery if the fall is inadequate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How does methotrexate treat an ectopic pregnancy, and what advice follows?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: It is a folate antagonist that stops trophoblast proliferation. Afterwards, avoid pregnancy for 3 months and take folic acid (it is teratogenic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What management options apply when hCG is 1500–5000 IU/L in a stable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A choice of methotrexate or surgery (if pain-free and able to follow up).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria mandating SURGICAL management of an ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Significant pain, or mass ≥35 mm, or a fetal heartbeat, or hCG ≥5000 IU/L, or rupture/instability, or inability to attend follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When is salpingectomy vs salpingotomy chosen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Salpingectomy (remove the tube) is first-line if the contralateral tube is healthy; salpingotomy (remove the pregnancy, preserve the tube) is used if there is an infertility risk (contralateral tube damaged), but ~1 in 5 need further treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the mnemonic to remember salpingectomy vs salpingotomy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: SalpingECTOMY = remove the tube; salpingOTOMY = you've still GOT the tube (tube preserved).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the anti-D rules for ectopic pregnancy management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Give anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU) to all Rhesus-NEGATIVE women having SURGICAL management; do NOT give it for solely medical/expectant management, and NICE says do NOT use a Kleihauer test here.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What GI symptoms can occur with an ectopic due to pouch of Douglas blood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Dyschezia (pain on defaecation) and diarrhoea, from blood irritating the pouch of Douglas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is miscarriage defined and classified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 24 weeks (most <12 weeks), classified by whether the cervical os is open/closed, whether products have been expelled, and whether the fetus is alive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What three questions frame a bleeding early pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: (1) Is the OS open or closed? (2) Have PRODUCTS passed (partially/fully)? (3) Is the fetus ALIVE?

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What does an open vs closed cervical os indicate about the miscarriage type?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: An OPEN os = miscarriage progressing (inevitable or incomplete); a CLOSED os = threatened (viable) or missed (dead but retained), or complete (all passed).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the mnemonic for the open-os miscarriage types?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: 'OPEN YOUR I's' — an OPEN cervical os means INEVITABLE or INCOMPLETE miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a threatened miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os, painless light bleeding, and a live fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe an inevitable miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Open os, heavy bleeding with clots and pain; an intrauterine sac is present with no cardiac activity, but products have not yet passed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe an incomplete miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Open os with only some products passed (retained products of conception), and ongoing pain and bleeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a complete miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os, little bleeding, with all products passed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a missed (delayed) miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os with a dead fetus retained; there are no symptoms of expulsion, pregnancy symptoms fade, and usually no pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the key risk of an incomplete miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Retained products of conception → risk of ongoing bleeding and infection → needs medical or surgical clearance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How does the pain/bleeding sequence help distinguish ectopic from miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: In ectopic, PAIN comes FIRST then bleeding; in miscarriage, bleeding typically comes first (± pain). Always confirm an intrauterine pregnancy on scan before assuming miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line, diagnostic investigation for miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — a crown-rump length (CRL) >7 mm with NO cardiac activity confirms miscarriage (or a mean sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What should be done if ultrasound findings for viability are borderline/uncertain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Repeat the scan in about 7–14 days before confirming miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When is serum βhCG used in suspected miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: When the pregnancy location is uncertain, to help exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line management for most miscarriages?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Expectant management — waiting 7–14 days for the miscarriage to complete, then repeating a pregnancy test/scan to confirm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When should medical or surgical management be preferred over expectant management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Increased risk of haemorrhage (late first trimester, coagulopathy, cannot have transfusion), previous adverse/traumatic pregnancy experience, or evidence of infection (or if unstable/haemorrhaging, do not wait).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the medical regimen for a MISSED miscarriage (2023 MifeMiso update)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Oral mifepristone 200 mg (a progesterone-receptor antagonist that primes/softens the cervix), then 48h later misoprostol 800 mcg (a prostaglandin causing contractions/expulsion), unless the sac has already passed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the medical regimen for an INCOMPLETE miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A single dose of misoprostol 600 mcg (vaginal/oral/sublingual).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why was the management of missed miscarriage changed to mifepristone plus misoprostol?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: The MifeMiso evidence showed the combination is more effective than misoprostol alone, resulting in fewer surgical procedures.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What supportive care and follow-up accompany medical management of miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Antiemetics and pain relief, and a pregnancy test at 3 weeks to confirm completion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What surgical options exist for miscarriage, and when are they used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Manual vacuum aspiration (local anaesthetic, outpatient) or surgical management in theatre (general anaesthetic) — used if the woman is unstable, expectant/medical management has failed, there is infection, or the woman prefers it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the anti-D rules in miscarriage management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Give anti-D immunoglobulin to Rhesus-negative women having SURGICAL management of miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Roughly how common is miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: About 1 in 5 pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A spectrum of conditions arising from abnormal proliferation of placental TROPHOBLAST tissue — from benign/premalignant molar pregnancies (complete and partial hydatidiform moles) to the malignant forms collectively called gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN): invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, and PSTT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why is a markedly elevated hCG the defining feature of GTD, and what does it explain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because trophoblast produces hCG. The very high hCG explains exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (severe hyperemesis), early pre-eclampsia, and hyperthyroidism (hCG structurally resembles TSH).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the genetic basis of a COMPLETE mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: An empty egg fertilised by sperm → ALL PATERNAL chromosomes, usually 46,XX (diploid). There is NO fetal tissue, hCG is very high, and malignant potential is higher.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the genetic basis of a PARTIAL mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A normal egg fertilised by TWO sperm → three sets of chromosomes (triploid, e.g. 69,XXY). There is some fetal tissue (often a non-viable fetus), hCG is moderately raised, and malignant potential is lower.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the GTD spectrum from benign to malignant?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Hydatidiform mole (complete/partial, premalignant) → invasive mole (invades myometrium) → choriocarcinoma (malignant, can follow a mole/miscarriage/ectopic/normal pregnancy, metastasises to lung) → placental-site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT, rare).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: The malignant end of the spectrum (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT), diagnosed when hCG persists or rises after evacuation of a mole.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the classic clinical features of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Painless bleeding in the first/early-second trimester, exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (e.g. hyperemesis), a uterus that is very large for dates, and a very high hCG; hypertension and hyperthyroidism may occur, ± grape-like vesicles and theca lutein cysts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why can hyperthyroidism occur in a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because the very high hCG structurally resembles TSH and can stimulate the thyroid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of a molar pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: First-trimester bleeding + uterus large for dates + very high hCG + snowstorm scan → molar pregnancy → evacuate + register + hCG follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the characteristic ultrasound appearance of a complete mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A 'snowstorm' or bunch-of-grapes appearance — numerous small anechoic spaces.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the definitive diagnostic investigation for GTD?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Histopathology of the evacuated products of conception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the method of choice for evacuating a complete mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Suction curettage (urgent uterine evacuation); a partial mole with fetal parts may require medical evacuation. Products must be sent for histological examination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What precautions apply during evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Give anti-D if Rhesus-negative, and avoid oxytocics before evacuation completes (risk of embolisation of trophoblastic tissue).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why must a woman with GTD be registered with a specialist GTD centre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: It is the UK standard of care, enabling serial hCG monitoring to detect persistent/malignant disease (progression to GTN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What follow-up is required after evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Serial hCG monitoring until it normalises (to detect persistent/malignant disease), plus effective contraception to avoid pregnancy during follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why should pregnancy be avoided during hCG follow-up after a mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because a new pregnancy's hCG would confuse the monitoring used to detect persistent/malignant disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: With chemotherapy — low-risk GTN with single-agent methotrexate; high-risk GTN with multi-agent chemotherapy (EMA-CO). GTN is highly chemo-sensitive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why is GTN described as the most curable gynaecological malignancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because it is highly chemo-sensitive, with cure rates over 90–95%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What indicates that a molar pregnancy has progressed to GTN?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Persistent or rising hCG after evacuation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Which pregnancy events can choriocarcinoma follow?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A molar pregnancy, a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, or a normal pregnancy; it is malignant and characteristically metastasises to the lung.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Inflammation of the breast tissue — most commonly lactational — caused either by MILK STASIS (duct obstruction → milk accumulation) or by INFECTION (Staph aureus commonest). It presents as a painful, red, warm area of breast ± fever.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why does mastitis usually start as milk stasis rather than infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: When milk is not removed (poor latch, blocked duct, missed feeds, engorgement), it backs up and the duct/tissue inflames — initially a sterile/inflammatory process. If stasis persists, bacteria (Staph aureus) can superinfect it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the first-line treatment for all mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Effective milk removal — continue breastfeeding (it is safe and therapeutic), with frequent feeding, good latch/positioning, and expressing if needed. Antibiotics are NOT first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the commonest organism in infective mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Staphylococcus aureus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What typically allows bacteria to enter and cause infective mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A nipple fissure/crack (often from a poor latch), which acts as a bacterial entry point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What happens if mastitis is left untreated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It can progress to a breast abscess (a fluctuant, very tender collection of pus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Give the reflex approach to a painful, red, wedge-shaped area of breast in a breastfeeding woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: This is mastitis → keep feeding + effective milk removal → add antibiotics only if she is systemically unwell, has an infected nipple fissure, is not improving after 12–24h, or has a positive culture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Contrast inflammatory (milk stasis) and infective mastitis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Inflammatory: caused by milk not being removed (blocked duct/poor latch/engorgement), mild/no systemic symptoms, intact nipple, improves with effective milk removal, no antibiotics. Infective: bacterial (Staph aureus) superinfection, fever/systemically unwell, often a nipple fissure, does not improve with milk removal alone, needs antibiotics.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What are the clinical features of mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Breast pain; focal, wedge-shaped/segmental erythema; local warmth and inflammation; ± nipple discharge and fever. It is typically unilateral and focal/segmental, following the affected duct/lobule.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How is mastitis diagnosed, and when is breast milk culture indicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It is a clinical diagnosis. Breast milk culture is indicated if it is not improving, the woman is systemically unwell, it is recurrent, or it is being treated in hospital.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When is ultrasound used in suspected mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: When a breast abscess (a fluctuant mass) is suspected.
