conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Massive obstetric haemorrhage (dominant risk), DIC, massive transfusion, hysterectomy (loss of fertility), bladder/ureteric/bowel injury (especially percreta), ICU admission, maternal death, and preterm birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the reflex approach when placenta praevia is found with a previous caesarean.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Screen for accreta antenatally (ultrasound ± MRI) and plan a specialist MDT caesarean-hysterectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) and its inheritance?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: An X-LINKED RECESSIVE disorder of end-organ RESISTANCE to testosterone, caused by a mutation in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. A genotypically male (46,XY) individual develops a female phenotype. It is a disorder of sex development (DSD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What single molecular defect underlies AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A non-functioning androgen receptor — so although the testes produce testosterone, tissues cannot respond to androgens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have female external genitalia despite being 46,XY with functioning testes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the androgen receptor doesn't work, tissues cannot respond to testosterone, so the external genitalia default to the female pattern (no virilisation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS develop breasts?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Testosterone is aromatised to OESTROGEN, and oestrogen-responsive tissues still respond — driving breast development and a female habitus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have no uterus, cervix, upper vagina or fallopian tubes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: The testes still produce anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which acts normally to suppress the Müllerian (female internal) structures.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have neither ovaries nor a uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: There are no ovaries because the gonads are testes (46,XY); and no uterus because AMH suppressed the Müllerian ducts — leaving a blind-ending vagina, no menstruation and infertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Summarise the three hormone signals that explain the AIS phenotype.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: (1) Testosterone is made but not sensed → female external genitalia + scant hair; (2) AMH is present and acts → no uterus/cervix/upper vagina/tubes; (3) oestrogen (aromatised from testosterone) acts → breast development.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What are the two forms of AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Complete AIS (CAIS) — a fully female phenotype; and partial AIS (PAIS) — ambiguous or undervirilised genitalia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How might AIS present in infancy/childhood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: With bilateral inguinal hernias or groin swellings in an apparent girl that turn out to contain testes (undescended) — a key trigger to investigate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does AIS typically present in adolescence?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Primary amenorrhoea in a normally developed phenotypic female (breasts present), with scant pubic/axillary hair and a short/blind-ending vagina.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is pubic and axillary hair scant in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because pubic and axillary hair growth is androgen-dependent, and androgens are not sensed — making scant hair a useful discriminator.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the classic reflex description of AIS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A phenotypic female with primary amenorrhoea, absent uterus, breast development, scant pubic/axillary hair, and inguinal 'hernias' (testes) → karyotype 46,XY.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does AIS (CAIS) differ from Müllerian agenesis (MRKH) in primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: AIS: 46,XY, high (male-range) testosterone, scant pubic hair, gonads are testes. MRKH: 46,XX, female-range/normal testosterone, NORMAL pubic hair, ovaries present. Karyotype, testosterone and pubic hair distinguish them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does 5α-reductase deficiency differ from AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Both are 46,XY with absent uterus and high testosterone, but in 5α-reductase deficiency DHT is low and affected individuals virilise at puberty, whereas in AIS androgens are not sensed at all (no virilisation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the key confirmatory investigation in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Karyotype showing 46,XY; androgen receptor gene sequencing confirms the mutation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the typical hormone profile in post-pubertal AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Testosterone in the normal/high MALE range; raised LH (no androgen negative feedback); oestrogen present; AMH detectable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What do pelvic imaging (USS/MRI) findings show in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Absent uterus and ovaries, testes in the abdomen or inguinal canal, and a blind-ending vagina.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the overall management approach to AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Multidisciplinary care (endocrine/gynae/urology/psychology/genetics) with sensitive counselling; usually female sex of rearing in CAIS; gonadectomy (timing now usually deferred to post-puberty); oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy; vaginal and psychological support.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is gonadectomy now typically deferred until after puberty in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the pre-pubertal malignancy risk of the intra-abdominal testes is low, and retaining the testes allows spontaneous puberty/feminisation via aromatisation; gonadectomy is a shared decision, with gonads often retained into early adulthood under surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the malignancy risk from retained intra-abdominal testes in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: An increased risk of gonadal (germ-cell) malignancy that rises with age; modern estimates of frank malignancy are lower than older figures (~1–2%, premalignant change ~6%), almost all occurring post-puberty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is oestrogen replacement given after gonadectomy in AIS, and why is progesterone not needed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Oestrogen maintains secondary sexual characteristics and protects bone (preventing osteoporosis) and cardiovascular/metabolic health. Progesterone is not needed because there is no uterus/endometrium to protect.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What additional supportive measures are important in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Vaginal dilation or surgery if the vagina is short (for sexual function), psychological support, genetic counselling (X-linked implications for relatives), and infertility counselling (cannot carry a pregnancy).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is fertility not possible in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: There is no uterus and no ovaries, so the individual cannot produce eggs or carry a pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What two parallel cycles make up the menstrual cycle, and what links them?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The OVARIAN cycle (follicular → ovulation → luteal) and the UTERINE/endometrial cycle (proliferative → secretory → menstruation). They are linked by ovarian hormones — oestrogen and progesterone drive the uterine changes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which axis governs the menstrual cycle and what is its overall feedback pattern?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, running cyclically. It is governed by NEGATIVE feedback throughout, except for one mid-cycle POSITIVE-feedback burst (high oestrogen) that triggers ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during the follicular phase (ovarian side)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: FSH rises and stimulates follicle development (several recruited, one becomes dominant); the growing follicle's granulosa cells produce rising oestrogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the uterine counterpart of the follicular phase, and which hormone drives it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The PROLIFERATIVE phase — oestrogen (from the developing follicle) causes endometrial proliferation/thickening and thins cervical mucus to make it fertile.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does FSH fall slightly during the mid/late follicular phase?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Rising oestrogen exerts negative feedback, lowering FSH; this helps select the single dominant follicle (which can survive the falling FSH).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What triggers ovulation, and what is unique about the feedback involved?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: When oestrogen reaches a critically high level, feedback switches from negative to POSITIVE, triggering a massive LH surge (with a smaller FSH surge). This is the ONLY positive-feedback loop in the cycle and one of the few in endocrinology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How long after the LH surge begins does ovulation occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The follicle ruptures and releases the egg approximately 24–36 hours after the LH surge begins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during the luteal phase (ovarian side)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (plus some oestrogen).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the effects of progesterone in the luteal phase?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It produces a SECRETORY endometrium (glands secrete, preparing for implantation), thickens cervical mucus, and raises basal body temperature (an ovulation marker).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the feedback effect of luteal-phase progesterone and oestrogen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: They suppress FSH and LH (negative feedback), preventing the development of new follicles during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is the luteal phase a fixed length, and what is the clinical implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan, so the luteal phase is reliably ~14 days. Therefore cycle-length variation comes from the FOLLICULAR phase, not the luteal phase — useful for dating ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The corpus luteum regresses (~day 24–28), so progesterone and oestrogen fall; the endometrium can no longer be maintained and sheds (menstruation). The falling hormones release feedback, so FSH rises again to start the next cycle.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the FSH pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: FSH rises early (follicular phase), has a small ovulatory surge, and is suppressed during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the LH pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: LH is low through the follicular phase, then shows a dramatic mid-cycle surge that triggers ovulation, and falls again in the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the oestrogen pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oestrogen rises through the follicular phase, peaks just before ovulation (triggering the LH surge), then has a second smaller rise during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the progesterone pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone is low in the follicular phase, rises in the luteal phase (from the corpus luteum), and falls if no pregnancy occurs — leading to menstruation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What raises basal body temperature after ovulation, and how is this used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone from the corpus luteum raises basal body temperature; a sustained temperature rise is used as a marker that ovulation has occurred.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens hormonally if the egg is fertilised and implants?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The embryo secretes hCG, which 'rescues' the corpus luteum so it keeps producing progesterone; the endometrium is maintained (no menstruation) and pregnancy continues.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of hCG, and when does the placenta take over progesterone production?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: hCG maintains the corpus luteum (and is the basis of pregnancy tests). The placenta takes over progesterone production at around weeks 8–12.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does the combined oral contraceptive pill work in terms of the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Its oestrogen and progesterone provide negative feedback, reducing FSH and LH, so there is no follicular development or ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does progesterone-only contraception work?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It thickens cervical mucus, thins the endometrium, and (depending on the type/dose) may inhibit ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What hormonal changes occur at menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Follicle depletion leads to falling oestrogen and a marked rise in FSH (loss of negative feedback from the ovary).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the hormonal picture in PCOS relevant to the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: A disrupted axis with a raised LH:FSH ratio and anovulation, producing irregular/absent cycles.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which two events should be anchored to understand the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: (1) The mid-cycle oestrogen peak → LH surge → ovulation; and (2) the luteal progesterone rise → secretory endometrium (then its fall → menstruation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the two broad purposes of maternal physiological adaptation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: (1) To SUPPLY the fetus (increased cardiac output, blood volume, ventilation) and (2) to PREPARE for delivery and lactation — driven by pregnancy hormones (hCG, progesterone, oestrogen, hPL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which organ becomes the main endocrine organ of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The placenta — it takes over as the principal source of pregnancy hormones (progesterone, oestrogen, hPL) after the early corpus-luteum phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of hCG in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It maintains the corpus luteum early (sustaining progesterone) until the placenta takes over at ~weeks 8–12, and is the basis of pregnancy tests.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are progesterone's key roles in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maintaining the endometrium/pregnancy, relaxing smooth muscle (the unifying cause of many adaptations), and preventing uterine contractions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which single hormonal effect explains many pregnancy adaptations, and give examples?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone-mediated SMOOTH MUSCLE RELAXATION — causing vasodilation (↓SVR), reduced gut motility (constipation/reflux), and ureteric dilation (hydronephrosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of human placental lactogen (hPL)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It increases maternal insulin resistance, diverting glucose to the fetus — the physiological basis of gestational diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: By how much does cardiac output rise in pregnancy and via what mechanisms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Cardiac output rises ~30–50%, through increased stroke volume and heart rate, to supply the uteroplacental circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: By how much does plasma volume increase in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Plasma volume rises ~50%, driven by RAAS activation and fluid retention.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens to systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone-mediated vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, so BP falls in the 1st/2nd trimester and returns towards normal by term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is a rising blood pressure or hypertension abnormal in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because BP normally FALLS in early–mid pregnancy (vasodilation); a rising BP or hypertension is abnormal and should prompt consideration of pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is aortocaval compression and how is it managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The gravid uterus compresses the IVC (and aorta) when the woman is supine, reducing venous return and causing hypotension (supine hypotensive syndrome). It is managed by nursing in the left lateral tilt.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Explain the physiological (dilutional) anaemia of pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Plasma volume increases (~50%) more than red cell mass (~25%), so the blood is diluted, producing a physiological fall in haemoglobin — a normal dilutional anaemia, not iron deficiency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is pregnancy a hypercoagulable state, and what is the consequence?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: There are increased clotting factors, reduced fibrinolysis, and venous stasis (Virchow's triad), raising VTE risk — a leading cause of maternal death, hence the importance of prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why are iron and folate requirements increased in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because of fetal demand; supplementation is used, and folate additionally prevents neural tube defects.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the respiratory adaptations of pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone increases tidal volume and hence minute ventilation, blowing off CO₂ to cause a mild (compensated) respiratory alkalosis; oxygen consumption rises with fetal/maternal demand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do many pregnant women feel breathless, and what must be excluded?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Physiological breathlessness results from increased ventilation and the uterus splinting the diaphragm. Pulmonary embolism must be excluded given the increased VTE risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens to GFR and serum creatinine/urea in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Renal blood flow and GFR rise ~50%, lowering serum creatinine and urea — so a 'normal' creatinine may actually be relatively high for pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is there an increased risk of UTI/pyelonephritis in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Physiological hydronephrosis (progesterone-induced ureteric relaxation plus uterine compression) causes urinary stasis, predisposing to UTI and pyelonephritis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does mild glycosuria occur in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The renal threshold for glucose is lowered, so mild glycosuria can occur and is usually benign.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What drives the insulin resistance of pregnancy, and what condition results if uncompensated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Insulin resistance is driven by hPL, progesterone and cortisol (diverting glucose to the fetus); if the maternal pancreas cannot compensate, gestational diabetes develops — typically in later trimesters when placental hormones peak.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does pregnancy affect the thyroid, and its clinical implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oestrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin and hCG stimulates the thyroid, increasing thyroid hormone demand — which is why levothyroxine doses often need increasing in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What GI adaptations occur in pregnancy and their mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle → reduced gut motility (constipation), reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone (reflux/heartburn), and gallbladder stasis (gallstones); nausea/vomiting is hCG-related.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is VTE prophylaxis/treatment managed in pregnancy, and why not warfarin/DOACs?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is used, because warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are not recommended in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How do the renal/volume changes of pregnancy affect drug handling?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Increased GFR raises drug clearance and the increased volume of distribution alters drug levels — both affecting dosing in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What four organ functions does the placenta perform for the fetus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Gas exchange (replacing the lungs), nutrition (replacing the gut), waste removal (replacing the kidneys), and endocrine function (hCG, progesterone, oestrogen, hPL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does the placenta achieve gas exchange, nutrition and waste removal?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: O₂ passes to the fetus and CO₂ away down gradients; glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, amino acids by active transport, and fatty acids to the fetus; urea/creatinine/CO₂ are cleared to maternal blood.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the key structural principle of the placenta regarding maternal and fetal blood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maternal and fetal blood come close but do NOT mix — they are separated by the placental membrane, across which exchange occurs by diffusion/transport.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which substances readily cross the placenta?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: O₂, CO₂, nutrients and water; IgG antibodies (giving neonatal passive immunity); many drugs (e.g. warfarin, alcohol); some pathogens (TORCH); and anti-D IgG.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which important substances do NOT cross the placenta well?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maternal red cells (normally), IgM (too large), and heparin — which is why heparin/LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is heparin/LMWH preferred over warfarin in pregnancy, in placental terms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic, whereas heparin does not cross — so LMWH is used for anticoagulation in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which antibody class crosses the placenta and what does it provide?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: IgG crosses the placenta, providing the neonate with passive immunity. IgM is too large to cross.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Explain the placental basis of rhesus disease.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and attacks fetal red cells, causing fetal haemolysis (haemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are TORCH infections in the context of placental transfer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Pathogens that can cross the placenta to cause congenital infection — Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, and others (e.g. herpes/'other') — hence 'TORCH'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the structure of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) and its key property?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: HbF is 2α2γ and has a HIGHER oxygen affinity than adult HbA (a left-shifted O₂ dissociation curve).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does HbF's higher oxygen affinity matter physiologically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It lets the fetus extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta — fetal Hb 'grabs' the O₂ that maternal Hb releases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do β-chain disorders like sickle cell and β-thalassaemia present after birth rather than in utero?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because HbF (which lacks β-chains) is gradually replaced by adult HbA after birth; as HbF wanes, the β-chain defects become manifest.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Name the three fetal shunts and what each connects.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Ductus venosus (umbilical vein → IVC), foramen ovale (right atrium → left atrium), and ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery → aorta).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the ductus venosus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the liver, sending oxygenated placental blood from the umbilical vein straight to the IVC and heart.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the foramen ovale?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the lungs by shunting blood from the right atrium to the left atrium across the atrial septum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the ductus arteriosus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the lungs by diverting blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What haemodynamic conditions drive the fetal shunt pattern?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: High pulmonary vascular resistance (fluid-filled, non-functional lungs) and low systemic vascular resistance (the large placental circulation) drive blood away from the lungs and through the shunts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Trace the path of oxygenated blood in the fetal circulation.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus (past the liver) → IVC → right atrium → most crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart → body/brain; blood in the pulmonary artery mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus to the aorta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What two events at birth transform the circulation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The first breath inflates the lungs → pulmonary vascular resistance falls dramatically (blood flows to the lungs); and cord clamping removes the low-resistance placenta → systemic vascular resistance rises.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the foramen ovale become after birth, and what triggers its closure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It becomes the fossa ovalis; closure is triggered when left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, causing the flap to close.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the ductus arteriosus become after birth, and what triggers its closure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; closure is triggered by rising O₂ and falling prostaglandins, constricting it (over days).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the ductus venosus become after birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The ligamentum venosum, following the loss of umbilical blood flow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How do prostaglandins affect the ductus arteriosus, and what is the clinical application?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus OPEN in utero. Clinically, prostaglandin (PGE) is used to keep it open in duct-dependent congenital heart disease, while NSAIDs/indometacin (which reduce prostaglandins) close a patent ductus arteriosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and how is it managed pharmacologically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close, causing a left-to-right shunt. Indometacin (reducing prostaglandins) is used to close it; PGE is used to keep it open when a duct-dependent lesion is present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Failure of the pulmonary vascular resistance to fall at birth, so the circulation does not transition normally to the lungs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the two hormonal arms of lactation and their distinct roles?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin (anterior pituitary) makes the milk (production/synthesis), and oxytocin (posterior pituitary) ejects it (the let-down reflex, by contracting myoepithelial cells). Both are sustained by the suckling stimulus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which hormone is responsible for milk PRODUCTION, and from where?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin, from the anterior pituitary — it drives milk synthesis in the alveolar cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which hormone is responsible for milk EJECTION (let-down), and from where?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oxytocin, from the posterior pituitary — it contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli to eject milk into the ducts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is the breast prepared for lactation during pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Placental oestrogen and progesterone develop the ducts and alveoli (glandular tissue), priming the breast for milk production.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the 'pregnancy paradox' of lactation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin rises through pregnancy, but the high oestrogen and progesterone BLOCK prolactin's milk-producing action — so no milk is made during pregnancy despite the priming.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What triggers milk production to begin after birth, and when does milk 'come in'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Delivery of the placenta causes oestrogen and progesterone to fall sharply, removing the block so prolactin can act; milk production begins around day 2–3 postpartum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is colostrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The protein- and antibody-rich (especially IgA) first milk, produced in the first few days before mature milk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the suckling reflex and its role in milk supply.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The baby suckling sends a sensory signal to the hypothalamus → increased prolactin (and oxytocin) → more milk made and ejected. This 'supply and demand' loop matches milk supply to the baby's demand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is prolactin normally controlled by dopamine?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin is under tonic INHIBITION by dopamine; suckling reduces this dopamine inhibition, allowing prolactin to rise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do dopamine antagonists (e.g. antipsychotics) raise prolactin?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin; blocking dopamine removes this inhibition, raising prolactin and potentially causing galactorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which drugs are used to SUPPRESS lactation, and why do they work?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Dopamine agonists — bromocriptine and cabergoline — because increasing dopamine activity suppresses prolactin and hence milk production.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the let-down (milk ejection) reflex pathway.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Suckling → signal to the hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases oxytocin → oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli → milk is ejected into the ducts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How can the let-down reflex be triggered or inhibited by non-suckling factors?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It can be triggered by a conditioned/neural stimulus such as the baby's cry or the sight of the baby, and inhibited by stress/pain (sympathetic activation) — which is why a relaxed environment aids breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Besides milk ejection, what other effect does oxytocin have postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It causes uterine contraction, helping the uterus involute after birth (and can cause 'afterpains' during breastfeeding).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is lactational amenorrhoea and its mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: High prolactin suppresses the HPG axis (↓GnRH → ↓LH/FSH), suppressing ovulation and causing amenorrhoea during breastfeeding — a natural but unreliable contraceptive effect.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does breastfeeding delay the return of fertility postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because high prolactin suppresses the HPG axis and ovulation (lactational amenorrhoea), delaying the return of menstruation and fertility, especially during exclusive breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What immune protection does breast milk provide the neonate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Secretory IgA, which provides mucosal protection for the neonate's gut and respiratory tract — a form of natural passive immunity; colostrum is especially antibody-rich.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is caution needed when prescribing drugs to a breastfeeding mother?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because many drugs pass into breast milk and can reach the infant, so prescribing during breastfeeding requires care over drug safety.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: In a non-pregnant person, what can cause hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: A prolactinoma or dopamine antagonists (e.g. antipsychotics) — raising prolactin, which causes galactorrhoea and suppresses the HPG axis (amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Summarise how supply is established and maintained in breastfeeding.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Suckling stimulates prolactin (production) and oxytocin (ejection); the more the baby feeds, the more milk is made and released — a demand-driven 'supply and demand' system.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A postmenopausal woman describes a feeling of 'something coming down' in the vagina, worse at the end of the day, with a visible bulge. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A bearing-down sensation with a vaginal bulge, worse on standing/end of day, is characteristic of pelvic organ prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman has descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall with urinary symptoms. What is this called?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall is a cystocele, associated with urinary symptoms; a rectocele involves the posterior wall/rectum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for pelvic organ prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Vaginal delivery and multiparity (especially instrumental/prolonged deliveries and large babies) are the biggest risk factors; age/menopause, obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure also contribute.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with a posterior vaginal wall prolapse reports constipation and needing to splint to empty her bowels. What type of prolapse is this?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A rectocele (rectum descending into the posterior vaginal wall) is associated with constipation, incomplete evacuation and splinting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: What is the first-line management for a woman with mild, symptomatic prolapse?
options: Conservative measures including pelvic floor muscle training
A vaginal pessary as first choice always
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.answer: Conservative measures including pelvic floor muscle training
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Conservative measures (weight loss, treating constipation/cough, PFMT ≥16 weeks, topical oestrogen) are first-line, especially for mild (POP-Q stage 1–2) prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: How often should a ring pessary be changed to prevent complications?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A vaginal pessary should be removed/changed at least every 6 months to prevent erosion, discharge, bleeding and fistula formation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with a symptomatic cystocele who has failed conservative treatment opts for surgery. Which procedure is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: An anterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair, without mesh) is used for a cystocele; posterior colporrhaphy is for a rectocele.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman develops a vault prolapse several years after a hysterectomy. Which surgical procedure is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Vault prolapse (top of the vagina after hysterectomy) is treated with sacrocolpopexy or sacrospinous fixation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: What is the current UK position on transvaginal mesh for prolapse repair?
options: Its use is highly restricted (research-only) due to serious complications
It is first-line for all repairs
It is recommended for cystocele repair
It is mandatory for vault prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.answer: Its use is highly restricted (research-only) due to serious complications
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Transvaginal mesh is highly restricted/paused in the UK (research-only per NICE IPG599) because of serious complications; native-tissue repairs are first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: How is asymptomatic pelvic organ prolapse managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Asymptomatic prolapse needs no treatment; observation is reasonable, with lifestyle advice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with symptomatic uterine prolapse wishes to preserve her uterus. Which surgical option is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Sacrohysteropexy is a uterus-preserving procedure for uterine prolapse; vaginal hysterectomy is the alternative when preservation is not desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: Which examination technique helps demonstrate a prolapse that is not visible at rest?
options: Examining while the woman bears down (± standing)
Examining only when supine and relaxed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.answer: Examining while the woman bears down (± standing)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Prolapse may only show when the woman bears down or stands, so examination is performed in these positions (a Sims speculum helps visualise each wall).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A frail elderly woman with significant prolapse who does not wish to retain sexual function is offered which definitive procedure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Colpocleisis (vaginal closure) is an option for frail women not wishing to retain sexual function, being a simpler, effective procedure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Under which legal ground are the vast majority of abortions in England performed?
options: Ground C (greater risk to the woman's health than termination, <24 weeks)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Ground C (greater risk to the woman's health than termination, <24 weeks)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Ground C — a greater risk to the woman's physical/mental health than termination — is used for the vast majority of abortions and applies up to <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which abortion ground has NO upper gestational time limit?
options: Ground E (substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Ground E (substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Grounds A (risk to life), B (grave permanent injury) and E (serious fetal abnormality) have no upper time limit; C and D apply <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: How many registered medical practitioners must agree to a non-emergency abortion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Two registered medical practitioners must agree in good faith that a legal ground is met; one is sufficient in an emergency to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: What is the mechanism of mifepristone in medical termination of pregnancy?
options: It is an anti-progesterone that breaks down the decidua and sensitises the uterus
It is a prostaglandin that causes contractions
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: It is an anti-progesterone that breaks down the decidua and sensitises the uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Mifepristone is an anti-progesterone; it blocks progesterone, breaking down the decidua and sensitising the uterus, after which misoprostol is given to expel the pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: In medical TOP, when is misoprostol typically given after mifepristone?
options: At the same time as the follow-up test
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Misoprostol (a prostaglandin analogue causing uterine contractions) is given 24–48 hours after mifepristone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which surgical method is used for TOP up to about 14 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Vacuum aspiration (manual or electric) is used up to ~14 weeks; dilatation & evacuation (D&E) is used for later gestations, with cervical priming beforehand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: A woman has a positive urine pregnancy test 5 weeks after a medical TOP. What does this suggest?
options: Incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast — investigate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast — investigate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: A urine test can stay positive up to ~4 weeks after TOP; a positive test beyond 4 weeks suggests incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast, warranting investigation (retained products/GTD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: How is the success of a medical TOP best confirmed?
options: A multi-level/quantitative serum β-hCG test at ~2 weeks
A urine test the next day
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: A multi-level/quantitative serum β-hCG test at ~2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Success is confirmed with a follow-up pregnancy test at ~2 weeks, ideally a multi-level/quantitative (serum β-hCG) test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: A RhD-negative woman has a surgical TOP. What should she receive?
options: No anti-D as it is not needed
Anti-D only if she is over 10 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Anti-D is given to RhD-negative women having a surgical abortion, and for medical abortion after 10 weeks; it is no longer needed for early medical abortion before 10 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: What is the current provision for early medical abortion via telemedicine?
options: Both pills can be taken at home after a remote consultation (up to 9⁺⁶ weeks)
Both pills must be taken in hospital
Only mifepristone can be taken at home
It is allowed up to 24 weeks at home
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Both pills can be taken at home after a remote consultation (up to 9⁺⁶ weeks)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Since the COVID provisions became permanent in 2022, early medical abortion up to 9⁺⁶ weeks can follow a remote consultation with both mifepristone and misoprostol taken at home.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which contraceptive can be inserted immediately after a surgical TOP?
options: Only after a negative pregnancy test at 4 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: An IUD/IUS can be inserted immediately after surgical evacuation; implants/injections/pills can be started at the time of medical TOP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which is a recognised complication specific to surgical (rather than medical) TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Uterine perforation and cervical trauma are complications specific to surgical TOP; retained products, infection, haemorrhage and failed termination can occur with either method.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which assessment is recommended before a termination of pregnancy (NICE NG140)?
options: Confirm/date the pregnancy, blood group & Rhesus, FBC, and STI screening
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Confirm/date the pregnancy, blood group & Rhesus, FBC, and STI screening
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Before TOP, the pregnancy is confirmed and dated, blood group/Rhesus and FBC are checked, STI screening is done, options discussed non-judgementally, and contraception planned.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Why can reduced fetal movements be a warning sign of fetal compromise?
options: A chronically hypoxic fetus reduces movement to conserve oxygen
The fetus moves less as it grows larger
Reduced movements indicate imminent normal delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: A chronically hypoxic fetus reduces movement to conserve oxygen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: A chronically hypoxic fetus redistributes blood to vital organs and reduces movement to lower oxygen consumption, so RFM is an important (if non-specific) marker of fetal condition.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: At what gestation is quickening (first perception of fetal movements) usually felt?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Quickening is usually felt around 18–20 weeks (earlier in multiparous women).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which statement about fetal movements at the end of pregnancy is correct?
options: Movements plateau after ~32 weeks and should NOT reduce
There is a fixed normal number of movements
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Movements plateau after ~32 weeks and should NOT reduce
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Movements increase until ~32 weeks then plateau; they should not reduce at the end of pregnancy — the idea that late movements decrease is a myth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman at 30 weeks reports reduced movements. On handheld Doppler, no fetal heartbeat is heard. What is the immediate next step?
options: Send home with a kick chart
Arrange a growth scan in 2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If no fetal heartbeat is detected on handheld Doppler, an immediate ultrasound is performed to confirm viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman at 32 weeks reports reduced movements and a fetal heartbeat is confirmed. What is the next step?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: With a confirmed heartbeat, a CTG (≥20 minutes) is done to assess fetal wellbeing; ultrasound follows if concern persists or risk factors are present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: What advice should be given to a woman after 28 weeks who is worried about reduced movements?
options: Lie on the left side, focus for 2 hours; if <10 movements, contact the unit immediately
Wait until the next day and re-count
Use a home Doppler for reassurance
Increase caffeine to stimulate the baby
Only worry if movements stop completely
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Lie on the left side, focus for 2 hours; if <10 movements, contact the unit immediately
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: She should lie on her left side and focus for 2 hours; fewer than 10 movements warrants contacting the maternity unit immediately, without waiting or relying on home Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which condition is most strongly associated with reduced fetal movements as a concerning cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: FGR/SGA is a concerning cause linked with ~29% of RFM cases; anterior placenta, obesity, distraction and sedatives are benign causes of reduced perception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman reports she has never felt fetal movements by 24 weeks. What is the appropriate action?
options: Refer to a fetal medicine unit
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Refer to a fetal medicine unit
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If movements have never been felt by 24 weeks, referral to a fetal medicine unit is indicated, with the heartbeat confirmed on handheld Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: What did the AFFIRM trial demonstrate about formal fetal movement awareness packages?
options: They did not reduce stillbirth and increased inductions/caesareans
They eliminated the need for CTG
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: They did not reduce stillbirth and increased inductions/caesareans
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: The AFFIRM trial showed a formal awareness-of-movements package did not significantly reduce stillbirth and increased interventions, so routine formal kick-counting is not recommended.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman with RFM has a normal CTG and normal growth scan. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure, advising immediate re-presentation if RFM recurs
Weekly CTG for the rest of pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Reassure, advising immediate re-presentation if RFM recurs
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If investigations are normal, reassure and advise the woman to re-present immediately if RFM recurs; recurrent RFM warrants ultrasound and closer surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which is a benign cause of reduced perception of fetal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: An anterior placenta (<28 weeks) cushions movements and reduces perception; the others are concerning/pathological causes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Why is recurrent reduced fetal movements clinically important?
options: It is a risk factor warranting ultrasound and a lower threshold for delivery discussion
It confirms the baby is well
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: It is a risk factor warranting ultrasound and a lower threshold for delivery discussion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Recurrent RFM is itself a risk factor, so it warrants ultrasound, closer surveillance and a lower threshold for a delivery discussion near term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman with RFM is found to have an SGA fetus with abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. How should she be managed?
options: As fetal growth restriction — increased surveillance and timed delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: As fetal growth restriction — increased surveillance and timed delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: RFM with SGA/abnormal Doppler/abnormal liquor is managed as fetal growth restriction (RCOG Green-top 31), with increased surveillance and timed delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 30 weeks reports a gush of vaginal fluid. Speculum shows pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Rupture of membranes before labour before 37 weeks, confirmed by pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix on sterile speculum, is PPROM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which examination should be AVOIDED in suspected PPROM, and why?
options: Digital vaginal examination — it introduces infection and shortens latency
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Digital vaginal examination — it introduces infection and shortens latency
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Digital vaginal examination is avoided in PPROM as it introduces infection and shortens the latency period; a sterile speculum is used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What prophylactic antibiotic is given in PPROM?
options: Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days reduces chorioamnionitis and delays delivery in PPROM; co-amoxiclav is avoided due to neonatal NEC risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which antibiotic is contraindicated in PPROM due to a risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Co-amoxiclav is associated with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in PPROM (ORACLE trials) and is avoided; erythromycin is used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman with stable PPROM at 31 weeks has no signs of infection. What is the recommended timing of birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Current RCOG guidance favours expectant management to 37⁺⁰ weeks in stable PPROM (better outcomes than early birth); deliver early only for infection/fetal compromise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman with PPROM develops a fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, and a raised CRP. What is the appropriate management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Signs of chorioamnionitis (maternal fever/tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, raised CRP) mandate immediate delivery regardless of gestation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: If no pooling of fluid is seen on speculum in suspected PPROM, which test can confirm the diagnosis?
options: PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 on vaginal fluid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 on vaginal fluid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: If pooling is not seen, biochemical tests (PAMG-1/IGFBP-1) on vaginal fluid help confirm PPROM; ultrasound may show supportive oligohydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which intervention is NOT recommended in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM (no clear benefit and may mask infection); steroids, erythromycin, MgSO₄ and infection monitoring are used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Up to what gestation are antenatal corticosteroids offered in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids are offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks to reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC and death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which fetal complication results specifically from severe, early oligohydramnios in PPROM?
options: Pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence if very early)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence if very early)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Severe/early oligohydramnios can cause cord/limb compression and pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence if very early), alongside cord prolapse and prematurity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: When is magnesium sulphate offered in PPROM, and for what purpose?
options: 24⁺⁰-29⁺⁶ weeks for neuroprotection if birth expected within 24h
At any gestation to prevent infection
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: 24⁺⁰-29⁺⁶ weeks for neuroprotection if birth expected within 24h
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate is given for fetal neuroprotection (reducing cerebral palsy) at 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶) when birth is expected within 24 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What is the main maternal complication of PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Chorioamnionitis is the main maternal complication of PPROM (cause or consequence), along with postpartum endometritis and sepsis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 29 weeks has regular painful contractions with cervical change, and clinical assessment suggests preterm labour. What is the appropriate management?
options: Treat with corticosteroids ± tocolysis without needing further tests
Wait for a fetal fibronectin result
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Treat with corticosteroids ± tocolysis without needing further tests
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: At ≤29⁺⁶ weeks, if clinical assessment suggests preterm labour, treat with steroids ± tocolysis without requiring further diagnostic tests.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 31 weeks has suspected preterm labour with intact membranes and an uncertain diagnosis. Which test helps predict birth within 48 hours?
options: Transvaginal cervical length OR fetal fibronectin
Both cervical length and fibronectin together
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Transvaginal cervical length OR fetal fibronectin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: At ≥30 weeks, either transvaginal cervical length (>15 mm unlikely) OR fetal fibronectin (≥50 ng/mL positive) is used — but not both together.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which is the strongest risk factor for preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: A previous preterm birth (and late miscarriage) is the strongest risk factor; multiple pregnancy, PPROM, infection and cervical incompetence also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What is the first-line tocolytic for preterm labour, and its aim?
options: Nifedipine — to delay birth ~48 hours for steroids and in-utero transfer
Nifedipine — to improve neonatal outcomes long-term
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Nifedipine — to delay birth ~48 hours for steroids and in-utero transfer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Nifedipine is first-line tocolysis (26⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks, intact membranes), aiming to delay birth ~48h for corticosteroids to work and to allow in-utero transfer; it does not improve outcomes alone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Antenatal corticosteroids in preterm labour reduce which complications, and up to what gestation are they offered?
options: RDS, IVH, NEC and neonatal death; up to 34⁺⁶ weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: RDS, IVH, NEC and neonatal death; up to 34⁺⁶ weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturity, reducing RDS, IVH, NEC and neonatal death, and are offered up to 34⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Magnesium sulphate is given in preterm labour for which purpose?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate is given for fetal neuroprotection (reducing cerebral palsy) when birth is expected within 24h at 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: When should antibiotics (erythromycin) be given in preterm labour?
options: Only if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM)
In all cases of preterm labour
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Only if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Per the ORACLE trials, erythromycin is given only if membranes have ruptured (PPROM); it is not given in preterm labour with intact membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A magnesium sulphate infusion causes loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression. What is the antidote?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Magnesium toxicity (loss of reflexes → respiratory depression) is treated with IV calcium gluconate; reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output are monitored.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which complication of prematurity is caused by over-oxygenation in infants born before 32 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity results from over-oxygenation causing abnormal retinal neovascularisation, in infants born <32 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: How is preterm birth prevented in a woman with a previous preterm birth and a short cervix?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: High-risk women (previous preterm birth, short cervix) are offered vaginal progesterone and/or cervical cerclage to prevent preterm birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which respiratory complication of prematurity results from surfactant deficiency?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: RDS results from surfactant deficiency in the preterm lung; chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) can follow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A fetal fibronectin swab is planned in a woman with suspected preterm labour. When should it be taken?
options: Only if the cervix is closed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: The fetal fibronectin swab must be taken before any digital vaginal examination, as digital examination alters the result.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman bleeds 1500 mL from the genital tract 2 hours after a vaginal delivery, and her uterus feels soft and 'boggy'. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A soft, boggy uterus that won't contract indicates uterine atony (Tone) — the commonest cause of PPH (~70%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the definition of postpartum haemorrhage by blood loss?
options: ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPH is defined as blood loss ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery; major PPH is >1000 mL or any volume with shock.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the FIRST-line intervention to stop bleeding in atonic PPH?
options: Bimanual uterine massage ('rub up' the fundus) and empty the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Bimanual uterine massage ('rub up' the fundus) and empty the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Mechanical measures are first-line — 'rub up' the fundus (bimanual massage) and empty the bladder — while resuscitation and medical measures proceed in parallel.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in a woman with pre-eclampsia during PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia; carboprost is avoided in asthma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which uterotonic should be avoided in a woman with asthma during PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Carboprost (PGF2α) can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma; ergometrine is avoided in hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: According to the WOMAN trial, which drug reduces death from PPH when given early?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The WOMAN trial showed tranexamic acid 1 g IV given early (within 3 hours) reduces death from PPH, so it is given early in all significant PPH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and fever 10 days after delivery. What is the likely cause of this secondary PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Secondary PPH (24 hours to 6–12 weeks) is typically due to retained placental tissue or endometritis; treat with antibiotics ± evacuation of retained products, guided by ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is the biggest single predictor of postpartum haemorrhage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A previous PPH is the biggest single predictor; an overdistended uterus, pre-eclampsia, praevia/accreta and emergency caesarean also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which intervention at delivery reduces PPH risk for all women?
options: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic IM oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic IM oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Active third-stage management with prophylactic IM oxytocin 10 IU reduces PPH by ~60% and is used for all births, since most PPH occurs without risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: If mechanical and medical measures fail to control atonic PPH, which tamponade device is used?
options: A Foley catheter in the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: An intrauterine (Bakri) balloon provides tamponade; further options escalate to B-Lynch suture, artery ligation/embolisation, and hysterectomy as a last resort.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman who had a severe PPH later fails to lactate and has amenorrhoea. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Severe PPH causing hypovolaemic shock can cause pituitary necrosis (Sheehan's syndrome), classically with failed lactation (low prolactin) and amenorrhoea (low gonadotrophins).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which of the 4 T's refers to retained placenta or membranes as a cause of PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: 'Tissue' refers to retained placenta or membranes, which prevent effective uterine contraction; Tone is atony, Trauma is tears/rupture, Thrombin is coagulopathy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman is bleeding <500 mL after delivery with no shock, and the bleeding is settling. What is this most likely to be?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Bleeding <500 mL with no shock is likely normal lochia (postpartum discharge reducing over ~6 weeks); persistent bleeding beyond 6 weeks warrants ultrasound for retained products.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 5 days postpartum has a fever of 38.5°C, lower abdominal pain, a tender uterus and offensive lochia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia postpartum is classic endometritis — the commonest cause of puerperal pyrexia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: IV clindamycin + gentamicin is first-line for endometritis, continued until the woman is afebrile for >24 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Caesarean section is the biggest risk factor for endometritis; prolonged ROM/labour, retained products and multiple vaginal exams also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A febrile postpartum woman is hypotensive and tachycardic with a raised lactate. What is the appropriate immediate management?
options: Initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Severe sepsis requires immediate initiation of the Sepsis Six and urgent escalation (RCOG GTG64), alongside identifying and treating the source.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which organism causing genital tract sepsis is particularly virulent and rapidly progressive postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Group A Streptococcus is a highly virulent, rapidly-progressive genital-tract pathogen postpartum, warranting a low threshold for aggressive treatment and infection control.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 3 days after caesarean has a fever and erythema with discharge from her abdominal wound. What is the likely source of her puerperal pyrexia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Erythema and discharge from a caesarean wound indicate a wound infection as the source; a systematic 'where is the source?' approach is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: How long is IV treatment for endometritis typically continued?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: IV clindamycin + gentamicin is continued until the woman is afebrile for >24 hours, and oral continuation is usually not needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A febrile postpartum woman has dysuria, frequency and loin pain. Which source should be investigated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Dysuria, frequency and loin pain point to a UTI/pyelonephritis; an MSU is sent and appropriate antibiotics given.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why is clindamycin added in severe Group A streptococcal genital tract sepsis?
options: For its antitoxin effect (reducing toxin production)
Because it is the only effective antibiotic
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: For its antitoxin effect (reducing toxin production)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Clindamycin is added for its antitoxin effect against Group A Strep, alongside broad cover such as piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the traditional temperature threshold defining puerperal pyrexia, and its timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal pyrexia is traditionally a temperature ≥38°C in the first 14 days after delivery (some definitions extend across the puerperium to 6 weeks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A postpartum woman has a fever with a unilateral tender, red, swollen breast. What is the likely source?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A unilateral tender, red, swollen breast indicates mastitis as the source of the fever; it is managed with milk removal ± antibiotics.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which investigation is most appropriate if retained products of conception are suspected as a cause of postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Pelvic ultrasound is used to assess for retained products/pelvic collection; evacuation of retained products (ERPC) may be needed if tissue is driving the infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A postpartum woman has a low-grade fever with calf swelling and breathlessness. Which source must be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Calf swelling and breathlessness with a low-grade fever raise concern for VTE (DVT/PE); Doppler/CTPA and anticoagulation are considered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman develops confusion, mania, and delusions centred on her baby 8 days after delivery. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Puerperal psychosis — urgent psychiatric admission (Mother & Baby Unit)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Puerperal psychosis — urgent psychiatric admission (Mother & Baby Unit)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Rapid-onset psychosis, mania, and delusions (often about the baby) within 2–3 weeks of birth is puerperal psychosis — a psychiatric emergency requiring urgent admission, ideally to a Mother & Baby Unit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Puerperal psychosis is most strongly associated with which underlying condition?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar disorder; a personal/family history of bipolar or previous puerperal psychosis is the biggest risk factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman is tearful, anxious and irritable on day 4 postpartum, with mild labile mood. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Baby blues (~60–70%, days 3–7) is mild and self-limiting, managed with reassurance and support, not medication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which screening tool is used for postnatal depression?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The EPDS (10-item, max 30; >13 suggests likely depressive illness) is used to screen for postnatal depression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which SSRI is preferred for a breastfeeding woman with postnatal depression, and which is avoided?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Sertraline and paroxetine are preferred in breastfeeding; fluoxetine is avoided due to its long half-life causing infant accumulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the preferred setting for admitting a woman with puerperal psychosis?
options: A general adult psychiatric ward without the baby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Admission to a Mother & Baby Unit is preferred, as it keeps mother and baby together to support bonding while maintaining safety.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which pharmacological treatments are used in puerperal psychosis?
options: Antipsychotics + a mood stabiliser (lithium), ± benzodiazepines; ECT if severe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Antipsychotics + a mood stabiliser (lithium), ± benzodiazepines; ECT if severe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis is treated with antipsychotics (olanzapine/quetiapine), a mood stabiliser (lithium), short-term benzodiazepines, and ECT for severe/resistant cases or high suicide risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What must be assessed and managed urgently in a woman with puerperal psychosis?
options: Risk to the mother (suicide) and to the baby (harm/neglect)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Risk to the mother (suicide) and to the baby (harm/neglect)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Risk to the mother (suicide) and baby (harm/neglect) must be assessed and managed urgently in puerperal psychosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Previous puerperal psychosis (and a personal/family history of bipolar disorder, primiparity, and stopping psychiatric medication in pregnancy) are risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What should be ruled out when assessing a woman with suspected puerperal psychosis?
options: Organic causes such as infection, thyroid disease and medication effects
Nothing — the diagnosis is always clear
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Organic causes such as infection, thyroid disease and medication effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Organic causes (infection, thyroid disorder, medication) must be excluded when assessing suspected puerperal psychosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman has low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and guilt starting 6 weeks postpartum. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
options: Postnatal depression — CBT (± SSRI if needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Postnatal depression — CBT (± SSRI if needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Low mood, anhedonia and guilt starting within the first months is postnatal depression, managed with CBT first-line and an SSRI if needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the prognosis of puerperal psychosis with treatment?
options: Generally good, but with high recurrence in future pregnancies
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Generally good, but with high recurrence in future pregnancies
