conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: With prompt treatment most women recover fully, but recurrence in future pregnancies is high, so pre-conception counselling and a perinatal mental health plan are important.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the typical onset time of puerperal psychosis after delivery?
options: Within 2-3 weeks (often within the first few days)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Within 2-3 weeks (often within the first few days)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis typically has an abrupt onset within ~2–3 weeks of birth, often within the first few days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 3 months postpartum has palpitations, tremor and anxiety; TFTs show ↑T4 and ↓TSH. Radioiodine uptake is low. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A thyrotoxic phase within months of delivery with LOW radioiodine uptake indicates the destructive thyrotoxicosis of postpartum thyroiditis, not Graves' (which has high uptake).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: How should the thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis be managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The thyrotoxic phase is destructive release, so it is managed symptomatically with propranolol; antithyroid drugs (which block synthesis) are not used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why are antithyroid drugs (e.g. carbimazole) not used in postpartum thyroiditis?
options: The thyroid is leaking stored hormone, not overproducing it
They are ineffective against TPO antibodies
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: The thyroid is leaking stored hormone, not overproducing it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT is a destructive thyroiditis (hormone release from a damaged gland), so antithyroid drugs, which block hormone synthesis, do not address the problem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which antibodies are characteristic of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: TPO antibodies are present in ~90% of PPT and predict its development; TRAb are characteristic of Graves' disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which feature distinguishes postpartum thyroiditis from Graves' disease?
options: Low radioiodine uptake in PPT vs high uptake in Graves'
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Low radioiodine uptake in PPT vs high uptake in Graves'
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT (destructive) has LOW radioiodine uptake and TPO antibodies with no eye signs; Graves' (stimulatory) has HIGH uptake, TRAb, and may have eye disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the classic triphasic course of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The classic pattern is thyrotoxic → hypothyroid → euthyroid, though not every woman goes through all three phases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 6 months postpartum has fatigue and cold intolerance with ↓T4 and ↑TSH, in keeping with the hypothyroid phase of PPT. How is she managed if symptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The hypothyroid phase is treated with levothyroxine if symptomatic (or if trying to conceive), then tapered at ~6–12 months as it is usually transient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which follow-up is recommended after postpartum thyroiditis, and why?
options: Annual TSH monitoring, as up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Annual TSH monitoring, as up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Up to ~50% of women with PPT develop permanent hypothyroidism in later years, so annual TSH monitoring is advised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which factor increases the risk of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Type 1 diabetes, previous PPT, and a personal/family history of autoimmune thyroid disease increase the risk of postpartum thyroiditis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What predicts which women will develop postpartum thyroiditis?
options: A low free T4 in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: TPO-positivity in pregnancy predicts PPT — about 50% of TPO-positive women develop it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why is postpartum thyroiditis frequently missed?
options: Symptoms are attributed to normal postnatal fatigue/stress
It causes no symptoms at all
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Symptoms are attributed to normal postnatal fatigue/stress
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT is easily missed because its symptoms are often dismissed as normal postnatal fatigue/stress.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman with postpartum thyrotoxicosis is breastfeeding. Which treatment is safe for symptom control?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Propranolol is safe in breastfeeding and controls the adrenergic symptoms of the thyrotoxic phase; antithyroid drugs and radioiodine are not appropriate for PPT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the recurrence risk of postpartum thyroiditis in future pregnancies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Postpartum thyroiditis has a high recurrence rate (~20–70%) in future pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and cervical motion tenderness on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Pelvic inflammatory disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Bilateral lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness in a young sexually active woman is classic PID (ascending infection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the most common causative organism of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Chlamydia trachomatis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of PID (often asymptomatic/insidious); gonorrhoea causes more severe disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for PID (BASHH)?
options: IM ceftriaxone 1 g + oral doxycycline 14 days + oral metronidazole 14 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: IM ceftriaxone 1 g + oral doxycycline 14 days + oral metronidazole 14 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: First-line is IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days; fluoroquinolone regimens are now second-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why are fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin/moxifloxacin) now second-line for PID?
options: MHRA safety advice on disabling tendon, muscle, joint and neurological effects
They are contraindicated in all women
They cause fewer side effects than ceftriaxone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: MHRA safety advice on disabling tendon, muscle, joint and neurological effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Following 2019 MHRA safety advice about serious adverse effects, fluoroquinolones became second-line, with the ceftriaxone-based regimen preferred first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which investigation must always be performed in a sexually active woman with suspected PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A pregnancy test (β-hCG)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: A pregnancy test must be done to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential, before diagnosing PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman with a suspected PID has a swab microscopy showing no pus cells. What does this suggest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: PID is unlikely
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: The absence of pus cells on microscopy makes PID unlikely — a useful rule-out, though PID remains a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman develops right upper quadrant pain in the context of PID, with 'violin-string' perihepatic adhesions. What is this complication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Perihepatitis with RUQ pain and violin-string adhesions is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, a classic complication of chlamydial/gonococcal PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman with a copper IUD develops mild PID. How should the device be managed?
options: It can usually be left in situ
It must always be removed immediately
It should be replaced with a new one
It should be removed only after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It can usually be left in situ
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: In mild PID the IUD can usually be left in situ; removal is considered in severe cases or if there is no improvement within 48–72 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature would make quinolone-based PID treatment inadvisable?
options: A high likelihood of gonococcal PID
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A high likelihood of gonococcal PID
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Quinolones are avoided when gonococcal PID is likely (partner with gonorrhoea, severe disease, contact abroad) because of high quinolone resistance in gonorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which is a recognised long-term complication of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Infertility from tubal scarring
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Tubal scarring from PID causes infertility (risk rising with each episode), ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why should PID be treated empirically without waiting for swab results?
options: It is a clinical diagnosis and the complications of untreated PID are serious
It is never caused by an STI
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is a clinical diagnosis and the complications of untreated PID are serious
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: PID is a clinical diagnosis with a low treatment threshold, because a negative swab does not exclude it and delayed treatment risks serious complications (infertility, ectopic, chronic pain).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: When should a woman with PID be admitted for IV antibiotics?
options: Severe disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, or failure of/inability to tolerate oral therapy
Only if she has an IUD
Never — PID is always managed as an outpatient
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Severe disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, or failure of/inability to tolerate oral therapy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Inpatient/IV treatment is indicated for severe disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, failure of oral therapy, or inability to tolerate oral treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman treated for PID should also receive which of the following?
options: GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: PID management includes GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment, plus advice to avoid intercourse until treatment is completed and screening for other STIs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman has a thin, white, homogenous vaginal discharge with a fishy odour but no itching. The vaginal pH is 5.0. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Bacterial vaginosis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Thin, white, homogenous, fishy discharge with a raised pH and no itch is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the underlying cause of bacterial vaginosis?
options: Loss of lactobacilli with overgrowth of anaerobes (Gardnerella)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Loss of lactobacilli with overgrowth of anaerobes (Gardnerella)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV results from loss of protective lactobacilli, raising the vaginal pH and allowing anaerobic overgrowth (chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which of Amsel's criteria is a microscopy finding characteristic of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Clue cells
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Clue cells (epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria) are the microscopy hallmark of BV; pseudohyphae suggest candida and motile flagellates suggest trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How many of Amsel's four criteria are needed to diagnose BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: 3 of 4
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV is diagnosed if ≥3 of the 4 Amsel's criteria (thin discharge, pH >4.5, clue cells, positive whiff test) are present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis?
options: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days is first-line; alternatives include a 2 g single dose or topical metronidazole/clindamycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman is prescribed metronidazole for BV. What advice should she be given?
options: Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment
Take it with alcohol to improve absorption
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Metronidazole is associated with a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so patients are advised to avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Is bacterial vaginosis a sexually transmitted infection, and should partners be treated?
options: It is not an STI, and partners are not routinely treated
It is an STI, and partners must be treated
It is an STI, but partners are not treated
It is not an STI, but partners must be treated
It only occurs after sexual contact
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is not an STI, and partners are not routinely treated
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV is not an STI (it is a flora disturbance), and treating male partners does not reduce recurrence, so partners are not routinely treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which pregnancy complication is associated with bacterial vaginosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Preterm birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV in pregnancy is associated with miscarriage, preterm birth, PROM, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight and postpartum endometritis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which preventive advice reduces recurrence of BV?
options: Avoid vaginal douching and internal soaps
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid vaginal douching and internal soaps
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Avoiding douching and internal soaps/shower gels preserves the protective lactobacilli and reduces BV; recurrence is common.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A pregnant woman has symptomatic BV. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose) or topical treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose) or topical treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Symptomatic BV in pregnancy is treated (given adverse outcomes) with oral metronidazole (avoiding the high-dose single 2 g regimen) or topical treatment; metronidazole is considered low-risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why does the fishy odour of BV worsen after intercourse or menstruation?
options: Alkaline semen and blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing amines
Blood is acidic and neutralises the discharge
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Alkaline semen and blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing amines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Alkaline semen and menstrual blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing the fishy amine odour, so it is worse after sex/menstruation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature distinguishes BV from vulvovaginal candidiasis?
options: BV has minimal itch with thin fishy discharge; candida has prominent itch with thick curdy discharge
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: BV has minimal itch with thin fishy discharge; candida has prominent itch with thick curdy discharge
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV causes a thin, fishy, homogenous discharge with minimal itch and a raised pH, whereas candida causes a thick, curdy, intensely itchy discharge with a normal pH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which increased risk is associated with BV due to the raised vaginal pH and loss of protection?
options: Acquiring sexually transmitted infections including HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Acquiring sexually transmitted infections including HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: The raised pH and loss of lactobacilli in BV increase the risk of acquiring STIs, including HIV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman has a frothy, yellow-green, offensive vaginal discharge with vulval itching and dysuria. Examination shows punctate cervical haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Trichomoniasis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Frothy yellow-green offensive discharge with itch and a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical haemorrhages) is classic trichomoniasis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What type of organism causes trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A flagellated protozoan parasite
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile, flagellated protozoan parasite — a sexually transmitted infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature most distinguishes trichomoniasis from bacterial vaginosis in management?
options: It is an STI, so partners must be treated and contact-traced
It has a normal vaginal pH
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is an STI, so partners must be treated and contact-traced
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Both raise vaginal pH and can smell fishy, but trichomonas is an STI requiring partner treatment/contact tracing, whereas BV is a flora disturbance where partners are not treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line treatment for trichomoniasis?
options: Oral metronidazole 400-500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole 400-500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole 400–500 mg BD for 5–7 days is first-line; a 2 g single dose is an alternative but less favoured (and avoided in pregnancy).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How is trichomoniasis best diagnosed in a woman?
options: Charcoal swab from the posterior fornix for microscopy, or NAAT
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Charcoal swab from the posterior fornix for microscopy, or NAAT
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: A charcoal swab from the posterior fornix shows motile trophozoites on microscopy; NAAT is the most sensitive test. A Pap smear is not diagnostic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why is a Pap smear not relied upon to diagnose trichomoniasis?
options: It gives false positives/negatives and is not a diagnostic test
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It gives false positives/negatives and is not a diagnostic test
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas may be an incidental Pap finding, but the Pap is not diagnostic (false positives/negatives), so a proper test is needed to confirm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A man's partner is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. He is asymptomatic. What is the appropriate management?
options: Treat him and arrange contact tracing (it is an STI)
No treatment, as he is asymptomatic
Treat only if he develops symptoms
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Treat him and arrange contact tracing (it is an STI)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas is an STI, so partners are treated and contact-traced regardless of symptoms (men are often asymptomatic but can transmit it).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which pregnancy complication is associated with trichomoniasis?
options: Preterm birth and low birth weight
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Preterm birth and low birth weight
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight; it also increases HIV transmission risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How should trichomoniasis be treated in pregnancy?
options: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose); topical gel is ineffective
A single 2 g metronidazole dose preferred
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose); topical gel is ineffective
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole is used in pregnancy (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen); topical/gel treatment is not effective for trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which vaginal pH finding is typical of trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: >4.5 (raised)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomoniasis (like BV) raises the vaginal pH above 4.5; candida has a normal pH (<4.5).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. What additional step is recommended?
options: Screen for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Screen for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Co-infection is common, so screening for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV) is recommended, along with partner treatment and GUM referral.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which advice accompanies metronidazole treatment for trichomoniasis?
options: Avoid alcohol during and shortly after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid alcohol during and shortly after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so alcohol should be avoided during and shortly after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the significance of asymptomatic trichomonas infection?
options: Asymptomatic carriers (up to ~50%, often men) act as a reservoir for transmission
It means no treatment is needed
It is not a true infection
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Asymptomatic carriers (up to ~50%, often men) act as a reservoir for transmission
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Up to ~50% of infections are asymptomatic (men usually), forming a reservoir for ongoing transmission, which is why partner treatment/contact tracing matter.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A 24-year-old with a known 5 cm ovarian cyst presents with sudden severe right pelvic pain and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting in a woman with an ovarian cyst is ovarian torsion until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which investigation must always be performed first in a woman with suspected ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: A pregnancy test is always done first to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: An ultrasound in a woman with severe pelvic pain shows normal Doppler flow to the ovary. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal Doppler does NOT exclude ovarian torsion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: Normal Doppler does NOT exclude ovarian torsion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Venous obstruction precedes arterial compromise in torsion, so Doppler flow may be normal/present in up to ~50% of cases; normal Doppler does not exclude torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which structures does the ovary twist around in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: The ovary twists on the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament (carrying the vessels) and the utero-ovarian ligament.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: At laparoscopy, a torted premenopausal ovary looks blue-black and ischaemic. What is the preferred management?
options: Detorsion and conservation of the ovary
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: Detorsion and conservation of the ovary
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Ovarian conservation with detorsion is preferred in premenopausal women even if the ovary looks ischaemic, as visual viability assessment is unreliable and blackened ovaries often recover.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which ultrasound finding is characteristic of ovarian torsion?
options: An enlarged, oedematous ovary with a whirlpool sign
A gestational sac in the tube
A normal-sized ovary with brisk flow
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: An enlarged, oedematous ovary with a whirlpool sign
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Torsion shows an enlarged, oedematous ovary, peripherally displaced follicles ('string of pearls'), a whirlpool sign (twisted pedicle) and free fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which group characteristically torses a NORMAL (non-enlarged) ovary?
options: Pregnant women with corpus luteum cysts
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Prepubertal girls, with long ovarian ligaments and mobile ovaries, can torse a normal ovary; adults usually torse an enlarged/abnormal ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for ovarian torsion?
options: An ovarian cyst or mass (especially a dermoid, ~5 cm+)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: An ovarian cyst or mass (especially a dermoid, ~5 cm+)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: An ovarian cyst/mass (especially dermoid cysts and cysts ~5 cm or larger) is the biggest risk factor, acting as a lever point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: When is oophorectomy indicated in ovarian torsion?
options: A frankly necrotic ovary or a suspicious mass (?malignancy), especially postmenopausal
Any torted ovary in a young woman
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: A frankly necrotic ovary or a suspicious mass (?malignancy), especially postmenopausal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Oophorectomy is reserved for a truly necrotic/non-viable ovary or a suspicious mass (possible malignancy), particularly in postmenopausal women; otherwise the ovary is conserved.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A woman with equivocal ultrasound findings has a high clinical suspicion of ovarian torsion. What is the appropriate next step?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: If clinical suspicion is high despite equivocal imaging, diagnostic laparoscopy is undertaken, as the definitive diagnosis is made at surgery and delay risks ovarian loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which procedure may be added to prevent recurrence in torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Oophoropexy (fixing the ovary) is used for recurrent torsion or torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments; cystectomy addresses an underlying cyst.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Why does delayed diagnosis of ovarian torsion matter?
options: It leads to ovarian infarction and loss of ovarian tissue with fertility consequences
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: It leads to ovarian infarction and loss of ovarian tissue with fertility consequences
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Delayed detorsion allows progression from venous congestion to arterial ischaemia and infarction, causing loss of ovarian tissue and fertility consequences — so timing is critical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A pregnant woman with ovulation-induced enlarged ovaries develops sudden unilateral pelvic pain. Besides OHSS, which complication must be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Enlarged ovaries (from OHSS/ovulation induction or pregnancy) are prone to torsion; sudden unilateral pelvic pain should prompt consideration of ovarian torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: How many antenatal appointments are recommended for an uncomplicated nulliparous pregnancy (NICE NG201)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: NICE NG201 recommends 10 appointments for nulliparous women and 7 for parous women in uncomplicated pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At what gestation is the fetal anomaly scan performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The anomaly scan is done at 18–20⁺⁶ weeks; the dating scan is at 10–13⁺⁶ weeks and the combined test at 11–13⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which test was removed from the booking blood panel in 2016?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Rubella screening was removed from the booking bloods in 2016; HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening continue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman with epilepsy taking antiepileptic drugs is planning pregnancy. What dose of folic acid should she take?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: High-dose (5 mg) folic acid is recommended for women with epilepsy on antiepileptics (and obesity, NTD history, diabetes, coeliac, thalassaemia trait); the standard dose is 400 micrograms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What vitamin D dose is recommended for all pregnant women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: All pregnant women are advised to take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily (note the unit is micrograms).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Why should pregnant women avoid liver and high-dose vitamin A?
options: Vitamin A is teratogenic in high doses
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Vitamin A is teratogenic in high doses
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: High-dose vitamin A (>700 mcg) is teratogenic, and liver is very high in vitamin A, so both are avoided in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: When are the two antenatal anti-D doses given to a RhD-negative woman?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks (or as a single dose), plus postnatally if the baby is RhD-positive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At which appointment is presentation checked and ECV offered if the baby is breech?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Presentation is checked at 36 weeks, and ECV is offered if the baby is breech.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman at 30 weeks has a new BP of 150/95. What is the appropriate action?
options: Start labetalol at home without referral
Ignore, as BP always rises in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: New BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks warrants referral within 24 hours; ≥160/110 needs same-day assessment. (BP normally falls in the first half of pregnancy.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What does the combined test screen for, and what does it include?
options: Down syndrome — nuchal translucency, βhCG and PAPP-A
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Down syndrome — nuchal translucency, βhCG and PAPP-A
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The combined test (11–13⁺⁶ weeks) screens for Down syndrome using nuchal translucency, βhCG and PAPP-A.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which supplement is NOT routinely offered to all pregnant women?
options: (All of folic acid and vitamin D are routine)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Iron is not routinely offered — only if the woman is anaemic; folic acid (to 12 weeks) and vitamin D are recommended for all.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: From what gestation is symphysis-fundal height measured and plotted?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Symphysis-fundal height is plotted from 24–28 weeks to monitor growth; a small measurement prompts a growth scan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: How is the onset of labour diagnosed?
options: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change
Irregular contractions with no cervical change
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Labour is diagnosed by regular painful uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change (effacement and dilatation), distinguishing it from Braxton Hicks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A term woman has irregular contractions every 20 minutes with no cervical change and is otherwise well. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure and send home (Braxton Hicks/false labour)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Reassure and send home (Braxton Hicks/false labour)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Irregular contractions without progressive cervical change are Braxton Hicks/false labour; a term, well woman can be reassured and sent home.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: The first stage of labour extends from onset to which point?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The first stage runs from onset to full dilatation (10 cm), with a latent phase up to ~4 cm and an active phase from ~4 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which management of the third stage of labour reduces postpartum haemorrhage (NICE NG235)?
options: Active management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Active management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Active third-stage management (a prophylactic uterotonic such as IM oxytocin plus controlled cord traction and delayed cord clamping) reduces PPH risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which is the correct order of the first three cardinal movements of labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The cardinal movements begin engagement → descent → flexion, then internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which is the commonest, and correctable, cause of failure to progress in labour?
options: Power (inadequate uterine contractions) — corrected with oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Power (inadequate uterine contractions) — corrected with oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Inadequate contractions ('Power') are the commonest cause of failure to progress and can be corrected with oxytocin; Passage and Passenger are the other two P's.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What is used to graphically monitor progress in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: A partogram graphically records cervical dilatation vs time, contractions, fetal heart and maternal observations, flagging when progress crosses the alert/action line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: In a low-risk labour, how is the fetal heart monitored?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Low-risk labour uses intermittent auscultation; continuous CTG is used if there are risk factors or concerns.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At approximately what rate does the cervix dilate in the active first stage of labour?
options: It does not dilate in the active phase
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: In the active first stage the cervix dilates approximately 0.5–1 cm per hour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: During which stage of labour do the cardinal movements (mechanism of labour) occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The mechanism of labour (cardinal movements) occurs during the second stage, from full dilatation to delivery of the baby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which analgesic option is the strongest listed for labour pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Analgesia in labour escalates from non-pharmacological measures to Entonox to epidural, the last being the strongest.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A 'show' during pregnancy refers to which of the following?
options: Passage of the blood-stained mucus plug
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Passage of the blood-stained mucus plug
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: A 'show' is passage of the blood-stained cervical mucus plug, one of the signs associated with the onset of labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which factor primarily determines the risk profile and management of a twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Chorionicity — not zygosity — determines management, because it decides whether the twins share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A first-trimester ultrasound shows a lambda (λ)/'twin peak' sign at the membrane junction. What does this indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: The lambda/twin peak sign (thick membrane with a wedge of placenta) indicates a dichorionic pregnancy; the T-sign indicates monochorionic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which twin type carries the highest risk due to cord entanglement, and how is it delivered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: MCMA twins (one placenta, one sac) are at highest risk from cord entanglement and are delivered by caesarean at 32+0 to 33+6 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A monochorionic twin pregnancy develops one twin with oligohydramnios and growth restriction and the other with polyhydramnios and polycythaemia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Unbalanced blood flow across placental anastomoses causes TTTS — the donor (oligohydramnios, anaemic, growth-restricted) and recipient (polyhydramnios, polycythaemic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: How is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome treated?
options: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the communicating placental vessels
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the communicating placental vessels
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: TTTS is treated with fetoscopic laser ablation of the shared communicating placental vessels.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which surveillance schedule is recommended for a monochorionic twin pregnancy?
options: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Monochorionic twins need fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks (amniotic fluid/Doppler) to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR; dichorionic twins are scanned less intensively (~4-weekly).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: What is the planned timing of birth for an uncomplicated DCDA twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Uncomplicated DCDA twins are delivered at 37+0 weeks; MCDA at 36+0 weeks; MCMA at 32+0 to 33+6 weeks by caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which is the dominant fetal risk in twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Preterm birth is the dominant risk — about 60% of twins deliver before 37 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A twin pregnancy is in labour with twin 1 in a cephalic presentation. What mode of delivery can be offered?
options: Vaginal birth (with 2 obstetricians, continuous CTG, epidural advised)
Forceps delivery of both without monitoring
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Vaginal birth (with 2 obstetricians, continuous CTG, epidural advised)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: If twin 1 is cephalic, vaginal birth can be offered with 2 obstetricians present, continuous CTG and epidural often advised; caesarean is for non-cephalic twin 1 or MCMA.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which statement about zygosity and chorionicity is correct?
options: All dizygotic twins are DCDA; monozygotic twins can be DCDA, MCDA or MCMA
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: All dizygotic twins are DCDA; monozygotic twins can be DCDA, MCDA or MCMA
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Dizygotic twins are always DCDA; monozygotic twins can be any chorionicity depending on the timing of the split.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which prophylactic medication is offered in twin pregnancy to reduce pre-eclampsia risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Multiple pregnancy is a moderate risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so aspirin prophylaxis is offered; iron and folate are also given for increased demand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Why is prophylactic oxytocin given at delivery of twins?
options: The overdistended uterus has a high PPH risk from atony
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: The overdistended uterus has a high PPH risk from atony
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Uterine overdistension in twin pregnancy predisposes to atony and PPH, so active third-stage management with prophylactic oxytocin is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A first-trimester scan shows a T-sign at the inter-twin membrane. What does this indicate, and what surveillance is needed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: A T-sign indicates a monochorionic pregnancy (shared placenta), requiring fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is heavy menstrual bleeding defined in current practice?
options: Menstrual loss that interferes with quality of life (impact-based)
Blood loss of ≥80 mL per cycle
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Menstrual loss that interferes with quality of life (impact-based)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: HMB is defined by its impact on quality of life, not a millilitre threshold; the old ≥80 mL figure and the term 'DUB' are obsolete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with HMB has a bulky, irregular, non-tender uterus. Which PALM-COEIN cause is most likely?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A bulky, irregular ('knobbly') uterus suggests fibroids (Leiomyoma); a tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus would suggest adenomyosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which blood test should be performed for all women presenting with HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A full blood count is done for all women with HMB (to detect anaemia); ferritin, hormones and TFTs are not routine, and coagulation testing only if the history suggests it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 16-year-old has had heavy periods since menarche and bruises easily. Which investigation is indicated?
options: Coagulation testing (e.g. for von Willebrand disease)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Coagulation testing (e.g. for von Willebrand disease)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: HMB since menarche with a bleeding history suggests a coagulopathy such as von Willebrand disease, warranting coagulation testing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the first-line treatment for HMB with no structural pathology, in a woman who accepts long-term treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The LNG-IUS is first-line for HMB (NICE NG88), being the most effective medical option, when there is no pathology (or fibroids <3 cm not distorting the cavity, or adenomyosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with HMB does not want contraception and has no dysmenorrhoea. Which non-hormonal treatment is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic with no cycle effect) is appropriate when contraception is not wanted; NSAIDs are used if dysmenorrhoea co-exists.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with HMB and painful periods does not want contraception. Which non-hormonal option reduces both bleeding and pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid reduce both menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhoea, making them a good choice when pain co-exists and contraception is not wanted.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which symptom in a woman with HMB should prompt exclusion of endometrial malignancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Intermenstrual, postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding (especially persistent) should prompt hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy to exclude malignancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which classification system is used to categorise the causes of HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PALM-COEIN classifies HMB causes into structural (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy) and non-structural (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not-classified).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 48-year-old woman with HMB has completed her family and failed medical treatment. Which definitive surgical option may be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: When medical treatment fails and the family is complete, endometrial ablation or hysterectomy (definitive) are options; fertility-sparing options are reserved for those wanting future fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which test is NOT routinely recommended in the assessment of HMB?
options: Coagulation testing if the history suggests it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Serum ferritin, routine female-hormone testing and routine TFTs are not recommended; FBC is done for all, and targeted tests are guided by the history.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is endometrial ablation contraindicated in a woman wanting future pregnancy?
options: It destroys the endometrium and is only used when the family is complete
It increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy
It is ineffective in young women
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It destroys the endometrium and is only used when the family is complete
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Endometrial ablation destroys the endometrium, so it is reserved for women who have completed their family and is not used if future fertility is desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with HMB has a tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus and dysmenorrhoea. Which PALM-COEIN cause is most likely?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus with dysmenorrhoea suggests adenomyosis; a knobbly irregular uterus would suggest fibroids.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 15-year-old has crampy lower abdominal pain starting with her period, beginning about 8 months after menarche, with a normal examination. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Pain with the period starting 6–12 months after menarche with a normal exam is primary dysmenorrhoea; NSAIDs (prostaglandin inhibitors) are first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 32-year-old develops progressively worsening period pain that starts days before her period and is associated with deep dyspareunia and subfertility. What type of dysmenorrhoea is this, and the likely cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Older onset, pain preceding the period, deep dyspareunia and subfertility indicate secondary dysmenorrhoea, classically due to endometriosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why are NSAIDs effective and first-line for primary dysmenorrhoea?
options: They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing myometrial contractions
They increase uterine blood flow directly
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing myometrial contractions
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Primary dysmenorrhoea is prostaglandin-driven, so NSAIDs (prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors) reduce contractions and pain and are first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which NSAID is now less favoured for dysmenorrhoea, and why?
options: Mefenamic acid — narrow therapeutic window and seizure risk in overdose
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Mefenamic acid — narrow therapeutic window and seizure risk in overdose
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Mefenamic acid is less favoured (no better efficacy, narrow therapeutic window, higher seizure risk in overdose); ibuprofen/naproxen are preferred.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with dysmenorrhoea fails to respond to NSAIDs and the combined pill. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Suspect a secondary cause (e.g. endometriosis) and investigate/refer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Suspect a secondary cause (e.g. endometriosis) and investigate/refer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Failure to respond to NSAIDs plus hormonal contraception should prompt suspicion of a secondary cause (especially endometriosis) and investigation/referral.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 22-year-old presents with new-onset pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and vaginal discharge. Which diagnosis must be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: New-onset pelvic pain with discharge in an under-25-year-old should prompt consideration of PID/chlamydia, with STI screening and swabs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the second-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea if NSAIDs are insufficient?
options: Hormonal treatment (e.g. combined oral contraceptive pill)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Hormonal treatment (e.g. combined oral contraceptive pill)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: If NSAIDs are insufficient, hormonal treatment (COCP, or LNG-IUS/progestogen) is second-line; NSAIDs and hormonal treatment can be combined.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which finding on examination would suggest secondary rather than primary dysmenorrhoea?
options: A fixed, retroverted uterus with adnexal tenderness
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A fixed, retroverted uterus with adnexal tenderness
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A fixed/retroverted uterus, pelvic mass, or adnexal tenderness suggests secondary dysmenorrhoea (e.g. endometriosis/adenomyosis); primary dysmenorrhoea has a normal exam.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which investigation is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis in secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Laparoscopy is the gold standard for endometriosis, though empirical medical treatment is supported before it; TVUS detects fibroids/adenomyosis/endometriomas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with a copper IUD develops worsening dysmenorrhoea. What is a reasonable management step?
options: Consider removal of the copper coil or an alternative
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Consider removal of the copper coil or an alternative
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The copper IUD is an iatrogenic (secondary) cause of dysmenorrhoea; considering its removal or an alternative contraceptive is reasonable if it is contributing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which non-drug measure can help primary dysmenorrhoea?
options: Bed rest for the whole period
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Local heat, TENS and gentle exercise are helpful non-drug measures for primary dysmenorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the characteristic timing of pain in primary dysmenorrhoea?
options: With or just before the period, lasting 1-3 days
Days before and after the period
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: With or just before the period, lasting 1-3 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Primary dysmenorrhoea causes pain with or just before the period, lasting 1–3 days; pain that precedes and outlasts the period suggests a secondary cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 28-year-old with secondary dysmenorrhoea is found to have a tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus and heavy periods. Which cause is most likely?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus with heavy menstrual bleeding suggests adenomyosis as the secondary cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 25-year-old with previously regular periods has had no menstruation for 5 months. What is the first investigation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Pregnancy must always be excluded first in secondary amenorrhoea before other investigations.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 16-year-old has never menstruated but has normal secondary sexual characteristics. At what age is primary amenorrhoea defined in this situation?
options: No period by age 15 (with normal secondary sexual characteristics)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: No period by age 15 (with normal secondary sexual characteristics)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Primary amenorrhoea is defined as no period by 15 with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A young woman with amenorrhoea, short stature and streak ovaries has a high FSH/LH. What is the likely diagnosis, and confirmatory test?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: High FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic) with short stature and streak ovaries suggests Turner syndrome/gonadal dysgenesis; a karyotype confirms it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A low-weight competitive runner has secondary amenorrhoea with low FSH and LH. What is the mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (low weight/over-exercise/stress) reduces GnRH, giving low FSH/LH (hypogonadotropic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is the commonest pathological cause of secondary amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PCOS is the commonest pathological cause of secondary amenorrhoea; pregnancy/lactation/menopause are excluded first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman has secondary amenorrhoea and a raised prolactin. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Repeat prolactin, and if persistently raised arrange a pituitary MRI
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Repeat prolactin, and if persistently raised arrange a pituitary MRI
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Prolactin is repeated (stress/food falsely raise it); if persistently raised, a pituitary MRI is arranged to look for a prolactinoma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman develops amenorrhoea and difficulty breastfeeding after a severe postpartum haemorrhage. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Sheehan's syndrome is pituitary necrosis after PPH, causing hypopituitarism (including amenorrhoea and failure of lactation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman develops amenorrhoea after a dilatation and curettage. What is the likely cause and treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Intrauterine adhesions after a D&C (Asherman's syndrome) cause amenorrhoea and are treated with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A hormone panel shows raised testosterone and a raised LH:FSH ratio in a woman with amenorrhoea and hirsutism. What is the likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Raised testosterone and a raised LH:FSH ratio with hirsutism and amenorrhoea suggest PCOS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with premature ovarian insufficiency has amenorrhoea. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: HRT (to maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: HRT (to maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: POI (and gonadal dysgenesis) is managed with HRT to develop/maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with hyperprolactinaemia causing amenorrhoea is to be treated. Which drug is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Hyperprolactinaemia is treated with a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline or bromocriptine, which lowers prolactin and can restore menses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: An adolescent has primary amenorrhoea with normal secondary sexual characteristics and cyclical lower abdominal pain but no menstrual flow. Which cause should be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Cyclical pain without menstrual flow and normal secondary sexual characteristics suggests an outflow obstruction such as an imperforate hymen, managed surgically.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: In amenorrhoea, what does a LOW FSH/LH pattern localise the problem to?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Low FSH/LH (hypogonadotropic) localises the problem to the hypothalamus/pituitary (e.g. stress, low weight, Sheehan's, prolactinoma); high FSH/LH points to an ovarian cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman reports irritability, bloating and breast tenderness in the 10 days before her period each month, resolving when menstruation starts, with a symptom-free week afterwards. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Cyclical luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menstruation and a symptom-free interval are characteristic of PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is a diagnosis of PMS best confirmed?
options: A prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles (e.g. DRSP)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles (e.g. DRSP)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PMS is confirmed with a prospective symptom diary (DRSP) over 2 cycles showing symptoms confined to the luteal phase; retrospective recall over-diagnoses it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman's mood symptoms are present throughout the whole cycle with no symptom-free interval. What does this suggest?
options: A primary mood disorder rather than PMS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A primary mood disorder rather than PMS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PMS is defined by luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menstruation; symptoms present throughout the cycle indicate a primary mood disorder, not PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is a recognised first-line treatment for moderate-severe PMS/PMDD?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: SSRIs (citalopram/escitalopram), given continuously or only in the luteal phase, are first-line for moderate-severe PMS/PMDD, alongside lifestyle/CBT and a drospirenone COCP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is distinctive about SSRI use in PMS compared with depression?
options: They can be given only in the luteal phase and have a rapid onset
They must be given for years
They must be combined with lithium
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: They can be given only in the luteal phase and have a rapid onset
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: In PMS, SSRIs have a rapid onset and can be given luteal-phase only (not just continuously), which is distinctive compared with their use in depression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which combined pill is recommended first-line to suppress ovulation in PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A continuous drospirenone-containing COCP is a first-line option to suppress ovulation in PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with severe, treatment-resistant PMS is started on a GnRH analogue. What must accompany this?
options: Add-back HRT to protect bone and cardiovascular health
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Add-back HRT to protect bone and cardiovascular health
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: GnRH analogues cause a hypo-oestrogenic state, so add-back HRT is needed to protect bone and cardiovascular health; they are third-line for severe/resistant PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the underlying cause of PMS symptoms?
options: Over-response to normal cyclical ovarian hormone changes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Over-response to normal cyclical ovarian hormone changes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PMS results from susceptibility to normal cyclical hormone changes (not abnormal levels), which is why suppressing ovulation or modulating serotonin both help.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)?
options: The severe, predominantly affective form of PMS — a formal psychiatric diagnosis
A type of depression unrelated to the cycle
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: The severe, predominantly affective form of PMS — a formal psychiatric diagnosis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PMDD is the severe, predominantly mood-based form of PMS and is a formal psychiatric diagnosis (DSM-5/ICD-11).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When the diagnosis of PMS is uncertain, which trial can help confirm it is ovulation-driven?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A 3-month GnRH-analogue trial switches off ovarian hormones; symptom resolution confirms the symptoms are ovulation-driven (PMS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which last-resort treatment removes ovarian cycling in the most severe, resistant PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (± HRT) removes ovarian cycling and is the fourth-line/last-resort option for the most severe, resistant PMS when the family is complete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which additional agent may help the bloating and breast tenderness of PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Spironolactone can help the bloating and breast tenderness of PMS; vitamin B6 has some evidence, and CBT is used throughout.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: The PMS treatment ladder works through which two mechanistic levers?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The ladder either suppresses ovulation (COCP → GnRH → surgery) or modulates serotonin (SSRIs) — the two mechanistic levers reflecting PMS's cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 48-year-old woman has 14 months of amenorrhoea with hot flushes and night sweats. How is menopause diagnosed?
options: Clinically — no blood tests are needed
FSH on two samples 6 weeks apart
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Clinically — no blood tests are needed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: For a woman ≥45 with typical symptoms, menopause is diagnosed clinically without blood tests, as FSH fluctuates and does not change management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 35-year-old woman has amenorrhoea and hot flushes. What is required to diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency?
options: An elevated FSH on two samples 4-6 weeks apart
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: An elevated FSH on two samples 4-6 weeks apart
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: POI (menopause <40) requires an elevated FSH (>30) on two samples 4–6 weeks apart, plus symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with POI. What is the recommended management regarding sex-steroid replacement?
options: Offer HRT or the COCP until at least ~51
No hormone treatment, as she is young
HRT only if she has severe symptoms
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Offer HRT or the COCP until at least ~51
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: POI warrants sex-steroid replacement (HRT or COCP) until ~51 to replace the missing oestrogen and protect bone and cardiovascular health; the older-woman HRT-risk narrative does not apply.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with an intact uterus needs HRT for menopausal symptoms. What type should she be given?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: With a uterus present, combined HRT is used — the progestogen protects the endometrium against unopposed oestrogen (hyperplasia/cancer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman who has had a hysterectomy needs HRT. What is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Without a uterus there is no endometrium to protect, so oestrogen-only HRT is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A menopausal woman has a BMI of 34 and a family history of VTE. Which HRT route is preferred, and why?
options: Transdermal — it does not raise VTE risk
Oral — it has no first-pass effect
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Transdermal — it does not raise VTE risk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first-pass metabolism and does not raise VTE risk, so it is preferred in women with VTE risk or BMI >30 (oral oestrogen raises VTE risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which statement about HRT and breast cancer is correct?
options: Combined HRT gives a small, duration-related increase that falls after stopping
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Combined HRT gives a small, duration-related increase that falls after stopping
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Combined HRT carries a small, duration-related increase in breast cancer risk that falls after stopping; oestrogen-only HRT carries little/no increase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Should HRT be prescribed to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia?
options: No — HRT is for symptoms and bone protection, not CVD/dementia prevention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: No — HRT is for symptoms and bone protection, not CVD/dementia prevention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The 2024 NICE guidance states HRT should not be offered for prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia; it is used for symptom relief and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with POI on HRT asks about contraception. What is the correct advice?
options: She still needs contraception, as HRT is not contraceptive and she may occasionally ovulate
She cannot conceive, so no contraception is needed
She should use HRT as emergency contraception
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: She still needs contraception, as HRT is not contraceptive and she may occasionally ovulate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Women with POI may occasionally ovulate and conceive; HRT is not contraceptive (the COCP is), so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is to be avoided.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which non-hormonal intervention is now recommended for vasomotor symptoms and low mood (2024 NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: CBT is recommended for vasomotor symptoms and low mood; SSRIs/SNRIs may be used cautiously for flushes, and topical vaginal oestrogen for GSM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which biochemical change is characteristic of the menopause?
options: Raised FSH (and LH) with low oestrogen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Raised FSH (and LH) with low oestrogen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Follicle depletion lowers oestrogen, removing negative feedback, so FSH (and LH) rise — a raised FSH with low oestrogen is characteristic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 30-year-old develops POI after chemotherapy. Which cause category does this represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Chemotherapy/radiotherapy/oophorectomy cause iatrogenic POI; other causes include idiopathic (commonest), autoimmune and genetic (Turner, Fragile X).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: For genitourinary symptoms of menopause (vaginal dryness, recurrent UTIs), what is the preferred safe long-term treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Topical vaginal oestrogen (± moisturisers/lubricants) is safe and effective long-term for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, with minimal systemic absorption.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A couple has failed to conceive after 12 months of regular intercourse. What is the appropriate initial investigation of the male partner?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Semen analysis is the core first-line test for the male partner; if abnormal it is repeated at ~3 months (spermatogenesis takes ~74 days).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is ovulation confirmed in a woman with a regular 28-day cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A mid-luteal progesterone (day 21 of a 28-day cycle, i.e. 7 days before the expected period) confirms ovulation when raised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is the first-line test for tubal patency in a woman with no suspected pelvic pathology?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: HSG is first-line for tubal patency (HyCoSy is an alternative); laparoscopy + dye is used when pelvic pathology is suspected. Chlamydia is screened before instrumentation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A 38-year-old woman and her partner have been trying to conceive for 8 months. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Wait until 12 months before any action
Reassure with no investigation for 2 years
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Investigation/referral is undertaken earlier (before 1 year) if the woman is ≥36, there is a known cause, or a predisposing history — because age is the dominant prognostic factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with PCOS and anovulation wishes to conceive. Which is an appropriate first-line ovulation-induction agent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: For PCOS anovulation, letrozole (increasingly first-line) or clomifene (± metformin) is used for ovulation induction; gonadotrophins are reserved for when oral agents fail.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A couple has unexplained infertility with all tests normal after 2 years. What is the appropriate management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: For unexplained infertility, clomifene/letrozole offer no benefit; couples continue regular intercourse and are offered IVF after 2 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A couple has severe male-factor subfertility (very low sperm count). Which assisted reproduction technique is most appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Severe male-factor subfertility is treated with ICSI (a single sperm injected into the egg); mild male factor may be managed with IUI/IVF.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is the leading cause of tubal-factor subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Chlamydia-related PID is the leading cause of tubal-factor subfertility; chlamydia screening is done before instrumentation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which WHO semen analysis value is within the normal reference range?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: WHO reference values include concentration ≥15 million/mL, motility ≥40%, normal forms ≥4%, and volume ≥1.5 mL; 20 million/mL is normal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with significant bilateral tubal damage wishes to conceive. What is often the preferred treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: IVF bypasses the tubes and is often preferred for significant tubal damage; tubal surgery may be considered for mild disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is a semen analysis repeated after ~3 months if the first is abnormal?
options: Spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so a repeat reflects a new cycle of sperm production
Because the first test is always wrong
To confirm the woman is ovulating
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so a repeat reflects a new cycle of sperm production
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so an abnormal semen analysis is repeated at ~3 months to assess a fresh cycle of sperm production.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which preconception advice is appropriate for a couple trying to conceive?
options: Folic acid, stop smoking, optimise BMI, intercourse every 2-3 days
Intercourse only on the day of ovulation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Folic acid, stop smoking, optimise BMI, intercourse every 2-3 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Preconception advice includes folic acid, stopping smoking/alcohol, optimising BMI (~19–30), and having intercourse every 2–3 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman has irregular cycles suggesting an ovulatory disorder. Which blood tests help identify the cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: With irregular cycles, day 2–5 FSH/LH, prolactin, TSH and testosterone (for PCOS) help identify the cause; a day-21 progesterone is used to confirm ovulation in regular cycles.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman develops abdominal distension, ascites and breathlessness 6 days after an IVF hCG trigger, with a haematocrit of 48% and oliguria. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Ascites, oliguria and haemoconcentration (haematocrit >45%) days after an hCG trigger indicate severe OHSS; torsion/rupture/ectopic must be excluded.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the underlying mechanism of OHSS?
options: hCG stimulates VEGF release, increasing vascular permeability and causing third-space fluid shift
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: hCG stimulates VEGF release, increasing vascular permeability and causing third-space fluid shift
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: hCG (trigger or endogenous) drives VEGF release, increasing vascular permeability so fluid leaks into the third space — causing ascites, hypovolaemia and haemoconcentration.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why does pregnancy worsen OHSS?
options: Endogenous hCG keeps the ovaries stimulated, causing more severe late OHSS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Endogenous hCG keeps the ovaries stimulated, causing more severe late OHSS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: OHSS is hCG-driven, so the endogenous hCG of an early pregnancy prolongs ovarian stimulation, producing more severe 'late' OHSS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is the most important complication to prevent in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: OHSS is strongly prothrombotic (haemoconcentration) and can kill via thrombosis — including at unusual sites — so VTE prophylaxis is essential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which woman is at highest risk of OHSS?
options: A young woman with PCOS and a high AMH
An older woman with a low antral follicle count
A woman with a high BMI and poor ovarian response
A woman not undergoing fertility treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A young woman with PCOS and a high AMH
