conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: PCOS, young age, low BMI and a high AMH/antral follicle count (a strong ovarian response) are key risk factors for OHSS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with severe OHSS has tense, painful ascites and breathlessness. Which intervention is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Paracentesis relieves tense/symptomatic ascites, improving pain, breathing and renal perfusion; surgery is reserved for torsion/rupture/ectopic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which analgesic should be avoided in OHSS with renal compromise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: NSAIDs are avoided if there is renal compromise in OHSS; paracetamol ± codeine is used for pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which measure helps prevent OHSS in high-risk women undergoing IVF?
options: Using a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG (± freeze-all embryos, cabergoline)
Immediate pregnancy in the same cycle
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Using a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG (± freeze-all embryos, cabergoline)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Prevention includes lower stimulation doses, a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG, 'freeze-all' embryos and cabergoline — all reducing the hCG/VEGF-driven fluid shift.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which blood test best reflects the severity (haemoconcentration) of OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Haematocrit reflects haemoconcentration and severity (>45% severe, >55% critical); FBC/U&Es/LFTs/albumin/coagulation are also monitored.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with OHSS develops sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain. Which complication must be excluded?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Enlarged OHSS ovaries are at risk of torsion (or rupture); sudden severe unilateral pain warrants exclusion of torsion — one of the few indications for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When is surgery indicated in OHSS?
options: Only for ovarian torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Only for ovarian torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Surgery in OHSS is reserved for torsion, rupture or ectopic pregnancy; otherwise the fragile ovaries are left alone and management is supportive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which of the following is a feature of CRITICAL OHSS?
options: Haematocrit >55% with VTE and organ failure
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Haematocrit >55% with VTE and organ failure
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Critical OHSS features tense ascites/large effusions, haematocrit >55%, WCC >25, oligo/anuria, VTE, ARDS and organ failure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the general management approach for mild OHSS?
options: Outpatient supportive care with analgesia, antiemetics, oral fluids and VTE risk assessment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Outpatient supportive care with analgesia, antiemetics, oral fluids and VTE risk assessment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Mild-moderate OHSS is managed as an outpatient with analgesia, antiemetics, oral fluids to thirst, monitoring, safety-netting and VTE risk assessment; it is usually self-limiting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman's 75g OGTT shows a fasting glucose of 5.9 mmol/L. What does this indicate?
options: Impaired fasting glucose only, not GDM
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Using the '5678' criteria, a fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L (or 2-hour ≥7.8) diagnoses GDM — either value alone is sufficient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman is diagnosed with GDM and has a fasting glucose of 8 mmol/L. What is the appropriate initial management?
options: Diet and exercise alone for 2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L at diagnosis is too high to wait for lifestyle measures, so immediate insulin (± metformin) is started.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with GDM has a fasting glucose of 6.2 mmol/L and diet/exercise targets are met. What is the first-line management?
options: A trial of diet and exercise with review of targets
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A trial of diet and exercise with review of targets
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: With a fasting glucose <7 mmol/L and no complications, diet and exercise are first-line, adding metformin then insulin if targets are missed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What are the recommended capillary glucose targets in gestational diabetes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: GDM targets are fasting <5.3, 1 hour post-meal <7.8, and 2 hours post-meal <6.4 mmol/L (keeping >4 if on insulin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is the appropriate screening test for GDM in a woman with risk factors?
options: A 75g oral glucose tolerance test at 24-28 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A 75g oral glucose tolerance test at 24-28 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: GDM is screened with a 75g OGTT (at 24–28 weeks, or ASAP after booking plus 24–28 weeks if previous GDM); urinalysis/HbA1c/fasting glucose are not used to screen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman has a trace of glucose on urine dipstick. What is the correct interpretation?
options: It can be normal in pregnancy; use an OGTT to assess for GDM
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It can be normal in pregnancy; use an OGTT to assess for GDM
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Trace glycosuria is normal in pregnancy due to increased GFR and reduced tubular reabsorption; GDM is diagnosed by OGTT, not dipstick.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the appropriate management of glucose-lowering treatment immediately after delivery in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: GDM resolves with delivery of the placenta, so all glucose-lowering treatment is stopped immediately after birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which fetal complication is associated with poorly controlled gestational diabetes?
options: Macrosomia (with shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Macrosomia (with shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia causes fetal macrosomia (risking shoulder dystocia) and neonatal hypoglycaemia after birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When should a woman with GDM on treatment be offered delivery?
options: By ~40-41 weeks (no later than 40⁺⁶ for elective birth)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: By ~40-41 weeks (no later than 40⁺⁶ for elective birth)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Timed delivery by ~40–41 weeks is recommended (elective birth no later than 40⁺⁶), earlier if on treatment or with complications.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What postnatal follow-up is recommended for a woman after gestational diabetes?
options: Fasting glucose/HbA1c at 6-13 weeks, then annual HbA1c
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Fasting glucose/HbA1c at 6-13 weeks, then annual HbA1c
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Because of the high future type 2 diabetes risk, a fasting glucose/HbA1c is done at 6–13 weeks postnatally, then annual HbA1c.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What neonatal complication should be monitored for after a GDM pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia persists briefly after birth, so the neonate must be monitored for hypoglycaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which hormones are chiefly responsible for the insulin resistance underlying gestational diabetes?
options: Human placental lactogen, cortisol and progesterone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Human placental lactogen, cortisol and progesterone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Human placental lactogen (with cortisol and progesterone) drives the insulin resistance of pregnancy, diverting glucose to the fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with previous gestational diabetes is now pregnant again. When should she have an OGTT?
options: As soon as possible after booking, and again at 24-28 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: As soon as possible after booking, and again at 24-28 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Women with previous GDM have an OGTT as soon as possible after booking and again at 24–28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman at 34 weeks has intense itching of her palms and soles, worse at night, with no rash. What is the most likely diagnosis and key test?
options: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — measure serum bile acids
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — measure serum bile acids
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Third-trimester itch of the palms/soles with no rash is classic ICP; serum bile acids are the key diagnostic and prognostic test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: In ICP, which factor drives stillbirth risk and delivery timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The bile-acid level (not the symptoms) drives risk; stillbirth risk is significantly raised at ≥100 micromol/L, guiding delivery timing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: At what peak bile-acid level is the stillbirth risk in ICP significantly raised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Stillbirth risk is significantly raised only at bile acids ≥100 micromol/L (severe ICP); mild (19–39) does not significantly raise it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman has severe ICP with bile acids of 120 micromol/L. When should delivery be planned?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Severe ICP (bile acids ≥100) is delivered at ~35–36 weeks; moderate (40–99) ~38–39 weeks; mild (<40) ~40 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What does current evidence (PITCHES trial) show about ursodeoxycholic acid in ICP?
options: It does not prevent stillbirth and has minimal benefit on itch, so is not routinely recommended
It lowers bile acids to normal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It does not prevent stillbirth and has minimal benefit on itch, so is not routinely recommended
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The PITCHES RCT showed UDCA does not prevent stillbirth and has only limited itch benefit, so it is no longer routinely recommended (individual consideration only).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which liver enzyme rises physiologically in pregnancy and is therefore not useful for diagnosing ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: ALP rises physiologically in pregnancy (placental source), so it is not useful; transaminases with pregnancy-adjusted ranges and bile acids are used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is ICP considered a diagnosis of exclusion?
options: Other causes (hepatitis, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, etc.) must be ruled out, and it resolves after delivery
It has a specific confirmatory test
It only occurs with a rash
It is confirmed by skin biopsy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Other causes (hepatitis, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, etc.) must be ruled out, and it resolves after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: ICP is a diagnosis of exclusion — viral hepatitis, autoimmune liver disease, pre-eclampsia/HELLP are excluded, and it is confirmed retrospectively by postnatal resolution.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When is vitamin K indicated in ICP?
options: If there is prolonged clotting or severe cholestasis
In all women with ICP routinely
Only if the itch is severe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: If there is prolonged clotting or severe cholestasis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Water-soluble vitamin K is given only if clotting is prolonged or cholestasis is severe, as fat-soluble vitamin absorption may be impaired, creating bleeding risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with mild ICP (bile acids 30 micromol/L) asks when she will be delivered. What is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Mild ICP (bile acids <40) is managed to ~40 weeks, as stillbirth risk is not significantly raised; severe disease is delivered earlier.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which supportive measure may soothe the itch of ICP?
options: Topical emollients (e.g. menthol in aqueous cream)
Topical steroid to the whole body
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Topical emollients (e.g. menthol in aqueous cream)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Topical emollients such as menthol in aqueous cream are safe and may soothe; a sedating antihistamine can help sleep, but neither reliably reduces bile acids or prevents stillbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman had ICP in her last pregnancy and is pregnant again. What should she be told about recurrence?
options: It only recurs if she has twins
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: ICP has a high recurrence rate (~45–90%) in future pregnancies, so surveillance is arranged.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the limitation of CTG in monitoring ICP?
options: It cannot reliably predict or prevent the sudden stillbirth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It cannot reliably predict or prevent the sudden stillbirth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: CTG is offered but cannot reliably predict or prevent the sudden stillbirth of ICP; serial bile acids and LFTs guide delivery timing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which feature helps distinguish ICP from other causes of itch in pregnancy?
options: Itch of the palms and soles with NO rash
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Itch of the palms and soles with NO rash
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: ICP characteristically causes itch (often of the palms/soles) with no rash (only excoriations), unlike the rashes of dermatoses of pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with a previous unprovoked VTE becomes pregnant. What thromboprophylaxis is appropriate?
options: LMWH throughout the antenatal period and for 6 weeks postnatal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: LMWH throughout the antenatal period and for 6 weeks postnatal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A previous VTE places a woman at highest risk, warranting LMWH throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks postnatally.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which anticoagulant is the agent of choice for VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice as it does not cross the placenta; warfarin (teratogenic) and DOACs are contraindicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is D-dimer not used to investigate suspected VTE in pregnancy?
options: It is only useful for DVT
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy, so it is not useful; the Wells score is also not validated in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman has a suspected DVT. What is the appropriate first investigation?
options: Compression duplex ultrasound of the leg
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Compression duplex ultrasound of the leg
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Suspected DVT in pregnancy is investigated with compression duplex ultrasound (often left-sided/iliofemoral); if negative but suspicious, repeat on days 3 and 7.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman presents with suspected PE and clinical signs of a DVT. Which imaging is preferred first, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: If DVT signs are present, a leg ultrasound is done first; a positive result confirms VTE and treats it, avoiding radiation from V/Q or CTPA.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When should treatment be started in a pregnant woman with clinically suspected PE?
options: Immediately with treatment-dose LMWH, before imaging
Only if the D-dimer is raised
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Immediately with treatment-dose LMWH, before imaging
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Treatment-dose LMWH should be started immediately on clinical suspicion of VTE, without waiting for imaging or a thrombophilia screen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman has an antenatal VTE risk score of 4. When should LMWH prophylaxis be started?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: An antenatal risk score of ≥4 warrants LMWH from the first trimester (plus 6 weeks postnatal); a score of 3 starts from 28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How long should treatment-dose LMWH be continued after a VTE diagnosed in pregnancy?
options: At least 3 months and until at least 6 weeks postnatal (whichever is longer)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: At least 3 months and until at least 6 weeks postnatal (whichever is longer)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: VTE treatment in pregnancy continues for at least 3 months and until at least 6 weeks postnatal, whichever is longer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman has an antenatal risk score of 3. What thromboprophylaxis is appropriate?
options: LMWH from 28 weeks plus 6 weeks postnatal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: LMWH from 28 weeks plus 6 weeks postnatal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: An antenatal score of 3 warrants LMWH from 28 weeks plus 6 weeks postnatal; a score ≥4 starts in the first trimester.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: When is anti-Xa monitoring of LMWH indicated in pregnancy?
options: At body-weight extremes (<50 or ≥90 kg) or renal impairment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: At body-weight extremes (<50 or ≥90 kg) or renal impairment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Anti-Xa monitoring is used only at body-weight extremes or in renal impairment, not routinely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman on treatment-dose LMWH for VTE goes into labour. What should happen to the LMWH?
options: Stop it at the onset of labour to allow safe regional anaesthesia timing
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Stop it at the onset of labour to allow safe regional anaesthesia timing
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: LMWH is stopped at the onset of labour (or before planned delivery) to allow safe timing of regional anaesthesia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman develops a massive, life-threatening pulmonary embolism in pregnancy. What is the appropriate management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Massive/life-threatening PE is managed with IV unfractionated heparin or thrombolysis, rather than prophylactic-dose LMWH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is warfarin avoided in pregnancy for VTE?
options: It is teratogenic (fetal warfarin syndrome) and crosses the placenta
It does not work in pregnancy
It is only avoided in the third trimester
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It is teratogenic (fetal warfarin syndrome) and crosses the placenta
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Warfarin is teratogenic (fetal warfarin syndrome) and crosses the placenta, so LMWH is used instead; DOACs are also contraindicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman at 9 weeks has severe vomiting with 6% weight loss, dehydration and hypokalaemia. What is the diagnosis?
options: Normal nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The RCOG triad — ≥5% weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance with onset before 16 weeks — defines hyperemesis gravidarum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the appropriate IV fluid for a dehydrated, hypokalaemic woman with hyperemesis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Normal saline with potassium chloride corrects dehydration and hypokalaemia; glucose/dextrose fluids are avoided as they can precipitate Wernicke's in a thiamine-deficient woman.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why must thiamine be given before any dextrose in an admitted woman with hyperemesis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Giving dextrose to a thiamine-deficient woman can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine is given first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: According to the RCOG GTG69 2024 update, what is the role of ketonuria in assessing hyperemesis severity?
options: Ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration/severity and should not be used
It is the best marker of dehydration
It determines the need for admission
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration/severity and should not be used
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The 2024 update states ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration and should not be used to assess severity; PUQE score, weight loss, clinical dehydration and electrolytes are used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which is a first-line antiemetic for hyperemesis gravidarum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: First-line antiemetics are antihistamines (cyclizine/promethazine), phenothiazines and doxylamine/pyridoxine; ondansetron and metoclopramide are second-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which severity tool is used to assess nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The PUQE score (≤6 mild, 7–12 moderate, 13–15 severe) assesses NVP/HG severity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which condition, driven by high β-hCG, must be excluded with ultrasound in severe hyperemesis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: High-β-hCG states such as multiple pregnancy and molar disease worsen HG, so ultrasound is always done to confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy and exclude them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman with hyperemesis develops confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia after receiving dextrose without thiamine. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: This triad is Wernicke's encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency, precipitated by giving glucose without thiamine — hence thiamine must precede dextrose.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which second-line antiemetic carries a small first-trimester cleft-palate risk that must be counselled?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Ondansetron carries a small first-trimester cleft-palate risk; it is second-line and its benefit is considered to outweigh this risk when needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Metoclopramide is used for hyperemesis but is limited to a maximum of how many days, and why?
options: 5 days, due to extrapyramidal/oculogyric crisis risk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: 5 days, due to extrapyramidal/oculogyric crisis risk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Metoclopramide is limited to a maximum of 5 days because of the risk of extrapyramidal effects/oculogyric crisis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) given to women admitted with hyperemesis?
options: Dehydration and immobility increase VTE risk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Dehydration and immobility increase VTE risk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Dehydration and immobility during HG admission raise VTE risk, so LMWH prophylaxis is given.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman's vomiting first begins at 18 weeks with abdominal pain and dysuria. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Search for another cause (e.g. UTI), as this is atypical for HG
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Search for another cause (e.g. UTI), as this is atypical for HG
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Vomiting starting after ~11–16 weeks or with pain/fever/dysuria is atypical for HG and should prompt a search for another cause such as UTI; HG is partly a diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which biochemical finding may occur in severe hyperemesis due to β-hCG mimicking TSH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: β-hCG structurally resembles TSH, so severe HG can cause transient biochemical hyperthyroidism.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman asks how much alcohol is safe to drink. What is the correct advice?
options: Avoid alcohol completely — there is no safe threshold
Up to 2 units per week is safe
Only avoid alcohol in the first trimester
One glass of wine daily is fine
Alcohol is only harmful if she is dependent
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Avoid alcohol completely — there is no safe threshold
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: UK guidance advises avoiding alcohol completely in pregnancy, as there is no safe threshold and risk is dose-related.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which combination of facial features characterises fetal alcohol syndrome?
options: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small palpebral fissures
Cleft lip and palate with polydactyly
A single palmar crease and epicanthic folds
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, small palpebral fissures
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The facial triad of fetal alcohol syndrome is a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip and small palpebral fissures, with growth restriction and neurodevelopmental effects.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman is dependent on opioids. What is the appropriate management?
options: Opioid substitution with methadone or buprenorphine, maintained throughout
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Opioid substitution with methadone or buprenorphine, maintained throughout
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Opioid dependence is managed with substitution (methadone or buprenorphine) via a specialist service; abrupt withdrawal risks fetal distress, miscarriage and preterm birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A neonate exposed to opioids in utero develops a high-pitched cry, jitteriness, poor feeding and diarrhoea. What is the diagnosis and assessment tool?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: This is neonatal abstinence syndrome (CNS/GI/autonomic features), assessed with Finnegan scoring and managed supportively, with weaning oral morphine if severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which obstetric complication is classically associated with cocaine use in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Cocaine causes vasoconstriction leading to placental abruption, as well as growth restriction and maternal hypertension/stroke/MI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which smoking-cessation drugs are avoided in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Varenicline and bupropion are avoided in pregnancy; NRT can be used if behavioural support fails, as it is safer than smoking.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is smoking addressed at the booking visit?
options: Ask about smoking, perform a CO breath test, and refer to Stop Smoking Services (opt-out)
Take no action unless she requests help
Refer only if she has complications
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Ask about smoking, perform a CO breath test, and refer to Stop Smoking Services (opt-out)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: At booking, women are asked about smoking, offered a CO breath test, and referred (opt-out) to Stop Smoking Services.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A pregnant woman who injects drugs should be screened for which infections?
options: Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Injecting drug use warrants screening for blood-borne viruses — hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which substances can generally be stopped abruptly (with support) in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Tobacco, cocaine/stimulants and cannabis can be stopped abruptly with support; opioids and alcohol/benzodiazepine dependence require substitution/supported withdrawal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A woman stable on methadone asks about breastfeeding. What is the appropriate advice?
options: Breastfeeding is only allowed after 6 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Breastfeeding is encouraged in women stable on methadone or buprenorphine.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the main fetal effect of maternal smoking in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Smoking causes chronic fetal hypoxia/vasoconstriction leading to growth restriction (low birth weight), along with abruption, praevia, preterm birth and stillbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is a non-judgemental, supportive approach emphasised in substance use in pregnancy?
options: A judged woman disengages from antenatal care
It avoids the need for safeguarding
It is legally required to prescribe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: A judged woman disengages from antenatal care
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Non-judgemental engagement (with MDT and safeguarding) keeps women in antenatal care; a judgemental approach risks disengagement and worse outcomes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A heavily alcohol-dependent pregnant woman needs to stop drinking. What is the safest approach?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Abrupt alcohol withdrawal risks seizures/delirium tremens, so dependent drinkers need supported detoxification with thiamine cover.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Why is the first RhD-positive pregnancy in an RhD-negative mother usually unaffected by Rhesus disease?
options: Sensitisation occurs during it, but the anti-D IgG produced affects the NEXT RhD+ fetus
Anti-D crosses immediately and harms the first fetus
The first fetus is always RhD-negative
Maternal antibodies are IgM and cannot cross
The placenta blocks all antibodies in a first pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Sensitisation occurs during it, but the anti-D IgG produced affects the NEXT RhD+ fetus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The first RhD+ pregnancy sensitises the mother (primary immune response), but the current baby is usually spared; the anti-D IgG then haemolyses a subsequent RhD+ fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: An RhD-negative woman at 20 weeks has an antepartum haemorrhage. What is the appropriate management?
options: Give anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours (≥500 IU, guided by Kleihauer)
Give anti-D only if she is already sensitised
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Give anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours (≥500 IU, guided by Kleihauer)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: APH is a sensitising event; anti-D should be given within 72 hours (≥500 IU from 20 weeks, with a Kleihauer test to size the dose).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (RAADP) regimen?
options: Anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks (500 IU each), or a single 1500 IU dose at 28-30 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks (500 IU each), or a single 1500 IU dose at 28-30 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: RAADP is either two doses (28 and 34 weeks, 500 IU each) or a single 1500 IU dose at 28–30 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What does fetal RHD genotyping using cell-free fetal DNA allow (NICE DG25)?
options: Avoiding anti-D if the fetus is RhD-negative
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Avoiding anti-D if the fetus is RhD-negative
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Non-invasive fetal RHD genotyping from ~11–16 weeks identifies RhD-negative fetuses, in whom anti-D is unnecessary (sparing ~40% of women).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: An RhD-negative woman has just delivered an RhD-positive baby. What should she receive, and when?
options: Anti-D only if she becomes symptomatic
No anti-D, as the baby is already born
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: If the baby is RhD-positive, the RhD-negative mother is given anti-D within 72 hours of delivery to prevent sensitisation for future pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which statement about anti-D immunoglobulin is correct?
options: It prevents sensitisation but does nothing once a woman is already sensitised
It is given only to sensitised women
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: It prevents sensitisation but does nothing once a woman is already sensitised
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Anti-D is purely preventive — it mops up fetal RhD+ cells before the immune system reacts; it is useless once the woman has already made her own anti-D antibodies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: What is the purpose of the Kleihauer test?
options: To quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage and size the anti-D dose
To confirm RhD status of the mother
To diagnose HDFN in the neonate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: To quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage and size the anti-D dose
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: The Kleihauer test quantifies the fetomaternal haemorrhage (adult HbA elutes, fetal HbF resists) to determine the required anti-D dose from ≥20 weeks/for large bleeds.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A positive direct Coombs test (DAT) on cord blood indicates what?
options: Maternal antibodies bound to the baby's red cells
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Maternal antibodies bound to the baby's red cells
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: A positive DAT indicates maternal antibodies are bound to the baby's red cells, confirming immune haemolysis (HDFN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is fetal anaemia monitored non-invasively in a sensitised pregnancy?
options: MCA (middle cerebral artery) Doppler — raised peak systolic velocity indicates anaemia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: MCA (middle cerebral artery) Doppler — raised peak systolic velocity indicates anaemia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity is a non-invasive marker of fetal anaemia in a sensitised pregnancy, alongside serial antibody titres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: How is significant fetal anaemia due to HDFN treated in utero?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Significant fetal anaemia from HDFN is treated with intrauterine (fetal) blood transfusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Which sensitising event requires anti-D in an RhD-negative woman?
options: Miscarriage after 12 weeks (or any surgically managed miscarriage)
A threatened miscarriage at 8 weeks with a viable pregnancy and no intervention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.answer: Miscarriage after 12 weeks (or any surgically managed miscarriage)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Sensitising events requiring anti-D include miscarriage >12 weeks (or surgically managed), delivery, TOP, ectopic, ECV, APH, invasive procedures and abdominal trauma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: A severely affected fetus with HDFN develops widespread oedema and effusions. What is this called?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Severe HDFN with fetal anaemia and heart failure causes hydrops fetalis (widespread fluid accumulation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.question: Besides anti-D, which antibody notably causes HDFN by suppressing erythropoiesis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.explanation: Anti-Kell causes HDFN and, notably, suppresses erythropoiesis; anti-c is another non-D antibody that causes HDFN.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A woman at 37 weeks has a persistent breech presentation confirmed on ultrasound. What should be offered first?
options: Await spontaneous labour with no intervention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: External cephalic version (ECV)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: For persistent breech at term, ECV is offered first (from 36 weeks nulliparous/37 weeks multiparous); if it fails, mode of delivery is decided.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which type of breech carries the highest cord-prolapse risk and contraindicates vaginal breech birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Footling breech
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Footling breech has the highest cord-prolapse risk (the presenting part doesn't fill the pelvis) and is a contraindication to vaginal breech birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which is the most common type of breech presentation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Frank (extended) breech
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Frank (extended) breech — hips flexed, knees extended — is the most common type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is the approximate success rate of external cephalic version?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: About 50%
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: ECV succeeds in about 50% of attempts (higher in multiparous women), improved by tocolysis, and reduces the caesarean rate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which is a contraindication to external cephalic version?
options: Antepartum haemorrhage in the last 7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Antepartum haemorrhage in the last 7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Contraindications to ECV include recent APH (<7 days), abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, placenta praevia, major uterine anomaly, and multiple pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: According to the Term Breech Trial, what is the recommended mode of delivery for persistent breech at term?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Planned caesarean section (lower perinatal mortality)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: The Term Breech Trial showed planned caesarean reduces perinatal mortality versus planned vaginal breech; vaginal breech remains an option only for selected women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A baby is born in breech presentation. Which screening investigation is indicated?
options: Hip ultrasound for developmental dysplasia of the hip
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Hip ultrasound for developmental dysplasia of the hip
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Breech is a major risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip, so hip ultrasound screening is indicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A woman is found to have a breech presentation at 33 weeks. What is the appropriate management?
options: Watch and wait, as most turn spontaneously
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Watch and wait, as most turn spontaneously
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Before 36 weeks, most breech babies turn spontaneously, so watchful waiting is appropriate; ECV is offered if breech persists at term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Immediately after a successful ECV, what is the approximate risk of needing an emergency caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: About 1 in 200
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: There is about a 1 in 200 risk of emergency caesarean immediately after ECV, which is why it is done where caesarean is available.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: On abdominal palpation, a hard ballotable mass is felt at the uterine fundus. What does this suggest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Breech presentation (head at the fundus)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: A hard, ballotable head at the fundus with an irregular mass in the pelvis suggests breech presentation; ultrasound confirms it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which statement about outcomes in breech presentation is correct?
options: Breech babies have worse outcomes than cephalic babies regardless of delivery mode
Breech babies always do well if delivered vaginally
Mode of delivery fully determines outcome
Breech has no association with fetal abnormality
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Breech babies have worse outcomes than cephalic babies regardless of delivery mode
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Breech babies do worse than cephalic babies whatever the mode of delivery, partly because the underlying cause contributes to the risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is the natural history of a fetus that is breech at 28 weeks?
options: Most turn ~180° to cephalic by term
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Most turn ~180° to cephalic by term
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: About 25% are breech at 28 weeks but only ~3–4% at term, as most perform a ~180° turn to cephalic by ~36 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A woman with a persistent footling breech at term requests vaginal breech birth. What is the appropriate advice?
options: Footling breech is a contraindication to vaginal breech birth; recommend caesarean
Vaginal breech is safe for footling breech
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Footling breech is a contraindication to vaginal breech birth; recommend caesarean
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Footling breech contraindicates vaginal breech birth due to the high cord-prolapse risk, so caesarean is recommended.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A woman at 38 weeks has a transverse lie. Why can she not deliver vaginally, and what is the main danger?
options: A transverse baby cannot pass through the pelvis; the main danger is cord prolapse
She can deliver vaginally with forceps
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: A transverse baby cannot pass through the pelvis; the main danger is cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: A transverse baby cannot deliver vaginally, and if the membranes rupture the cord (or an arm) can prolapse — the feared complication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A fetus is found to be in a transverse lie at 32 weeks. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure — most revert to longitudinal spontaneously
Admit for the rest of pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Reassure — most revert to longitudinal spontaneously
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Before 36 weeks most abnormal lies revert to longitudinal spontaneously, so reassurance is appropriate; intervention is timed near term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is the key management step for a persistent transverse/unstable lie at ~37 weeks?
options: Elective admission to guard against cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Elective admission to guard against cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Elective admission from ~37 weeks allows immediate caesarean if labour starts or the membranes rupture, given the high cord-prolapse risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: An abnormal lie persisting at term should prompt a search for which underlying causes?
options: Oligohydramnios and fetal growth restriction only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Placenta praevia, fibroids/pelvic mass, polyhydramnios
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: An abnormal lie at term is often not chance and should prompt a search for placenta praevia, fibroids/pelvic mass, polyhydramnios and other causes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: A woman with a transverse lie has spontaneous rupture of membranes at 38 weeks. What is the appropriate management?
options: Expedite delivery by caesarean (high cord-prolapse risk)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Expedite delivery by caesarean (high cord-prolapse risk)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Ruptured membranes with an abnormal lie carries a high cord-prolapse risk, so delivery is expedited by caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which patient classically develops an unstable lie?
options: A multiparous woman with a lax uterus
A woman with an engaged cephalic head
A primigravida with a firm uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: A multiparous woman with a lax uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Unstable lie (the lie keeps changing near term) is classically seen in the multiparous woman with a lax uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is the feared end-point of a neglected transverse lie in labour?
options: Obstructed labour leading to uterine rupture
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Obstructed labour leading to uterine rupture
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: A neglected transverse lie leads to obstructed labour and, ultimately, uterine rupture — the feared end-point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which is a limitation of ECV for unstable/abnormal lie?
options: The lie tends to revert, so ECV alone is often insufficient
ECV is contraindicated in all abnormal lies
ECV can only be done under general anaesthetic
ECV causes cord prolapse in most cases
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: The lie tends to revert, so ECV alone is often insufficient
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Abnormal/unstable lie tends to revert after ECV, so ECV alone is often insufficient; elective caesarean is used for persistent abnormal lie.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is 'stabilising induction' for selected unstable lie?
options: ECV to cephalic followed immediately by amniotomy and oxytocin, in theatre with caesarean standby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: ECV to cephalic followed immediately by amniotomy and oxytocin, in theatre with caesarean standby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Stabilising induction is a specialist option: ECV to cephalic then immediate amniotomy and oxytocin, done in theatre with caesarean standby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: How is the fetal lie defined?
options: The relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis
The relationship of the presenting part to the pelvis
The position of the fetal head
The station of the presenting part
The attitude of the fetal head
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: The relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Lie is the relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis; normal is longitudinal, and transverse/oblique are abnormal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: On abdominal examination of a woman at term, neither the head nor buttocks is felt at the fundus or pelvis, and the fetus is felt lying across. What is the likely lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Transverse lie
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Neither pole at the fundus/pelvis with the fetus felt lying across suggests a transverse lie, confirmed on ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Why should amniotomy be avoided with a high/mobile presenting part in an abnormal lie?
options: It risks cord or arm prolapse
It always fails to rupture the membranes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: It risks cord or arm prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Amniotomy with a high/mobile presenting part risks cord or arm prolapse, so it is avoided in abnormal lie.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman is being assessed for induction of labour and has a Bishop score of 4. What is the appropriate first step?
options: Cervical ripening with vaginal dinoprostone (or mechanical)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Cervical ripening with vaginal dinoprostone (or mechanical)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A Bishop score ≤6 (unfavourable) requires cervical ripening first (dinoprostone/misoprostol or mechanical); ARM + oxytocin is reserved for a favourable cervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman has a Bishop score of 9 and a cephalic presentation. What is the appropriate method of induction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A favourable cervix (Bishop >6/≥8) is managed with amniotomy plus oxytocin, titrated to ~4 contractions per 10 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the commonest indication for induction of labour, and when is it offered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Prolonged pregnancy is the commonest indication; induction is offered at 41–42 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: During an oxytocin induction, the CTG shows fetal distress with 7 contractions in 10 minutes. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Uterine hyperstimulation — stop oxytocin and consider tocolysis (terbutaline)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Uterine hyperstimulation — stop oxytocin and consider tocolysis (terbutaline)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Excessive contractions with fetal distress indicate uterine hyperstimulation; management is to stop/remove the agent (stop oxytocin), consider tocolysis, continue CTG, and escalate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is the standard first-line pharmacological agent for cervical ripening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Vaginal dinoprostone (PGE2) is the standard first-line ripening agent; low-dose oral misoprostol is an alternative, and mechanical methods are used when prostaglandins are unsuitable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman with a previous caesarean scar requires cervical ripening for induction. Which method is often preferred, and why?
options: A mechanical balloon catheter — it causes less hyperstimulation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: A mechanical balloon catheter — it causes less hyperstimulation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: With a previous caesarean, mechanical methods (balloon) are often preferred as they cause less hyperstimulation than prostaglandins, reducing uterine-rupture risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a recognised contraindication to induction of labour (favouring caesarean)?
options: Prelabour rupture of membranes at term
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Placenta praevia (and vasa praevia, cord presentation, transverse lie, classical caesarean, active primary genital herpes) contraindicate vaginal delivery/induction; the others are indications for IOL.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which complication is a specific risk of amniotomy during induction, especially with a high presenting part?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Amniotomy with a high, poorly-applied presenting part risks cord prolapse, as the cord can descend below the presenting part.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What contraction rate is targeted when titrating oxytocin during induction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Oxytocin is titrated to about 4 contractions per 10 minutes; more frequent contractions risk hyperstimulation and fetal distress.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A membrane sweep is best described as which of the following?
options: An adjunct offered from ~39-41 weeks, not formal induction
A method of cervical ripening equivalent to dinoprostone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: An adjunct offered from ~39-41 weeks, not formal induction
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A membrane sweep is an adjunct offered from ~39–41 weeks to promote spontaneous labour, distinct from formal induction methods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What monitoring is essential during active induction with prostaglandins or oxytocin?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Continuous CTG is used during active induction to detect fetal distress and uterine hyperstimulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: An induction fails to establish labour despite ripening and oxytocin. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Re-attempt ripening or proceed to caesarean section
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Re-attempt ripening or proceed to caesarean section
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Failed induction is managed by re-attempting cervical ripening or proceeding to caesarean section.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which statement about the Bishop score is correct?
options: A score ≤6 indicates an unfavourable cervix needing ripening; >6 indicates a favourable cervix for ARM + oxytocin
A score ≤6 means the cervix is favourable
A high score means caesarean is needed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: A score ≤6 indicates an unfavourable cervix needing ripening; >6 indicates a favourable cervix for ARM + oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The Bishop score (dilatation, effacement, consistency, position, station) determines readiness: ≤6 unfavourable (ripen first), >6 favourable (ARM + oxytocin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman in labour develops a cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia. Which category of caesarean and what decision-to-delivery target apply?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Cord prolapse with an immediate threat to the baby is a Category 1 (crash) caesarean, with a decision-to-delivery target of 30 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the decision-to-delivery target for a Category 2 caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Category 2 (compromise not immediately life-threatening) has a 75-minute audit target, though acute fetal compromise is pushed toward 30 minutes where possible.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which type of caesarean incision is used in ~99% of cases and carries a lower future rupture risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The lower segment transverse (LSCS) incision is used in ~99% of caesareans and has a lower future rupture risk, less bleeding and better healing than a classical incision.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which structure is NOT cut during a caesarean section?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The rectus abdominis is separated at the linea alba and retracted laterally, not cut; the sheath, peritoneum and uterus are incised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman had a previous classical (vertical) caesarean. Regarding VBAC, what is correct?
options: VBAC has the same rupture risk as after LSCS
She should be induced with prostaglandins
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A previous classical scar (or previous uterine rupture) contraindicates VBAC because of the high uterine rupture risk; VBAC is appropriate after a single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the main serious risk of attempting VBAC?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Uterine rupture is the feared complication of VBAC (~0.5% absolute risk, higher than elective repeat caesarean); VBAC success is ~72–75%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a placental indication for caesarean section?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Major placenta praevia (and accreta, vasa praevia) is a placental indication for caesarean; the others are not, in themselves, indications for caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Why does the risk of placenta praevia/accreta increase with each caesarean section?
options: The placenta can implant abnormally over the uterine scar
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: The placenta can implant abnormally over the uterine scar
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Abnormal placental implantation over the uterine scar increases the risk of praevia and accreta with each successive caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which postoperative complication requires routine thromboprophylaxis after caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Caesarean increases VTE risk, so thromboprophylaxis is essential; other complications include haemorrhage, infection, ileus and organ injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A CTG shows persistent fetal bradycardia with suspected uterine rupture. What category of caesarean is indicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Suspected uterine rupture with fetal bradycardia is an immediate threat to life — a Category 1 caesarean with a 30-minute target.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Planned VBAC is most appropriate in which situation?
options: A single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks
Two previous caesareans with a vertical scar
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: A single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: VBAC is appropriate with a single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks; previous rupture or a classical scar contraindicate it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which neonatal complication is more common after caesarean (especially elective, pre-labour)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn is more common after caesarean (retained lung fluid), and iatrogenic prematurity can occur if dates are wrong.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a recognised indication for a classical (vertical) caesarean incision rather than LSCS?
options: Anterior placenta praevia/accreta or very preterm delivery
A previous LSCS with a favourable cervix
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Anterior placenta praevia/accreta or very preterm delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Classical incisions are reserved for situations such as very preterm delivery, some transverse lies, anterior praevia/accreta, or obstructing fibroids, where the lower segment is inaccessible/unsuitable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A tear after vaginal delivery involves the perineal muscle but not the anal sphincter. What degree is it, and how is it managed?
options: Second degree — sutured on the ward
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Second degree — sutured on the ward
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A tear involving the perineal muscle but sparing the anal sphincter is second-degree and is sutured on the ward; sphincter involvement (3rd/4th degree, OASIS) requires theatre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A tear involves the anal sphincter complex and the rectal mucosa. What degree is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A tear involving the anal sphincter complex plus the rectal (anorectal) mucosa is a fourth-degree tear; third-degree involves the sphincter without the rectal mucosa.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What does the term OASIS refer to?
options: Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears (anal sphincter injury)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears (anal sphincter injury)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: OASIS (obstetric anal sphincter injury) comprises third- and fourth-degree tears; these are repaired in theatre, whereas 1st/2nd degree are managed on the ward.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A third-degree tear involves more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness but not the internal sphincter. How is it subclassified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: 3a is <50% of EAS, 3b is >50% of EAS, and 3c is EAS plus IAS torn; here >50% EAS with intact IAS is 3b.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is the strongest risk factor for OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Primigravida/first vaginal birth is the strongest risk factor (OASIS ~6% in primips vs ~1.7% in multips).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A rectal mucosal tear is found with an intact anal sphincter. How should this be classified?
options: A buttonhole tear — NOT a fourth-degree tear/OASIS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: A buttonhole tear — NOT a fourth-degree tear/OASIS
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A buttonhole tear (rectal mucosa torn, sphincter intact) is a separate entity documented separately — it is NOT a fourth-degree tear/OASIS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Where should a third- or fourth-degree perineal tear be repaired?
options: On the ward under local anaesthesia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: OASIS (3rd/4th degree) is repaired in theatre by a trained clinician under regional/general anaesthesia; 1st/2nd degree are managed on the ward.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which instrumental delivery is associated with a higher risk of OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Forceps delivery carries a higher OASIS risk than ventouse; instrumental delivery overall is a risk factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the appropriate post-OASIS bowel management?
options: Laxatives (to reduce dehiscence), avoiding a routine bulking agent
Nil by mouth for a week
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Laxatives (to reduce dehiscence), avoiding a routine bulking agent
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: After OASIS repair, laxatives are used to reduce wound dehiscence; a routine bulking agent is avoided. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, physiotherapy and a rectal exam are also part of care.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which type of episiotomy is recommended to help prevent OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A mediolateral episiotomy (~60° from the midline) is used where indicated to reduce OASIS, especially in instrumental delivery; midline episiotomy increases OASIS risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the feared long-term complication of a third/fourth-degree perineal tear?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Faecal urgency/incontinence is the feared long-term complication of OASIS; flatus incontinence, dyspareunia and rectovaginal fistula (4th degree) can also occur.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A first-degree perineal tear is identified after delivery. What is the appropriate management?
options: Usually no repair — it heals spontaneously
Immediate caesarean for the next birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Usually no repair — it heals spontaneously
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A first-degree tear (skin/superficial tissue only) usually needs no repair and heals spontaneously.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: When uncertain whether a tear is 3a or 3b, what should the clinician do?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: If in doubt about the grade of a third-degree tear, classify it higher to ensure appropriate repair and follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Immediately after artificial rupture of membranes in a woman with a high presenting part, the CTG shows sudden fetal bradycardia. What is the most important next step?
options: Perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse
Give maternal oxygen and re-check in 30 minutes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Sudden fetal bradycardia after ARM (especially with a high presenting part) should prompt a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman has a palpable pulsating cord in the vagina after her membranes rupture, with fetal bradycardia. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency caesarean
Push the cord back inside the uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency caesarean
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Cord prolapse is managed by relieving cord compression (elevate the presenting part, positioning ± bladder filling), stopping oxytocin, and category 1 caesarean; the cord must not be forcibly replaced.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What distinguishes cord prolapse from cord presentation?
options: Cord prolapse occurs with ruptured membranes; cord presentation with intact membranes
Cord prolapse occurs with intact membranes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Cord prolapse occurs with ruptured membranes; cord presentation with intact membranes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Cord prolapse requires ruptured membranes (the cord descends past/alongside the presenting part); with intact membranes the same anatomy is cord presentation, a warning sign.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why should the umbilical cord not be handled excessively or forcibly replaced in cord prolapse?
options: Handling and cold provoke arterial vasospasm, worsening fetal hypoxia
It has no effect either way
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Handling and cold provoke arterial vasospasm, worsening fetal hypoxia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Handling and cold provoke cord vasospasm, further cutting off fetal blood flow; the cord is kept warm/moist and not replaced, while pressure is relieved and delivery expedited.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the default mode of delivery for cord prolapse when the cervix is not fully dilated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The default is a category 1 emergency caesarean (delivery within 30 minutes); instrumental vaginal delivery is used only if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which technique can relieve cord compression when delivery or transfer is delayed in cord prolapse?
options: Filling the bladder with ~500 mL warm saline via a Foley catheter
Lying the woman flat on her back
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Filling the bladder with ~500 mL warm saline via a Foley catheter
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Bladder filling with ~500 mL warm saline elevates the presenting part off the cord and is useful if delivery/transfer is delayed (empty before delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for cord prolapse?
options: Post-term pregnancy with an engaged head
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Abnormal lie (transverse/unstable), breech, prematurity, polyhydramnios, twins, a high presenting part and ARM predispose to cord prolapse, as a poorly-applied presenting part leaves a gap.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A midwife at a home birth finds a cord prolapse. What should she advise while awaiting the ambulance?
options: Adopt a knee-chest position, call 999, and elevate the presenting part
Push the cord back and continue at home
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Adopt a knee-chest position, call 999, and elevate the presenting part
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: In the community, advise a knee-chest position, call 999, and elevate the presenting part; midwives carry a Foley catheter for bladder filling.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which position is preferred for ambulance transfer of a woman with cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Exaggerated Sims is preferred for transfer because the knee-chest position is unsafe in a moving ambulance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What medication should be stopped, and what may be considered, in cord prolapse with a delay to delivery?
options: Start magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Oxytocin is stopped and tocolysis (e.g. terbutaline) considered if there is fetal compromise and delivery is delayed, to reduce contractions compressing the cord.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the central danger to the fetus in cord prolapse?
options: Cord compression and vasospasm causing fetal hypoxia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Cord compression and vasospasm causing fetal hypoxia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The central danger is cord compression and vasospasm cutting off fetal blood flow, causing hypoxia that can lead to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, cerebral palsy or death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: In which situation is instrumental vaginal delivery (rather than caesarean) appropriate for cord prolapse?
options: When the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent
When the woman is only 4 cm dilated
When the presenting part is high
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: When the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Instrumental vaginal delivery is appropriate only when the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent; otherwise category 1 caesarean is the default.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A CTG shows variable decelerations shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes in a woman with polyhydramnios. What complication should be actively excluded?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Variable decelerations/bradycardia after ROM — especially with polyhydramnios (a risk factor) — should prompt a vaginal exam to exclude cord prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: After the fetal head delivers, it retracts tightly against the perineum and the shoulders fail to deliver with routine traction. What is the first-line manoeuvre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The turtle-neck sign indicates shoulder dystocia; McRoberts' (hyperflexing the hips) is first-line, ~90% effective and least invasive, typically combined with suprapubic pressure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which action is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Fundal pressure worsens the impaction and risks uterine rupture; suprapubic (not fundal) pressure is used, along with McRoberts' and internal manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Excessive downward traction on the fetal head during shoulder dystocia most commonly causes which injury?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Excessive/downward traction is the main cause of brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy, C5–C6, 'waiter's tip'); only routine axial traction should be used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What does the 'H' in the HELPERR mnemonic stand for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: HELPERR: H = call for Help, E = Evaluate for episiotomy, L = Legs (McRoberts'), P = suprapubic Pressure, E = Enter (internal rotation), R = Remove posterior arm, R = Roll (all-fours).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which manoeuvre involves rotating the fetal shoulders and is performed with a hand inserted vaginally?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Internal rotation manoeuvres — Rubin II and Woods' screw — are performed with a vaginal hand to rotate/reduce the shoulder diameter; McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure are external.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which single factor is the most important associated risk factor for shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Maternal diabetes (with associated macrosomia) is the most important associated risk factor, though most shoulder dystocia is unpredictable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A neonate after shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The 'waiter's tip' posture is Erb's palsy (C5–C6), a common brachial plexus injury after shoulder dystocia that usually resolves; Klumpke's (C8–T1) gives a claw hand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which is the last-resort manoeuvre involving replacing the fetal head into the uterus for emergency caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The Zavanelli manoeuvre (replacing the head into the uterus then caesarean) is a last resort if all other manoeuvres fail, along with cleidotomy/symphysiotomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia is highly effective by reducing the shoulder diameter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Delivering the posterior arm sweeps it across the chest, reducing the diameter and freeing the impaction — a highly effective manoeuvre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What are the main MATERNAL complications of shoulder dystocia?
options: Uterine inversion and amniotic fluid embolism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The main maternal risks are postpartum haemorrhage and perineal tears; symphyseal separation/femoral neuropathy can also occur from McRoberts'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which statement about predicting shoulder dystocia is correct?
options: Most cases are unpredictable, so every attendant must be prepared
It can be reliably predicted from risk factors
All macrosomic babies have shoulder dystocia
Prediction alone justifies caesarean for all at-risk women
It never occurs in diabetic mothers
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Most cases are unpredictable, so every attendant must be prepared
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Most shoulder dystocia is unpredictable; risk factors are weak predictors, so every birth attendant must be ready, and prediction alone does not justify routine induction/caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the role of episiotomy in managing shoulder dystocia?
options: It creates room for internal manoeuvres but does not relieve the bony impaction
It replaces the need for McRoberts'
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It creates room for internal manoeuvres but does not relieve the bony impaction
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Episiotomy does not relieve the bony impaction itself but creates space to perform internal (vaginal) rotation and posterior-arm manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which documentation is essential after a shoulder dystocia?
options: Time of head/body delivery, manoeuvres and order, anterior shoulder, cord gases, and staff present
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Time of head/body delivery, manoeuvres and order, anterior shoulder, cord gases, and staff present
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Because of the medicolegal significance, the time of head/body delivery, manoeuvres performed and their order, which shoulder was anterior, cord gases, and staff present must all be documented.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks. What mode of delivery is appropriate?
options: Delivery must be delayed until viral load rises
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: An undetectable viral load (<50) makes vaginal birth safe; planned caesarean is reserved for higher viral loads (≥400, or consider at 50–399).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of 800 copies/mL at 36 weeks. What is recommended?
options: Await spontaneous labour with no intervention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A viral load ≥400 copies/mL warrants a planned caesarean, plus combination neonatal PEP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: How is HIV screening offered to pregnant women in the UK?
options: To all women at booking on an opt-out basis
Only to women with risk factors
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: To all women at booking on an opt-out basis
